(Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal filed by M/s. Saudi Arabian Airlines and set aside the penalty imposed for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax (FTT), holding that delayed payment of FTT cannot be equated with failure or non-payment of tax for the purposes of Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979. The Court held that while Section 38(3) deals with non-payment of FTT, delayed deposit falls within Section 38(4) read with the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. It further held that imposition of penalty under Section 38 is not automatic merely because a statutory timeline has been breached. The dispute arose from six instances of delayed deposit of FTT collected by the appellant airline. In five instances, the delay ranged from one day to eleven days, though the demand drafts had been purchased before the respective due dates. The appellant explained that the drafts could not be deposited because of security restrictions. In the sixth instance, involving December 1995, there was a delay of 63 days, which was attributed to the concerned employee being on emergency leave. The initial adjudication order had imposed a penalty of Rs.12,000 for the six cases of late payment, but after remand the penalty was enhanced drastically to Rs.71,29,140. Examining Section 38(3), the Supreme Court emphasised the expressions “fails to pay the foreign travel tax” and “the amount of the tax not so paid”. The Court held that “failure to pay” means non-payment and cannot be equated with delay in making payment. If Parliament intended Section 38(3) to cover delayed payment, it could have used language to that effect. In interpreting fiscal statutes, courts cannot expand statutory expressions by importing meanings not used by the legislature. The Court drew support from U.S. Technologies International Private Limited Vs Commissioner of Income Tax, where the Supreme Court had interpreted Section 271C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and held that mere belated remittance of TDS after its deduction did not amount to failure to deduct TDS and therefore did not attract penalty under Section 271C. Applying the same interpretative approach, the Court held that delayed payment of FTT could not be treated as non-payment for invoking Section 38(3). The Supreme Court thereafter examined Section 38(4) of the Finance Act along with Rules 4 and 9 of the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979. Rule 4 required FTT collected by a carrier to be deposited within 30 days from the end of the month but empowered the Collector of Customs, on sufficient cause being shown and having regard to the carrier’s accounting system, to allow a longer period. Rule 9 similarly prescribed the timeline for filing monthly returns while permitting extension of time. The Court held that this statutory framework demonstrated that the timelines were not inflexible. The Court explained that payment made before issuance of a show-cause notice would constitute delayed payment rather than non-payment. It further observed that where delay was condoned under the proviso to Rule 4, no question of penalty for such delay would arise. Consequently, the view of the authorities below and the Bombay High Court that penalty followed automatically upon breach of the prescribed timeline was held to be incorrect. On the question whether penalty was mandatory, the Supreme Court examined Rule 12, which requires a written show-cause notice, opportunity to make a representation and reasonable opportunity of hearing before penalty can be imposed. According to the Court, such an adjudicatory mechanism necessarily gives the authority discretion to decide whether penalty should be imposed. Treating penalty as automatic would render the statutory opportunity of representation and hearing largely meaningless. The Supreme Court clarified that exclusion of mens rea and automatic imposition of penalty are separate concepts. Certain statutory penalties may not require proof of mens rea, but it does not follow that penalty must automatically be imposed whenever a statutory breach occurs. Whether penalty is automatic depends upon the statutory scheme and the adjudicatory process prescribed by the legislation. The power to impose penalty includes, in an appropriate case, the power not to impose it. Referring to Hindustan Steel Ltd. Vs State of Orissa, the Court reiterated that penalty for failure to perform a statutory obligation is a matter requiring judicial exercise of discretion after consideration of relevant circumstances and that even

rows.title: Income Tax | PMS Charges Deductible Under Section 48 Amid Divergent Views: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12573 Case Name Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ameeta Jagdish Thackersey Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the assessee’s appeal concerning the allowability of Portfolio Management Service (PMS) charges while computing capital gains under section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The appeal arose from the order of the Ld. CIT(A), dated 28.08.2025, which had sustained the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer under section 143(3) for Assessment Year 2011-12. The assessee had returned total income of Rs. 72,26,297/- from salary, short term capital gain and income from other sources. In computing capital gains, the assessee claimed Rs. 8,42,360/- towards fees and charges paid to Trust Investment Advisors Pvt. Ltd. for portfolio management services. The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount on the ground that the expenditure could not be regarded as expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer of the capital asset within the meaning of section 48. The CIT(A) sustained the disallowance, relying principally upon the Mumbai Tribunal decision in ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah, where PMS fees and performance-linked charges had been held not deductible under section 48. Before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the issue was unsettled because different coordinate Benches had adopted divergent views. Reliance was placed upon KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT, where PMS fees were allowed as a deduction while computing capital gains. The assessee also submitted that although the Revenue had challenged KRA Holding and Trading before the Bombay High Court, the substantial question raised before the High Court concerned whether PMS income was assessable under the head “capital gains” or “profit and gains of business or profession”; the allowability of PMS charges under section 48 was not raised as a substantial question of law. The assessee further relied upon Zarah Rafik Malik v. ITO and ACIT v. Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd., both of which had taken a view favourable to deduction of PMS expenses in the circumstances considered by those Benches. The Revenue, on the other hand, relied upon ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah and contended that PMS charges were composite in nature, relating to advisory, management and consultancy services rather than being directly relatable to acquisition or transfer of particular securities. The Tribunal noted that divergent views existed. The Mumbai Bench in Apurva Mahesh Shah had held PMS fees not deductible under section 48, whereas the Pune Bench in KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd., the Mumbai Bench in Zarah Rafik Malik and the Delhi Bench in Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd. had allowed such deduction on the facts before them. The Tribunal then applied the principle laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. [(1973) 88 ITR 192 (SC)]. It held that where two reasonable and plausible constructions of a taxing provision are possible, the interpretation favourable to the assessee should be adopted, particularly where no binding decision of the jurisdictional High Court or Supreme Court directly settles the controversy. The Tribunal found that the Revenue had not brought to its notice any binding decision of the Hon’ble Bombay High Court or the Hon’ble Supreme Court specifically holding that PMS charges were not deductible under section 48. Accordingly, following the assessee-favouring principle, it adopted the favourable view and held that the PMS charges of Rs. 8,42,360/- were allowable as a deduction while computing capital gains under section 48. The orders of the revenue authorities were set aside on this issue and the Assessing Officer was directed to allow the assessee’s claim. The appeal was consequently allowed. Cases Discussed KRA Holding and Trading Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT — Pune ITAT decision allowing PMS fees as deduction while computing capital gains. ACIT v. Apurva Mahesh Shah — Mumbai ITAT decision holding PMS and performance-linked fees not deductible under section 48. Zarah Rafik Malik v. ITO — Mumbai ITAT decision relied upon for allowing PMS expenses in the circumstances discussed. ACIT v. Vireet Investment Pvt. Ltd. — Delhi ITAT decision allowing PMS-related expenditure on the facts considered. CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. [(1973) 88 ITR 192 (SC)] — Supreme Court principle that where two reasonable constructions of a taxing provision are possible, the construction favourable to the assessee should be adopted. Vs Union of India (Kerala High Court) Summary: The Kerala High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by AVT McCormick Ingredients Pvt. Ltd. challenging an assessment order dated 15.10.2018 to the extent it disallowed refund of input tax credit lying in the Electronic Credit Ledger under the head SGST credit. The petitioner, engaged in export of spice extracts and oleoresins, was earlier registered under the Kerala Value Added Tax Act, 2003 and had filed Form GST TRAN-1 for transitioning excess input tax credit from its VAT ledger to its Electronic Credit Ledger. According to the petitioner, TRAN-1 was filed in November 2017 and the transitional credit was reflected in the Electronic Credit Ledger on 27.12.2017. For November 2017, the petitioner sought refund of ITC. The Department rejected the claim on the ground that transitional credit was not credit earned during the relevant period and therefore did not qualify as “Net ITC” under Rule 89(4) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as clarified by Circular No.37/11/2018-GST dated 15.03.2018. The respondents also objected to maintainability of the writ petition because the petitioner had not exhausted the statutory remedy and had approached the High Court after expiry of the limitation period for appeal. The petitioner argued that an appeal would be futile because the adjudicating authority had acted on a departmental circular that would also bind the appellate authority. It relied upon Filterco and another v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, Madhya Pradesh and another. On merits, reliance was placed upon M/s Ford India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India and others and M/s Intas Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Union of India and Others to contend that refund could not be denied by ignoring transitional credit appearing in the Electronic Credit Ledger. The Court examined Section 140 of the CGST Act and Rule 117 of the CGST Rules. It observed that transitional credit representing the closing balance of eligible taxes lying in the last return under the erstwhile regime as on 30.06.2017 would be carried forward as credit in the Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. Consequently, unutilised input tax credit under the erstwhile regime as on 30.06.2017 would be available as the opening balance of unutilised ITC on 01.07.2017. However, the Court found a crucial evidentiary deficiency in the petitioner’s case. The petitioner had not produced a copy of the declaration in Form GST TRAN-1 required to be filed within the prescribed period and had not produced satisfactory material proving the credit in its Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. The adjudicating authority could allow the refund only upon proof that the amount claimed stood credited in the Electronic Credit Ledger as on 01.07.2017. In the absence of such satisfactory material, the Court found no reason to interfere with the impugned adjudication order. The High Court also dealt with the belated invocation of its writ jurisdiction. It noted that Sections 107 and 108 of the CGST Act provide statutory remedies of appeal and revision against orders of the adjudicating authority and that the present writ petition had admittedly been filed after expiry of the statutory appeal period. The Court further noticed that the Allahabad High Court judgment in Moriroku UT India Pvt. Ltd., relied upon by the petitioner, had subsequently been set aside by the Supreme Court in Moriroku UT India (P) Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. Relying on A.V. Venkateswaran, Collector of Customs, Bombay v. Ramchand Sobhraj Wadhwani and another, the Court reiterated that a litigant who, by his own fault, allows the prescribed period for availing the statutory remedy to expire cannot use that failure as a ground for invoking the discretionary jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226. It further relied upon Rikhab Chand Jain v. Union of India, where the Supreme Court held that although Article 226 itself carries no prescribed limitation period, writ jurisdiction must be invoked with utmost expedition and within a reasonable period; the statutory limitation applicable to the alternative remedy can provide an indication of what constitutes a reasonable period. The Court also referred to Assistant Commissioner (CT) LTU v. Glaxo Smith Kline Consumer Health Care Ltd., in which the Supreme Court explained that the width of Article 226 jurisdiction does not mean that a High Court should issue a writ inconsistent with the legislative scheme governing the statutory remedy and its limitation. Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Hyderabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Central Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: The CESTAT Hyderabad partly allowed the appeal of Lahari Holiday Homes Ltd. against an Order-in-Original confirming service tax of Rs.1,63,15,458/- with interest under “Club or Association Service”, besides penalties under Sections 76, 77 and 78 of the Finance Act, 1994 and smaller demands under Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service and Renting of Immovable Property Service. The appellant operated Lahari Resorts and had introduced a Time Share Holiday Scheme under which customers acquired a contractual right to occupy specified accommodation for one week every year for 12 years against predetermined consideration. The Tribunal examined whether persons enrolled under the Time Share Scheme could be regarded as “members” of a club or association merely because the agreement used that terminology. It held that taxability must depend upon the real legal and commercial character of the arrangement rather than nomenclature. The customers acquired no proprietary, voting, management or shareholding rights in the appellant company. Their relationship with the appellant remained that of customer and service provider, and they merely purchased accommodation rights for specified periods. The Tribunal also noted that the appellant was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and that the time-share customers did not become members of the company in accordance with that Act. They neither subscribed to the memorandum, became shareholders, nor had their names entered in the register of members. Therefore, the foundation for treating them as members of a “Club or Association” was held to be legally unsustainable. The Tribunal relied heavily upon State of West Bengal Vs Calcutta Club Ltd. and noted that the Supreme Court had explained that incorporated clubs and associations constituted under statutory enactments stood on a different footing and that charging provisions must be interpreted strictly. The Tribunal further observed that commercial hospitality arrangements could not become “Club or Association Service” merely because customers were described as members. It also relied upon Bharat Hotels Ltd. and Adarsh Realty & Hotel Pvt. Ltd., where loyalty or membership programmes of hotels were treated as commercial hospitality arrangements rather than club membership. A further significant factor was the introduction of “Short Term Accommodation Service” under Section 65(105)(zzzzw) of the Finance Act, 1994 with effect from 01.05.2011. According to the Tribunal, creation of this specific taxable category supported the conclusion that hotel and resort accommodation was not intended to be taxed earlier under “Club or Association Service”. The dominant object of the appellant’s Time Share Scheme was accommodation, not the provision of club facilities or privileges. On the facts, the consideration paid by each customer was directly linked to the category of accommodation selected. Customers acquired only a contractual right to occupy accommodation for one week each year during the tenure of the scheme. No evidence established separate consideration for recreational facilities, sports, club privileges or similar amenities. The Tribunal therefore held that the Time Share Scheme did not satisfy the essential ingredients of “Club or Association Service”, and the principal service-tax demand under that category was set aside. As regards Mandap Keeper Service, Internet Café Service, Rent-a-Cab Scheme Operator Service and Renting of Immovable Property Service, the appellant had voluntarily paid the entire service tax together with applicable interest before issuance of the show-cause notice. The Department did not dispute either the quantum or the fact of payment. In the absence of evidence of deliberate fraud or wilful suppression, the Tribunal held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of Section 73(3) of the Finance Act, 1994. The Tribunal also rejected the finding of suppression. The appellant maintained regular books of account, its Time Share receipts were reflected in audited financial statements, agreements were maintained in the ordinary course of business and the Department’s case itself was founded on documents produced by the appellant. The dispute arose from classification and interpretation rather than concealment or clandestine activity. Accordingly, penalties under Sections 76, 77 and 78 were held unsustainable. rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12569 Case Name Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Pranavbhai Ambalal Patel Vs Additional Director General (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court allowed a writ petition challenging the prolonged detention and subsequent seizure of a Toyota Land Cruiser imported from Japan. The petitioner purchased the vehicle for USD 54,000, filed Bill of Entry No.7472252 dated 26.12.2024 and paid customs duty of Rs.99,78,795. Out-of-charge was granted on 02.01.2025. On 07.02.2025, however, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the petitioner’s residence, prepared a Panchnama and directed him not to deal with or part with the vehicle. No contemporaneous seizure order under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 was passed. During pendency of the writ petition, the DRI ultimately issued a seizure memo only on 17.04.2026, more than one year after the original detention, followed by a show-cause notice dated 08.05.2026 under Section 124 read with Section 28(4). The Department also passed a provisional release order on 18.05.2026 requiring a bond for Rs.85,95,860 and a bank guarantee of Rs.1.20 crore by relying upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs dated 16.08.2017. The High Court noted that the relied-upon part of the Circular had already been struck down by the Delhi High Court in Shanus Impex Vs Union of India & Ors. to the extent it curtailed the adjudicating authority’s discretion. The Gujarat High Court strongly deprecated the Department’s continued reliance upon that paragraph. The Court rejected the Department’s attempt to attribute the delay in initiating Section 110 proceedings to pendency of the writ petition. It examined the sequence of interim orders and found that the High Court had never restrained the DRI from investigating or proceeding under the Customs Act. On the contrary, the Court repeatedly directed completion of the investigation. The High Court characterised the statement that pendency of the writ petition prevented initiation of Section 110 proceedings as a bald assertion and observed that the record showed that time had instead been consumed by the Department. The Court relied substantially upon Union of India & Ors. Vs Jatin Ahuja, where the Supreme Court held that where goods are seized under Section 110(1), notice under Section 124(a) must be given within six months, subject to a permissible extension of another six months under Section 110(2); absent such notice even within the extended period, the seized goods have to be released. The Gujarat High Court emphasised the legal distinction between “detention” and “seizure”. Merely recording in a Panchnama that the owner should not remove, part with or otherwise deal with the goods cannot substitute for an order contemplated by Section 110. Where seizure is undertaken, the proper officer must record reasons to believe that the goods are liable to confiscation. Where physical seizure is not practicable, the statutory provisos themselves prescribe the manner in which custody or restrictions are to be imposed. Relying upon Worldline Tradex Pvt. Ltd., the Court reiterated that detention through a Panchnama cannot automatically be treated as a seizure under Section 110(1). The Court also examined Instruction No.01/2017-Cus. dated 08.02.2017, which specifically directs field formations that whenever goods are seized, an appropriate seizure memo/order must be passed in addition to the Panchnama and must clearly record the reasons to believe that the goods are liable to confiscation. Where immediate seizure is impracticable, an appropriate statutory order restricting dealings with the goods has to be served and investigation must be fast-tracked. Construing these statutory requirements together, the High Court held that the seizure order must be coterminous with, or follow the Panchnama without permitting indefinite detention. Customs authorities cannot keep goods detained for an unlimited period and subsequently issue a Section 110(1) seizure order merely to restart the six-month limitation period under Section 110(2). In the present case, time began running from the actual detention of the vehicle under the Panchnama dated 07.02.2025. The seizure memo issued on 17.04.2026, after more than one year, could not enable the DRI to reap the benefit of its own inaction by thereafter issuing the Section 124 notice on 08.05.2026. The Court further declared the provisional release order dated 18.05.2026 illegal because its conditions were based upon paragraph 2 of Circular No.35/2017-Customs, already struck down in Shanus Impex. It consequently directed the respondents

rows.title: Excise Duty | CENVAT Credit Cannot Be Denied When Manufacturer’s Invoice Names Assessee as Consignee: CESTAT Kolkata
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12568 Case Name Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. Vs Commissioner of CGST & C.Ex. (CESTAT Kolkata) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Kolkata Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. Vs Commissioner of CGST & C.Ex. (CESTAT Kolkata) Summary: CESTAT Kolkata allowed the appeal filed by Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. and set aside the demand for reversal of CENVAT credit of Rs.83,839. The appellant had availed credit on the basis of three invoices, two issued in 2011 and one dated 22.01.2014. The Department sought reversal on the ground that the appellant had purchased the goods through M/s Ashis Enterprise, which did not possess dealer registration. The appellant contended that the invoices issued by M/s Roshanlal Bhagirathmal specifically showed Hindustan Engineering & Industries Ltd. as the consignee, while Ashis Enterprise was shown as the buyer. The goods were directly dispatched to the appellant and were duly accounted for in RG 23A Part I. Ashis Enterprise separately issued a commercial invoice to facilitate payment, which could be correlated with the invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. On examining the invoices, the Tribunal found that the appellant was expressly shown as the consignee and that all particulars required for an invoice under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were fulfilled. The Tribunal further noted that there was no allegation that the goods had not actually been received by the appellant. The goods had also been accounted for in RG 23A Part I after receipt at the appellant’s factory. In these circumstances, the Tribunal held that the Revenue had failed to establish any contravention of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The demand was accordingly set aside, the appeal was allowed and the appellant was held eligible for consequential relief, if any, in accordance with law. FULL TEXT OF THE CESTAT KOLKATA ORDER The appellant has taken the Cenvat Credit of Rs.83,839 on the basis of the Dealer’s invoice. The credit was taken in respect of of 2 invoices issued in the year 2011 and one invoice issued on 22.01.2014. 2. On the ground that the appellant has bought goods from a Dealer, who did not have Dealer’s Registration, a Show Cause Notice was issued to the appellant seeking reversal of Rs.83,839. After due process, the lower authorities have confirmed the demand. Hence, the appellant is before the Tribunal. 3. The Ld. Consultant appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the appellant has received the invoices clearly showing the present appellant as the Consignee and the dealer M/s. Ashis Enterprise, as the Buyer. The goods have been directly despatched by M/s. Roshanlal Bhagirathmal with proper Dealer’s Invoice, based on which the appellant has taken the Cenvat Credit. The appellant has also properly accounted for the inputs in the RG 23A Part I as can be observed from the Invoices. The Dealer Ashish Enterprise has issued a separate Invoice so that the payment can be made by the appellant to him. The Invoice issued by Ashish can be correlated with the Dealer’s Invoice issued by Roshanlal Bharatmal. Therefore, it is prayed that the appeal may be allowed. 4. The Ld. Authorized Representative submits that the Ashish Enterprise has not taken the Dealer’s registration. The goods have been received from Roshanlal with this invoice, who is the main seller and the buyer is Ashsish, who has not issued the Dealer’s Invoice. Therefore, it is submitted that the appellant has taken irregular cenvat credit. Therefore, he justifies the confirmed the demand. 5. Heard both the sides. 6. I have gone through the copy of the Invoices produced by the appellant. The sample copy is produced below: 7. From the above Invoice issued by Roshanlal Bhagirathmal, I find that the present appellant is shown as the Consignee. The buyer of the goods is mentioned as Ashis Enterprise. I observe that all the details required under an invoice to issued in terms of Rule 9 of CCR, 2004 have been fulfilled in the invoice raised by the Roshanlal Bhagirathmal. 8. Further, there is no allegation that the goods in question have not been received by the appellant. It is seen that the appellant has accounted for the goods received in RG 23A part I, after the same is received at his factory. 9. Therefore, I do not find any case has been made out by the Revenue towards any contravention of provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules 2004. Hence, I set aside the demand and allow the appeal. 10. The appellant would be eligible for consequent relief if any, as per law. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); ECI BJCL JV Vs Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax (CESTAT Hyderabad) Summary: CESTAT Hyderabad dismissed the appeal filed by ECI BJCL JV and upheld the Commissioner (Appeals)’ order dismissing its service tax appeal for failure to comply with a direction requiring pre-deposit of 50% of the adjudged demand. The appellant had executed EPC/works contracts relating to construction of dams, reservoirs, canals and allied structures for the Government of Andhra Pradesh during June 2007 to March 2012. A show-cause notice dated 23.10.2012 demanded service tax of Rs.43,86,471/- under Works Contract Service, which was confirmed by the adjudicating authority on 09.01.2014. The appellant challenged the order and sought waiver of pre-deposit. The Commissioner (Appeals) fixed the stay application for hearing on 12.06.2014; although the appellant sought an adjournment, the request was declined and, by order dated 13.06.2014, it was directed to deposit 50% of the service tax demand. The appellant subsequently requested a speaking order considering its legal submissions and precedents, but did not comply with the pre-deposit condition. Its appeal was consequently dismissed on 23.07.2014. Before the Tribunal, the appellant argued that its appeal had been dismissed without adjudication on merits and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had failed to consider its prima facie case, balance of convenience and financial hardship. It relied, inter alia, upon Lanco Infratech Ltd., Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd., DSM Sugar, Pennar Industries Ltd., Amber Anuruddha Mufti, Surya Pharmaceutical Ltd., B. Rama Rao & Company and Thermopads Pvt. Ltd. The Revenue maintained that adequate opportunity had been provided, the adjournment request had been considered and declined for recorded reasons, and failure to satisfy the pre-deposit condition justified dismissal. The Tribunal found that the Commissioner (Appeals) had granted an opportunity of personal hearing and had expressly considered the appellant’s request for an adjournment of about one month. The request was declined having regard to the statutory requirement of expeditious disposal, and the stay order recorded reasons for directing a 50% pre-deposit. It therefore rejected the contention that the stay order had been passed mechanically or without reasons. The decisions relied upon by the appellant concerning absence of adequate hearing or reasoned orders were held factually distinguishable. The Tribunal further held that the amended provisions of Section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 prescribing a mandatory 10% pre-deposit came into force only from 06.08.2014 and operated prospectively. Since the impugned appellate order had been passed before that amendment, the parties’ rights and obligations continued to be governed by the unamended provision. Consequently, a subsequent deposit of 10% could not cure the appellant’s earlier failure to comply with the 50% conditional stay order. The Tribunal reiterated that the right of appeal is statutory and subject to conditions prescribed by the statute. Under the then applicable Section 35F, the Commissioner (Appeals) could insist upon an appropriate pre-deposit while considering waiver, and once such a condition was imposed, the appellant had either to comply or seek appropriate relief from a competent forum. The Tribunal also rejected the plea of violation of natural justice, observing that a request for adjournment did not create an indefeasible right to obtain it and that the Commissioner (Appeals) had exercised discretion judicially by recording reasons. Subsequent compliance with the amended 10% requirement could not retrospectively validate an appeal already dismissed under the earlier statutory regime. The Tribunal accordingly held that the Commissioner (Appeals) committed no legal error in dismissing the appeal for non-compliance with the pre-deposit condition under the unamended Section 35F and dismissed ECI BJCL JV’s appeal. Badve Helmets India Pvt. Ltd. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vodafone Idea Limited Vs ACIT (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court allowed the connected writ petitions filed by Vodafone Idea Limited, seeking release of pending TDS refunds with applicable interest for Assessment Years 2003-04, 2008-09 to 2013-14. The petitions stated that the refunds had remained unpaid for about two years even after orders of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and subsequent orders passed by the Assessing Officer giving effect to those appellate decisions. For AY 2012-13, the Tribunal’s order dated 05.06.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 30.10.2024, with refund quantified by the assessee at Rs.11,06,37,172; the Form 26B applications dated 25.04.2025 were rejected. For AY 2013-14, the Tribunal’s order dated 30.04.2024 was followed by an appeal-effect order dated 14.10.2024, with refund quantified at Rs.7,57,50,048; the Form 26B application dated 01.02.2025 was rejected. For AYs 2003-04 and 2008-09 to 2011-12, the relevant Tribunal orders were dated 26.11.2024 and 03.02.2025, followed by an appeal-effect order dated 15.05.2026, with refund quantified at Rs.34,45,69,250. The total amount found payable by the Assessing Officer was Rs.53,09,56,470. The petitioner argued that Section 200A, Section 201, Rule 31A and Form 26B address the processing of TDS statements and refunds arising from excess or incorrect deduction/deposit. According to the petitioner, they do not govern a refund that crystallises after an assessment under Section 201 or after an appellate order. The respondents relied on departmental practice and the Standard Operating Procedure dated 23.03.2023 issued by the Centralized Processing Cell (TDS), contending that Form 26B was sought whenever TDS refunds were issued, including refunds consequent upon court or appellate orders. They also relied on the SOP’s treatment of outstanding demands against sister associated TANs. The respondents stated that about Rs.924,57,20,992 was outstanding against the petitioner’s PAN and sister TANs, of which Rs.913,66,12,715 was stayed and Rs.10,91,08,277 was not subject to stay. The petitioner disputed that figure and asserted that only Rs.27,63,141 was outstanding. The Court expressly left that factual dispute to the authorities. The Court examined the statutory scheme and held that Sections 200A and 201 operate in entirely different fields. It held that Section 201 deals with assessment of TDS, whereas Section 200A deals with adjustment of TDS before assessment at the CPC level; Rule 31A provides the procedure for that adjustment and Form 26B facilitates it. Once a competent Assessing Officer has made an assessment under Section 201 and/or an appellate authority has passed an order giving rise to a refund, the assessee has a vested and crystallised right to the refund with applicable interest, subject to the Department’s right to challenge the order in accordance with law. The Court further held that, after an assessment under Section 201, Rule 31A does not apply and the AO or CPC cannot compel an assessee to furnish Form 26B. The refund arising after giving effect to an appellate order must therefore be paid with applicable interest, subject to withholding or adjustment by a legally passed order under Section 245. In the present case, no such order under Section 245 had been shown. The Court therefore held the withholding of the refund on the basis of outstanding demands against the petitioner’s PAN and sister TANs to be untenable in law, arbitrary and violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(g) and 300A of the Constitution. The writ petitions were allowed. The respondents were directed to pay Rs.53,09,56,470 to the petitioner with applicable interest under Sections 244A and 244A(1A) on or before 30.09.2026. If the amount was not credited by that date, the entire amount would carry additional interest at 1% per month over and above statutory interest. All pending applications were also disposed of. Agrawal Vs Union of India (Chhattisgarh High Court) Summary: The High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur has held that the petitioners were entitled to interest on income-tax refunds arising from excess self-assessment tax from the date on which the tax was paid, up to 01.06.2016. The Court also noted that interest for the period from 01.06.2016 to 30.07.2018 had already been paid by the Income-Tax Department. The petitioners had paid self-assessment tax for AY 2009-10 and subsequently succeeded before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), which held that the land transferred by them did not constitute a capital asset. Consequently, substantial additions were deleted and refunds became payable. The Court relied upon the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Tata Chemicals Ltd., 2014 (6) SCC 335, and the Karnataka High Court in Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Vijaya Bank, holding that where excess tax paid by an assessee becomes refundable, interest is payable on such excess payment from the date of payment where the case falls outside the specific situations covered by Section 244A(1)(a). Facts of the Case The petitioners had filed their returns for Assessment Year 2009-10 declaring total incomes of Rs.68,27,080/- and Rs.89,40,150/- respectively. They claimed deduction under Chapter VI-A of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and claimed credit for tax deducted at source. They paid self-assessment tax under Section 140A of the Act amounting to Rs.17,27,000/- and Rs.23,56,000/- respectively on 25.02.2010. Initially, they claimed nominal refunds of Rs.230/- and Rs.110/- respectively. During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer disallowed their claims for exemption under Section 54-B and made additions of Rs.2,01,51,363/- and Rs.1,02,27,293/- respectively. The petitioners challenged the assessments before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals). By orders dated 31.08.2012, the appellate authority held that the land transferred by the petitioners did not constitute a “capital asset” within the meaning of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and directed exclusion of the gains from their taxable income. As a result, the taxable income was reduced to Rs.8,88,070/- in WPT No.114 of 2023 and Rs.9,80,885/- in WPT No.115 of 2023. Although the appellate orders had been passed, the assessed income was not reduced in the departmental records due to inadvertence. The mistake was subsequently rectified under Section 154 by order dated 09.05.2013. Following the rectification, refunds of Rs.16,09,310/- and Rs.21,64,020/- became payable to the petitioners. The Department ultimately paid the refund amounts on 30.07.2018. Interest at 6% plus 3% per annum was subsequently paid for the period from 01.06.2016 to 30.07.2018 on 16.06.2020. Issue Whether the petitioners were entitled to interest on the refund arising from excess self-assessment tax from the date of payment of such tax, and whether additional interest under Section 244A(1A) was payable in respect of the delayed refund. Submissions of the Petitioners The petitioners contended that they were entitled to interest on the refund from the date on which the self-assessment tax was paid. It was submitted that although the CIT (Appeals) passed orders on 31.08.2012, the orders were given effect to only subsequently and the departmental records were ultimately rectified on 09.05.2013. The refund itself was paid only on 30.07.2018. The petitioners accordingly claimed interest under Sections 244A and 244A(1A), including interest at 6% plus additional interest at 3% per annum. Submissions of the Revenue The Revenue argued that the tax liability had been self-assessed by the petitioners and that, before the amendment introduced by the Finance Act, 2016, Section 244A did not specifically provide for interest on refunds arising from self-assessment tax. It was contended that the amended provisions could not be applied retrospectively. The Revenue further submitted that the appellate orders had been given effect to and that interest had already been paid for the period from 01.06.2016 to 30.07.2018. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Chalamala Narasa Reddy Vs Special Deputy Collector LAO Somasila Project (Andhra Pradesh High Court) Summary: The Andhra Pradesh High Court disposed of Civil Revision Petition Nos. 448, 446, 447 and 449 of 2026 by a common order, as the issue involved in all the cases was identical. The petitioners were decree holders in Land Acquisition Original Petitions and had filed Execution Applications in Execution Petitions under Rules 231 to 235 of the Civil Rules of Practice seeking transfer of the awarded amounts through the CFMS online system to their accounts. The Special Deputy Collector-cum-Land Acquisition Officer, Somasila Project, Unit-IV, Rajampet, opposed the applications on the ground that the applications concerned cheques for compensation awarded for structures and that income tax was therefore required to be deducted. Reliance was placed on Union of India v. Hari Singh, (2018) 15 SCC 201, contending that while compensation for acquisition of agricultural land was not subject to deduction, structures standing on agricultural lands remained taxable. The Executing Court, by order dated 29.12.2025, partly allowed the applications and granted liberty to the petitioners to claim exemption before the competent authority under Section 197 of the Income Tax Act. The petitioners challenged those orders before the High Court. Before the High Court, learned counsel for the petitioners relied upon Circular No. 36 of 2016 dated 25.10.2016. The Circular clarifies that compensation received in respect of an award or agreement exempted from levy of income tax under Section 96 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR Act) is not taxable under the Income Tax Act. The Court considered Section 96 of the RFCTLARR Act, which provides that no income tax or stamp duty shall be levied on an award or agreement made under that Act, except under Section 46. The Court also considered Section 194LA of the Income Tax Act. Its second proviso expressly provides that no deduction is to be made where payment is made in respect of an award or agreement exempted from levy of income tax under Section 96 of the RFCTLARR Act. The Explanation to Section 194LA distinguishes “agricultural land” from “immovable property”, with immovable property meaning any land other than agricultural land or any building or part of a building. The High Court noted that the RFCTLARR Act came into effect from 1st January, 2014. It held that Section 96 provides that income tax shall not be levied on any award or agreement made under the RFCTLARR Act, except those made under Section 46, and that the proviso to Section 194LA also reflects the same exemption. Accordingly, compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land under the RFCTLARR Act, except compensation relating to awards or agreements under Section 46, is exempt from levy of income tax. Consequently, the impugned orders dated 29.12.2025 passed by the Executing Court were set aside and the matters were remanded to the Executing Court to consider the issue afresh in accordance with the observations made by the High Court and law. The Executing Court was directed to expedite the hearing. The Civil Revision Petitions were disposed of with no order as to costs, and pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, were closed. The petitioner was a company engaged in the trading, sale and purchase of steel products and had been assigned a GSTIN by the Department. A show-cause notice dated 09.10.2025 was issued proposing cancellation of its registration under Rule 21(a) of the Chhattisgarh Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 on the ground that the petitioner was not conducting business from its declared place of business, or that the declared place of business was not found. The Assistant Commissioner of State Tax, Raipur-7 subsequently cancelled the registration on 27.10.2025 with retrospective effect from 11.12.2020. Before the High Court, the petitioner challenged both the show-cause notice and the cancellation order. It was contended that the show-cause notice did not specify the date and time on which the petitioner was required to appear before the authority for personal hearing. The petitioner further contended that there was no provision under Section 29 of the CGST/SGST Act or the Rules permitting cancellation of registration with retrospective effect in the manner adopted by the authorities. Reliance was placed on the decision in Nairson Multiventures (P) Ltd. vs. State of Chhattisgarh, reported in (2026) 183 taxmann.com 369 (Chhattisgarh). The respondents opposed the writ petition. They submitted that the Office of the Commissioner, State GST, had been informed that the petitioner was not conducting business from its declared place of business. A communication dated 03.10.2025 had been sent to the concerned authority and physical verification was thereafter carried out. According to the respondents, the show-cause notice and cancellation proceedings were undertaken in accordance with Rule 22 of the Rules of 2017. It was also argued that the petitioner had an alternative remedy of approaching the competent authority for revocation of cancellation and, therefore, the writ petition was not maintainable. The High Court examined the show-cause notice dated 09.10.2025 and found that although the petitioner had been granted seven days’ time to file a reply, the authority had not specified any date and time for personal hearing. The Court referred to Rule 22(1), read with Form GST REG-17, which requires the notice to provide an opportunity to furnish a reply within seven working days and also to appear before the authority on a specified date and time. The prescribed form itself states that, in case of failure to furnish a reply or appear for personal hearing, the matter may be decided ex parte on the basis of available records and on merits. The Court therefore held that the show-cause notice issued by respondent No.2 was contrary to the requirements of Form GST REG-17. Merely granting seven working days to file a reply did not satisfy the requirement to afford an opportunity of personal hearing by specifying the date and time for such hearing. The Court further considered Rule 25 of the Rules of 2017 concerning physical verification of the business premises. Under the rule, where physical verification is carried out, the verification report together with other documents, including photographs, is required to be uploaded in FORM GST REG-30 on the common portal within fifteen working days following the date of verification. In the present case, physical verification had allegedly been carried out on 21.08.2025 and 19.08.2025, but the relevant documents had not been uploaded until the final orders were passed. The Court held that the show-cause notice and final orders were consequently contrary to Rule 25 as well. On the objection concerning availability of an alternative remedy, the Court relied upon the Supreme Court decision in Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. vs. Excise and Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority and Others, reported in 2023 SCC OnLine SC 95. rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12561 Case Name Commissioner CGST & CX Vs Power Tech Global Private Limited (GSTAT) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GST Appellate Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Commissioner CGST & CX Vs Power Tech Global Private Limited (GSTAT) Summary: The Kolkata Bench of GSTAT has held that the amendment introduced by Notification No. 14/2022 dated 5 July 2022 to Explanation 1 of Rule 43 of the CGST Rules, whereby the value of specified duty credit scrips was excluded from the aggregate value of exempt supplies for ITC reversal, cannot be applied retrospectively to transactions undertaken during FY 2017-18 to FY 2019-20. The Tribunal noted that although the rule-making authority had statutory power to give the amendment retrospective effect, the notification expressly brought it into force from 5 July 2022. The amendment therefore operated prospectively. However, the Tribunal separately held that the Revenue had failed to establish fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts with intent to evade tax. The taxpayer had disclosed its transactions and its claim of ITC; the Department was also aware of the taxpayer’s dealings in duty credit scrips. Consequently, invocation of Section 74(1) was held unsustainable. Applying Section 75(2) of the CGST Act, the Tribunal directed the proper officer to determine the tax liability as if the notice had been issued under Section 73, after providing an opportunity of hearing to the taxpayer. Facts of the Case The Revenue filed three appeals against a common Order-in-Appeal dated 8 July 2025, by which the first appellate authority had set aside the adjudication order and exonerated the taxpayer from the liabilities. The adjudicating authority had directed Power Tech Global Private Limited to reverse proportionate ITC of ₹74,75,604 for the three financial years 2017-18 to 2019-20 and to pay applicable interest together with an equivalent penalty. The Department’s case concerned the taxpayer’s dealings in MEIS duty credit scrips and the treatment of their value for purposes of proportionate ITC reversal under Section 17(2) read with Rules 42 and 43 of the CGST Rules. The SCN demanded: IGST: ₹17,07,578 CGST: ₹28,84,013 SGST: ₹28,84,013 Total ITC: ₹74,75,604 together with interest and penalty under Section 74. Contentions of the Taxpayer The taxpayer contended, inter alia, that: 1. apportionment of ITC under Section 17(2) ought to have been restricted to taxable supplies, including zero-rated supplies; 2. the value of duty credit scrips ought not to have been included in exempt supplies for the purpose of ITC reversal; 3. reversal of ITC on sale of duty credit scrips would run contrary to the Government’s export-promotion objective; and 4. Section 74(1) was wrongly invoked because there was no wilful suppression or misstatement. The taxpayer also relied upon the 2022 amendment to Rule 43 and contended that the amendment should receive retrospective application. Order of the First Appellate Authority The first appellate authority accepted the taxpayer’s contention. It considered that sale of MEIS licences fell within exempt supplies but relied upon the insertion of clause (d) in Explanation 1 to Rule 43 by Notification No. 14/2022 dated 5 July 2022, under which the value of supply of duty credit scrips was excluded from the aggregate value of exempt supplies. On that basis, it held that the taxpayer was entitled to the benefit of the amended provision and set aside the ITC reversal. The appellate authority relied upon Supreme Court decisions including Sedco Forex International Drill Inc., Hitendra Vishnu Thakur, Suchitra Components Ltd. and Allied Motors (P.) Ltd. The Revenue challenged this approach before GSTAT. Questions Before the Tribunal The Tribunal identified three questions: 1. Whether the appeals were entertainable in view of CBIC Circular No. 207/1/2024-GST dated 26 June 2024, prescribing a monetary limit of ₹20 lakh for departmental appeals before GSTAT. 2. Whether the first appellate authority was correct in applying the 5 July 2022 amendment to Rule 43 retrospectively to transactions undertaken during 2017-20. 3. Whether the Revenue was legally justified in invoking Section 74(1) against the taxpayer. Tribunal’s Findings 1. Monetary limit for departmental appeals The Tribunal considered CBIC Circular No. 207/1/2024-GST. The circular prescribed monetary limits of: ₹20 lakh for appeals before GSTAT; ₹1 crore for appeals before the High Court; and ₹2 crore for appeals before the Supreme Court. The Tribunal nevertheless found that the present appeals could be entertained, particularly having regard to the fact that the three appeals arose from the same composite order and involved an issue concerning interpretation of the statutory provision

It had been availing refund of IGST paid on exports under Rule 96 of the CGST Rules, 2017. The first respondent issued a notice dated 28.09.2020 stating that the petitioner was not a holder of an EPCG licence and was therefore not eligible for export with payment of tax and to claim IGST refund benefits on exported goods. The notice also recorded that the petitioner had availed IGST refunds between 09.10.2018 and 31.03.2020 and that grant of IGST refund for subsequent shipping bills pertaining to the IEC had been suspended for further enquiry. During pendency of the writ petition, the suspension relating to the IEC code was revoked. The petitioner therefore sought permission to produce the necessary documents relating to its refund claim before the second respondent and requested a direction for consideration of the refund claim. The respondents raised no serious objection to this limited relief. The Madras High Court, without expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, permitted the petitioner to produce the necessary documents relating to the IGST refund claim before the second respondent, in terms of the notice dated 28.09.2020, within two weeks from receipt of the order. The second respondent was directed to consider the documents on merits and in accordance with law and pass appropriate orders within six weeks thereafter. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of without costs. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF MADRAS HIGH COURT The petitioner has filed this writ petition seeking issuance of Writ of Certiorarified Mandamus, calling for the records of the first respondent’s notice dated 28.09.2020 in DIN 20200973MZ00002RB587 in F.No. S.Misc/10/2020/IGST-Refunds-(CH.IV) and quash the same, and consequently direct the respondents to process the petitioner’s refund claim of IGST paid on export in accordance to Section 54 of CGST Act, 2017 read with Rule 96 of CGST Rules, 2017. 2. The learned counsel appearing for the petitioner submitted that the petitioner company is engaged in the business of processing of granite slabs/ tiles/ panels and other stone products. The petitioner had been availing refund of IGST paid on export as per the provisions of Rule 96, CGST Rules, 2017. However, the first respondent issued the impugned notice stating that the petitioner is not a holder of EPCG license, thus not eligible for export with payment of tax and to claim for IGST refund benefits on exported goods, however, the petitioner availed IGST refunds between 09.10.2018 to 31.03.2020 on exported goods and that grant of IGST refund for subsequent shipping bills pertaining to IEC has been suspended for further enquiry and challenging the same, the petitioner has filed this writ petition. 4.The learned Senior Panel Counsel appearing for the respondents raise no serious objection. 5.Considering the limited relief now sought for by the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner, this Court, without expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, permits the petitioner to produce necessary documents with regard to the claim of refund of IGST before the second respondent, as per the impugned notice dated 28.09.2020, within a period of two weeks from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. On receipt of such documents, the second respondent shall consider the same, on merits and in accordance with law, and pass appropriate orders, within a period of six weeks thereafter. 6.The writ petition is disposed of. No costs. Saravanan Vs Assistant Commissioner (ST) (Madras High Court) Summary: The Madras High Court considered a writ petition challenging an order dated 23.08.2023 passed under Section 73 read with Section 16(4) of the GST law in relation to Financial Year 2018-2019. The petitioner had filed the return for March 2019 on 30.10.2019, ten days after the prescribed due date of 20.10.2019. Although the return was filed belatedly and the applicable late fee under Section 47 had been paid, the respondent denied the Input Tax Credit (ITC) claimed in the return and consequently levied interest and penalty. The petitioner relied upon the retrospective insertion of sub-sections (5) and (6) in Section 16 of the CGST Act by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 (Act 15 of 2024). Section 16(5), inserted retrospectively with effect from 01.07.2017, provides a relaxation from the time limit under Section 16(4) for invoices or debit notes pertaining to Financial Years 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20 and 2020-21, where the relevant return under Section 39 is filed up to 30.11.2021. The petitioner contended that the case was covered by this extended statutory period. The learned Additional Government Pleader appearing for the Revenue did not dispute the legal position. The Court noted that the petitioner admittedly filed the relevant return on 30.10.2019, well before the extended statutory cut-off of 30.11.2021. It observed that Parliament had inserted Section 16(5), considering, among other things, that the GST enactment had come into force only in 2017 and dealers were not accustomed to the procedures. The Court reproduced Section 16(5), which operates notwithstanding Section 16(4) and covers ITC pertaining to Financial Years 2017-18 through 2020-21 where the return under Section 39 was filed up to 30.11.2021. The Court also recorded that Notification No.17 of 2024-Central Tax, dated 27.09.2024 and Circular No.237/31/2024-GST, dated 15.10.2024 were issued in furtherance of the amendment. The Court held that the petitioner was entitled to the benefit of the retrospective amendment, subject to fulfilment of the other statutory requirements for availment of ITC. The Court relied upon its earlier decision in Sri Ganapathi Pandi Industries vs. The Assistant Commissioner (State Tax), in which the Court had held that the extended period under Section 16(5) would be available to eligible registered persons following the retrospective amendment. Consequently, the Court found that the impugned order dated 23.08.2023 could not be sustained insofar as the ITC claim was barred under Section 16(4) but fell within the period prescribed by Section 16(5). The order was set aside to that extent. The respondent-Department was restrained from initiating or continuing recovery proceedings against the petitioner on the issue of limitation. The Court further directed that, if any amount had already been recovered from the petitioner pursuant to the impugned assessment order through the cash ledger, credit ledger or any other prescribed mode, the same should be refunded or utilised/adjusted towards future tax. The writ petition was accordingly allowed, with no order as to costs, and the connected miscellaneous petitions were closed. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mehadia & Sons C & F Division Vs Assistant Commissioner of CGST & Central Excise (Bombay High Court) Summary: The Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench, considered a challenge to a show cause notice dated 24/04/2025 issued under Section 73 of the CGST Act, concerning Financial Years 2021-22 to 2023-24. The notice alleged suppression of taxable value and consequent short payment of Central GST. The petitioner contended that clubbing the periods while issuing a notice under Section 73 was impermissible and relied upon the Bombay High Court judgment in M/s. Milroc Good Earth Developers Vs. Union of India & Ors., Writ Petition No. 2203/2025, decided on 9/10/2025. The Court in that case had held that there was no scope for consolidating various financial years/tax periods while issuing a show cause notice under Section 73. The Court also noted the subsequent decision in Rite Water Solutions (India) Ltd. Vs. Joint Commissioner, CGST & Central Excise, Nagpur and Ors., Writ Petition No. 466/2025, decided on 28/11/2025, which reiterated that position. The respondents opposed the contention and relied upon M/s Mathur Polymers Vs. Union of India & Ors., W.P.(C) 2394/2025, decided by the Delhi High Court on 26/8/2025. The Delhi High Court had held that, in cases involving allegations of fraudulent availment of ITC where transactions were spread across several years, a consolidated notice could be required to establish the alleged illegal modality adopted by businesses and entities, and that the legislation did not itself prevent issuance of an SCN or order for multiple years in a consolidated manner. The respondents further submitted that the Delhi High Court judgment had been challenged before the Supreme Court in Special Leave Petition (Civil) Diary No. 50279/2025, but the Supreme Court declined to interfere. The Bombay High Court acknowledged that the Delhi High Court judgment had attained finality, but held that the doctrine of merger did not apply because the Supreme Court had dismissed the petition in limine and not on merits. The Court further held that its judgments in Milroc Good Earth Developers and Rite Water Solutions would prevail within its jurisdiction because the Supreme Court had neither stayed nor overruled those decisions. The Court identified the reasons underlying the Bombay High Court’s earlier view: the GST scheme is based on tax periods and annual returns for each financial year; the statutory limitation framework operates separately for each year; consolidation of different years would aggregate periods having different due dates and limitation periods; Section 2(106) of the CGST Act defines “tax period” as the period for which the return is required to be furnished; and year-wise treatment is reflected in provisions including Sections 37, 39, 44 and 50, together with Section 73 and Section 74. The respondents also informed the Court that the Bombay High Court’s judgments in Milroc Good Earth Developers and Rite Water Solutions were under consideration for challenge before the Supreme Court and that the issue of clubbing notices had been referred to a Larger Bench by order dated 17-4-2026 in M/s. Rollmet LLP Vs. The Union of India and ors., Writ Petition No. 16848/2025, with connected writ petitions. The Court therefore granted liberty to the respondents to seek revival of the petition if the earlier Bombay High Court judgments were set aside or if the Larger Bench took a different view. Consequently, for the reasons set out in Milroc Good Earth Developers and Rite Water Solutions, the petition was partly allowed. The show cause notice dated 24/04/2025 was quashed and set aside, while the respondents were given liberty to re-issue notice strictly in terms of Section 73 of the CGST Act, if there was no other legal impediment. The petition was disposed of with no order as to costs. Cases Discussed M/s. Milroc Good Earth Developers Vs. Miny Zachariah (High Court of Kerala) Summary: The High Court of Kerala considered a preliminary objection on limitation in Company Claim No.1384 of 2023 filed by the Official Liquidator of M/S Appletree Chits India (P) Ltd. against Smt. Miny Zachariah. The Company Claim sought recovery of Rs.62,548/-, inclusive of interest, allegedly payable by the respondent to the company under liquidation. The claim was instituted under Section 446 read with Section 458A of the Companies Act, 1956, with the claimant also seeking future interest at 12% per annum on the principal amount of Rs.28,750/- from 14.08.2013 and costs. The respondent filed a counter affidavit dated 23.04.2026 denying the liability and contending that the demand was barred by limitation. The principal controversy before the Court at this stage was therefore the date from which the limitation period applicable to the Official Liquidator’s claim was required to be computed. The respondent’s counsel submitted that the alleged default occurred on 14.08.2013 and that, under Article 137 of the [Limitation Act, 1963](https://taxguru.in/corporate-law/section-7-ibc-limitation-date-default-acknowledgment-revival-claims.html), steps ought to have been taken within three years. It was contended that the winding-up proceedings commenced on 10.02.2014 and remained on hold until the Company Court passed the winding-up order on 08.11.2019. According to the respondent, after excluding the period from 10.02.2014 to 08.11.2019 under Section 458A of the Companies Act, 1956, and taking into account the additional one-year period under that provision, the claim ought to have been presented by 12.05.2023. Since the Company Claim was presented only on 05.09.2023, it was argued to be barred by limitation. Reliance was placed on the Supreme Court judgment in Karnataka Steel and Wire Products and Ors. V. Kohinoor Rolling Shutters and Eng. Works and Ors. [(2003) 1 SCC 76]. For the Official Liquidator, it was submitted that the right to sue arose only when the winding-up order was passed on 08.11.2019. On that basis, the Official Liquidator contended that the claim could be filed within four years, comprising three years under Article 137 of the Limitation Act and the additional one-year period under Section 458A of the Companies Act. The claim presented on 05.09.2023 was therefore stated to be within limitation. Reliance was placed on the Full Bench judgment in Ulahannan v. Wandoor Jupiter Chits (P) Ltd. [1998 (2) KLT 636 (F.B.)]. The Court noted that Article 137 requires an application to be presented within three years from the date on which the “right to apply” arises. The Court then considered when the Official Liquidator becomes entitled to institute the claim. Referring to Section 446 of the Companies Act, 1956, the Court observed that it is only when the winding-up order has been made, or the Official Liquidator has been appointed as provisional liquidator, that proceedings can be commenced with the leave of the Tribunal/Court. In the present case, the winding-up order was passed on 08.11.2019 and, accordingly, the Court held that the Official Liquidator’s entitlement to institute the Company Claim had to be reckoned with reference to that date. The Court considered the Supreme Court’s decision in Karnataka Steel and Wire Products and Ors. V. Kohinoor Rolling Shutters and Eng. Works and Ors. The judgment explained that the Supreme Court had considered whether a claim already barred on the date when the winding-up application was filed could be revived merely because an order was subsequently made in the winding-up proceedings. The Supreme Court held that Section 458A could not be construed as reviving a time-barred debt. At the same time, in respect of a legally enforceable claim that could have been made by the company on the date on which the winding-up application was made, the Official Liquidator could lodge the claim within four years from the date of winding up by taking the benefit of Section 458A, including the three-year period under Article 137. That case involved winding-up proceedings commencing on 16.10.1989 and a winding-up order dated 04.04.1990, following which the Official Liquidator instituted claims under Section 446(2) of the Companies Act. Vs Commissioner of Karnataka State GST (GSTAT Bengaluru) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench dismissed the appeal filed by Rodman Technologies Pvt Ltd and upheld the interest and penalty confirmed under Section 73(9) of the CGST/KGST Acts, 2017. The dispute concerned whether the appellant could obtain waiver of interest and penalty under Section 128A in respect of an excess Input Tax Credit demand that was reported in GSTR-3B for December 2020, although the appellant contended that the underlying debit notes related to FY 2018-19. The appellant was engaged in trading in garments manufacturing and was registered under the KGST Act, 2017. On scrutiny of returns for 2020-21, the department compared ITC available in GSTR-2A with ITC claimed in GSTR-3B for December 2020 and identified excess ITC of Rs 68,573 as IGST, Rs 2,46,747 as CGST and Rs 2,46,747 as SGST. A notice under Section 61 in Form GST ASMT-10 was issued on 08.02.2024, followed by Form GST DRC-01A on 02.07.2024. Thereafter, a show cause notice in Form DRC-01 dated 15.11.2024 was issued under Section 73, proposing recovery of the excess ITC together with interest of Rs 3,23,753 under Section 50 and penalty of Rs 69,350. The disputed excess ITC of Rs 5,62,067 was paid through Form DRC-03 on 09.01.2025, while interest and penalty remained unpaid. The adjudicating authority thereafter confirmed the interest and penalty under Section 73(9). The First Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal, holding that its jurisdiction under Section 107 was confined to the order appealed against and that considering FY 2018-19 would require fresh examination of facts and debit notes. It also held that the beneficial character of Section 128A could not enlarge appellate jurisdiction or permit the tax period to be re-characterised. The Tribunal appeal followed. The appellant argued that although the liability was declared and paid in December 2020, the underlying transaction related to FY 2018-19. According to the appellant, the relevant debit note had been issued and recorded in GSTR-1 in FY 2018-19, but because the earlier return could not be reopened, the liability was declared in the annual return for 2019-20 and discharged in December 2020. It was further argued that the repeated declaration in GSTR-1 for December 2020 produced a duplicate declaration of the same transaction. The appellant relied on the fact that the tax had been discharged suo motu and submitted that there was no intention to evade tax. The respondent contended that the excess ITC confirmed in the adjudication proceedings pertained to 2020-21 because it was identified from the December 2020 GSTR-3B. The respondent also submitted that Section 128A is confined to the period from 1 July 2017 to 31 March 2020 and that the appellant had admitted and paid the excess ITC through DRC-03 on 09.01.2025, leaving the confirmed interest and penalty payable. The Tribunal examined Section 128A, inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 01.11.2024. It emphasised that the waiver is subject to cumulative statutory conditions and is confined to amounts pertaining to the period from 1 July 2017 to 31 March 2020 or a part thereof. The Tribunal noted that payment of tax alone does not establish eligibility; the demand must itself arise from a notice, statement or order covered by Section 128A, must pertain to the specified period, and the prescribed payment and procedural conditions must be fulfilled. The Tribunal also noted the relevance of the procedure under Rule 164 and the prescribed application in Form GST SPL-01. The Tribunal held that the fact that the Section 73 notice was triggered by the December 2020 GSTR-3B was not by itself conclusive. It examined the records to determine the actual period to which the disputed ITC demand pertained. The decisive finding was that the excess ITC forming the subject matter of the demand was claimed in GSTR-3B for December 2020. It was not ITC availed in FY 2018-19 and carried forward through subsequent monthly returns. Consequently, the demand confirmed under Section 73(9) pertained to the ITC claim made in December 2020 and fell outside the temporal scope of Section 128A. The Tribunal considered the Karnataka High Court decision in Wipro Limited India v. the Assistant Commissioner of Central Taxes, Writ Petition No. 16175 of 2022 (T-Res), dated 06.01.2023. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Radhey Shyam Rishipal Factory Vs Principal Commissioner of Customs Import (Delhi High Court) Summary: The present batch comprises three Customs Appeals under Section 130 of the Customs Act, 1962, with CUSAA 89/2026, filed by M/S Radhey Shyam Rishipal Factory, treated as the lead matter. The appeals challenged the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi’s Common Miscellaneous Order Nos. 50042–50044/2026 dated 07.01.2026, by which applications seeking condonation of delay in appeals against Order-in-Original No. 19/2021/SG/Pr. Commr./ICD-Import/TKD dated 07.12.2021 were rejected and the appeals dismissed. The connected matters concerned Deepak Kumar and Radhey Shyam and arose from the same adjudication proceedings. The appellants stated that the Order-in-Original had not been served upon them and that they came to know of it only when bank-account freezing proceedings were initiated on 27.02.2024. They stated that a copy was ultimately furnished electronically on 02.07.2024 and appeals were filed before CESTAT on 01.08.2024. Since the appeals were beyond the period prescribed by Section 129A, applications seeking condonation of approximately 968 days’ delay were filed. The Department relied upon dispatch of the order to the address on record, electronic communication to the counsel who represented the appellants, the corrigendum communication and display of the order on the notice board under Section 153(e) of the Customs Act. The appellants contended that communication to their erstwhile counsel did not establish communication to them, that they had acted diligently after learning of the order, and that the question of service had been left open by an order dated 07.02.2025 in W.P.(C) No. 12704/2024. The Department contended that the appellants had participated in the adjudication through the same counsel, had not made any enquiry regarding the outcome for nearly three years, and had not shown sufficient cause for the delay. The High Court emphasised the limited jurisdiction under Section 130, under which interference is warranted only where a substantial question of law arises. Referring to Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, the Court considered the distinction between a substantial question of law and mere re-appreciation of factual findings, and noted the reiteration of those principles in Commissioner of Customs (Preventive), Odisha v. Satish Kumar Subudhi. On condonation, the Court noted that Section 129A(3) prescribes three months for filing an appeal from communication of the order and sub-section (5) permits admission after expiry where sufficient cause is shown. Relying upon Esha Bhattacharjee v. Managing Committee of Raghunathpur Nafar Academy and Basawaraj v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, the Court held that a liberal, justice-oriented approach does not dispense with bona fides, diligence and a satisfactory explanation for the entire period of delay. It also considered the appellants’ reliance on Rafiq v. Munshilal, but distinguished that principle on the basis that the present record disclosed prolonged inactivity by the appellants themselves. The Court found that CESTAT had considered the appellants’ participation in the adjudication, the Department’s attempts to communicate the order, electronic communication to counsel, notice-board display and, importantly, the absence of any enquiry for nearly three years. The Court further noted that the same counsel who had received the electronic communication later filed the appeals and condonation applications, and that no satisfactory explanation was furnished despite the Tribunal’s specific opportunity to explain the omission. The Court held that the subsequent receipt of the Order-in-Original on 02.07.2024 and filing of appeals on 01.08.2024 did not by themselves cure the preceding inaction. Ultimately, the High Court found no perversity, disregard of material evidence or error of law in CESTAT’s exercise of discretion. The question whether sufficient cause ought to have been accepted on these facts was treated as a matter within the Tribunal’s discretion, and no substantial question of law warranting interference under Section 130 was established. The three appeals were accordingly dismissed, and pending applications, if any, were also disposed of. Cases Discussed Commissioner of Customs (Preventive), Odisha v.
