rows.title: Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules Non-banking finance companies have sought clarity from the Reserve Bank of India on whether recovery calls fall under the service-call category permitted through the 1600 numbering series, amid concerns that customers increasingly block calls originating from the series, sources part of the discussion told ETBFSI. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:31 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133737944; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The issue was raised by NBFC CEOs and industry representatives during a meeting with RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu on Thursday, where the industry flagged concerns around the implementation of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) mandatory 1600-series framework for regulated financial entities.“Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source told ETBFSI.The 1600 series was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. TRAI, in November 2025, subsequently mandated a phase-wise migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the series, with the objective of allowing consumers to distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional and potentially fraudulent calls. Advt For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks were required to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026, while large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks and small finance banks were given a February 1, 2026 deadline. Remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks and other entities were required to migrate by March 1, 2026.RBI regulated entities covered by the mandate are not permitted to initiate service or transactional voice calls from numbers other than those allocated under the 1600 series, even where they have explicit or inferred customer consent.TRAI's stated objective is to prevent promotional calls from being made under the guise of service or transactional calls and to give BFSI entities a distinct identity that allows consumers to make informed decisions about whether to answer a call.However, NBFCs said the framework does not clearly address recovery communications. Lenders typically make large volumes of calls to borrowers regarding overdue payments, repayment schedules and other recovery-related matters, and the industry wants to know whether such calls qualify as service calls under the 1600 framework.“The distinction between a sales call, a service call and a recovery call is important. I agree that a sales call should not be made through 1600. But whether a recovery call is considered a service call is not clear,” the NBFC CEO said.The concern is compounded by the possibility of customers blocking calls originating from the 1600 series. Industry participants said that while the dedicated series is intended to help consumers identify genuine financial-sector calls, borrowers may still block such numbers as unwanted or spam, particularly when they receive repeated recovery calls. Advt “If you are doing mass recovery calls and people are blocking those numbers, the whole purpose is lost,” the source said.According to the industry, the problem becomes particularly acute when a borrower does not respond to repeated calls from a lender’s 1600 number.“Imagine a 1600 call. If the customer does not pick up, how will a banker communicate? If we try once or twice and the number is blocked, can we then call from our normal number? That is the question,” the CEO said. rows.title: Lenders challenge NCLT approval of Subhash Chandra repayment plan
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Lenders challenge NCLT approval of Subhash Chandra repayment plan HDFC Bank, LIC Housing Finance and Union Bank of India (UK) are set to challenge the NCLT’s approval of Zee founder Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan, which was cleared with 80.81 per cent of the creditors’ voting share despite opposition from several banks and public financial institutions. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Aug 31, 2026 at 12:55 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133636503; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Lenders including HDFC Bank, LIC Housing Finance and Union Bank of India (UK) are moving against the NCLT’s approval of Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan, with the lenders questioning the voting process and the eligibility of certain creditors who backed the proposal.Union Bank of India (UK) said it had rejected the plan along with lenders including Canara Bank and LIC Housing Finance and would "immediately" challenge the NCLT decision before the NCLAT. LIC Housing Finance said it would file an appeal along with other public financial institutions. HDFC Bank, which had a 3.17 per cent voting share, said it had opposed and voted against the resolution and was exploring an appeal. Advt The repayment plan, submitted by Chandra on October 16, 2024, was approved with 80.814 per cent of the voting share. The largest votes in favour came from World Crest Advisors (28.49 per cent), Lemonade Capital Advisors (16.85 per cent), Catalyst Trusteeship (11.85 per cent), Corpcall Capital Advisors (10.30 per cent) and Veena Investments (4.99 per cent).Among those voting against were LIC Housing Finance (6.09 per cent), IDBI Trusteeship representing Franklin Templeton (3.36 per cent), HDFC Bank (3.17 per cent), Axis Bank (2.86 per cent), Canara Bank (1.60 per cent), Union Bank of India (UK) (0.76 per cent) and RBL Bank (0.55 per cent). Creditors representing another 4.10 per cent did not vote.The dissenting lenders had argued that five entities - Veena Investments, Direct Media Distribution Ventures, World Crest Advisors, Lemonade Capital Advisors and Corpcall Capital Advisors, were associates of Chandra and should therefore not have been allowed to vote. Together, the five represented about 61.78 per cent of the voting share.They also raised concerns over the speed of the process. Chandra submitted the plan on October 16, the Resolution Professional filed his report on October 17, and the creditors’ meeting was held on October 24. Creditors were asked to evaluate claims of around Rs 21,697 crore, with the voting period later extended to October 31. Advt The lenders had also questioned the adequacy of Chandra’s asset disclosures and sought an independent forensic audit and asset-tracing exercise. They pointed to earlier net-worth certificates showing his wealth at Rs 45,888 crore in 2017 and Rs 40,562 crore in 2018, compared with a current net worth of around Rs 31.79 crore cited in the proceedings.The NCLT itself saw a split in the matter. The Technical Member had found procedural violations, including the shortened timeline for the creditors’ meeting, and questioned the participation of alleged associates in the voting process.The Judicial Member, however, held that the creditors had sufficient practical opportunity to examine the plan, noting that the voting period had been extended and that the creditors ultimately approved the plan by the requisite majority. Advt The matter was subsequently referred to a Third Member because of the difference between the two members. The Third Member backed approval of the repayment plan, subject to certain directions including exclusion of specified claims from the final creditor list. rows.title: Extension of timeline for implementation of SEBI Circular dated February 04, 2025 on ‘Safer participation of retail investors in Algorithmic trading’
rows.summary:
SEBI has issued Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/132 on September 30, 2025, which extends the implementation timeline for the earlier SEBI Circular dated February 4, 2025 on “Safer participation of retail investors in Algorithmic trading.” The substance of this document is a timing change: it does not introduce new substantive algo-trading rules in the text provided, but delays when the February 4, 2025 framework must be implemented.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that any obligations, controls, operational changes, or market-participant procedures required under the February 4, 2025 circular now have a later effective implementation date than previously scheduled. This extension applies to the retail-investor algorithmic trading framework addressed by SEBI, so firms involved in offering, facilitating, enabling, or overseeing algorithmic trading for retail investors should treat the original requirements as still pending but subject to the revised timeline.

No specific thresholds, rates, quantitative limits, or additional procedural changes are stated in the document excerpt provided. Accordingly, the compliance action item is to track the revised implementation deadline under the February 4, 2025 circular and adjust internal project plans, system readiness, client-facing communications, and control testing accordingly.

The compliance impact is that all SEBI-regulated entities remain subject to mandatory digital accessibility compliance under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 and the associated rules. The substantive obligation is to ensure digital services, platforms, and online interfaces are accessible in line with the accessibility requirements already referenced in the underlying July 31, 2025 circular.

Because only the heading and citation are shown, no additional procedural deadlines, phased timelines, exception criteria, reporting formats, or certification requirements are visible in the supplied content. For a compliance team, the key takeaway from the provided text is to treat this September 25, 2025 circular as implementation guidance for the existing mandatory accessibility regime and to verify that all entity digital touchpoints are aligned with the July 31, 2025 SEBI circular and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act framework.

rows.title: Ease of doing investment - Smooth transmission of securities from Nominee to Legal Heir
rows.summary:
This SEBI circular, titled **“Ease of doing investment - Smooth transmission of securities from Nominee to Legal Heir”** and dated **19 September 2025** as **Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/130**, signals a procedural change intended to make the transfer of securities from a nominee to the rightful legal heir smoother. Based on the content provided, the circular is focused on the **transmission process after the death of a securities holder**, specifically where a **nominee is named but the securities ultimately need to be passed to the legal heir**.

For a compliance team, the key point is that this appears to be a **regulatory facilitation measure affecting intermediaries and depository/market participants involved in securities transmission**—for example, entities handling client holdings, death claims, and account/beneficiary transfers. The document title indicates that SEBI is addressing the process by which securities are moved from the nominee’s control or recognition to the **legal heir’s entitlement**, suggesting a need for firms to ensure their internal transmission procedures, client communication, and operational workflows align with whatever updated SEBI requirements or clarifications the circular contains.

The material compliance implication is that firms should review how they currently handle **death-of-holder cases involving both nominees and legal heirs**, because the circular is explicitly about improving “smooth transmission” in that scenario. In practice, this means checking whether account-opening disclosures, nomination records, succession documentation requirements, and transmission processing steps need to be updated so that securities are not delayed or misdirected when a legal heir is entitled to them. If the circular introduces any new submission, verification, or timeline requirements, those would apply to the affected securities intermediaries from the effective date of the circular, which in the document provided is **19 September 2025**.

Because only the title and date are provided here, the exact operational requirements, forms, thresholds, or timelines are not visible in the excerpt. However, the document clearly concerns the **transfer of securities upon death**, and compliance teams should treat it as a prompt to verify whether their current nominee/transmission processes now require additional steps to reconcile the nominee’s role with the legal heir’s ultimate ownership rights.

rows.title: Framework on Social Stock Exchange

rows.title: Relaxation from certain provisions for units allotted to an employee benefit trust for the purpose of a unit based employee benefit scheme, Alignment of timelines for making distribution by InvITs and Format of Quarterly Report and Compliance Certificate – Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs)
rows.summary:

First, it grants a relaxation from certain InvIT regulatory provisions for units that are allotted to an employee benefit trust specifically for implementing a unit-based employee benefit scheme; this means such units will be treated with modified regulatory expectations rather than the standard provisions that otherwise apply to ordinary InvIT unit holdings. Second, it aligns the timeline for making distributions by InvITs, so any distributions required under the InvIT framework must now be made in accordance with the harmonized schedule set by SEBI, rather than any differing timing that may previously have existed under separate provisions. Third, SEBI has prescribed a specific format for the quarterly report and compliance certificate, which means InvITs and their compliance teams must prepare and submit these documents in the newly mandated structure.  

The circular is dated November 13, 2024 and is identified as Circular No. SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS-PoD-2/P/CIR/2024/159. The affected entities are Infrastructure Investment Trusts and, for the first item, employee benefit trusts holding InvIT units for the purpose of a unit-based employee benefit scheme. Compliance officers should verify whether their InvIT uses an employee benefit trust structure, update distribution calendars and internal control timelines to reflect the aligned distribution deadline, and ensure quarterly reporting/compliance certificate processes are revised to match the prescribed format.

rows.summary:

For compliance teams, the practical impact is that issuers, intermediaries, and listing/issue-processing workflows for these instruments will need to be capable of completing post-issue listing formalities within a much shorter window when the new option is used. The document’s material change is specifically the compression of the listing timeline for these two categories of securities; it does not indicate a change to the securities covered beyond debt securities and NCRPS, and it does not specify any monetary thresholds, rates, or other quantitative filing conditions beyond the **T+6 to T+3** shift. Compliance teams should therefore prepare for issuer-level process changes, tighter coordination among issue participants, and revised internal checklists/timelines to avoid late listing once the **T+3** framework is selected or becomes mandatory after the initial one-year optional period.

This affects entities offering Margin Trading Facility to clients and the associated risk/margin monitoring processes they use to ensure ongoing margin adequacy.

For compliance purposes, firms using MTF must update their margin management and collateral handling procedures so that securities obtained through cash collateral funding are recognized and tracked as eligible maintenance margin where permitted under the circular. The operational implication is that brokers must ensure systems, client margin statements, and internal controls properly distinguish these securities from other funded or pledged positions and apply the new treatment consistently. rows.title: (a) Ease of Doing Investments- Non-submission of ‘Choice of Nomination’  (i) Doing away with freezing of Demat Accounts and Mutual Fund Folios for existing investors; (ii) To remove freeze on payment of corporate benefits and service of physical folios; (b) Only 3 fields to be provided mandatorily for updating Nomination Details
rows.summary:
SEBI’s June 10, 2024 circular (SEBI/HO/MIRSD/POD-1/P/CIR/2024/81) relaxes the earlier nomination-compliance regime for existing investors by removing the freeze that had been used to enforce submission of the “choice of nomination” in demat accounts and mutual fund folios. In practical terms, demat accounts and mutual fund folios of existing investors will no longer be frozen merely because the investor has not completed the nomination choice process, and the earlier restriction on payment of corporate benefits and servicing of physical folios is also being removed. This means intermediaries, depositories, registrars/transfer agents, and mutual fund houses should stop treating non-submission of the nomination choice as a basis for blocking these investor services.

The circular also simplifies nomination-detail updates by requiring only three fields to be mandatorily provided when an investor updates nomination details. The document provided here does not list the three fields themselves, but the operational obligation is that only those three specified data points can be insisted upon as mandatory for nomination updates, reducing the documentation burden on investors and the compliance verification burden on market intermediaries. For a compliance team, the key action item is to align account-opening, nomination-update, and service-activation workflows with these relaxed rules so that accounts/folios are not inappropriately frozen and corporate benefits or physical-folio services are not withheld due to missing nomination-choice submission.

rows.title: Framework for providing flexibility to Foreign Portfolio Investors in dealing with their securities post expiry of their registration
rows.summary:
SEBI’s June 5, 2024 circular, titled “Framework for providing flexibility to Foreign Portfolio Investors in dealing with their securities post expiry of their registration,” introduces a post-expiry exit/transition framework for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) whose registration has lapsed. The document is aimed at giving FPIs flexibility to continue dealing with their securities for a limited period after registration expiry, rather than forcing an immediate and potentially disruptive liquidation or transfer process. In compliance terms, this means firms that are FPIs, their designated depository participants, custodians, and intermediaries servicing FPI accounts need to be prepared to apply the new post-expiry handling rules once an FPI’s registration term ends.

The key compliance point is that the circular creates a formal mechanism under which an FPI can deal with its securities after the expiry of its registration, subject to the conditions and procedures laid down by SEBI in the framework. The document does not, in the title-level information provided here, specify the detailed operational steps, time window, or any quantitative thresholds; however, the substance of the change is that expiry of registration no longer necessarily means an immediate halt to all securities-related activity. Compliance teams should therefore treat expired-registration cases as a regulated transition scenario requiring monitoring of registration status, controls around permitted dealing activity, and coordination with the relevant market intermediaries.

Because this is a SEBI circular, affected entities should verify whether their internal onboarding, renewal tracking, trade processing, and custody procedures need updating to reflect post-expiry permissions. The practical obligation is to ensure that any FPI whose registration has expired is handled strictly in accordance with the framework SEBI has prescribed, rather than under standard active-registration assumptions. rows.title: Disclosures of Material Changes and Other Obligations for Foreign Portfolio Investors
rows.summary:

The document indicates that FPIs have continuing disclosure obligations to report any “material changes,” meaning changes that could affect the accuracy or completeness of the information already provided to SEBI/DPs in connection with FPI registration or eligibility. In practical terms, a compliance team should treat this as a reminder that FPI-related records cannot remain static after onboarding; if there is any significant change in ownership, control, constitution, regulatory status, structure, or any other information relied on for registration/eligibility, it must be identified and reported promptly through the prescribed channel.

It requires covered intermediaries in the securities market to maintain systems for customer identification, client due diligence, recordkeeping, monitoring of transactions, and reporting of suspicious activity in order to detect and prevent money laundering and terrorist financing risks. The circular applies to securities market intermediaries subject to PMLA obligations, so firms dealing in securities or broking-related activities should treat it as directly relevant to their onboarding, surveillance, and compliance controls.

A compliance team should note that the circular is framed as “guidelines” on AML standards and CFT obligations, meaning the key operational requirement is to implement risk-based procedures that can identify customers, verify identities, understand the nature of the business relationship, and monitor transactions for unusual or suspicious patterns. It also indicates that intermediaries must preserve the relevant records and be able to furnish them as required under the PMLA framework. In practice, this means procedures for client acceptance, ongoing due diligence, escalation of suspicious indicators, and reporting workflows need to be in place and aligned with the statutory rules.

rows.title: Master Circular for Stock Exchange - Cash Market
rows.summary:
This document is SEBI’s **Master Circular for Stock Exchanges on the Trading Part (Part I)**, which is a compilation of all then-applicable circulars issued by SEBI’s Market Regulation Department **up to March 31, 2010**. It applies to **stock exchanges** and came into force **from the date of its issue**; for a compliance team, the key point is that it consolidates prior operative requirements rather than creating a single new standalone rule, so exchanges and connected market participants must treat the circular as the current reference point for the covered topics.

Substantively, the circular organizes the cash-market trading framework into several compliance areas that exchanges must implement and supervise: **bulk deals and block deals**, **index-based market-wide circuit filters and scrip-wise price bands**, and **uniform security-specific action across stock exchanges**. It also contains detailed requirements for **margin trading**, including which securities are eligible, the conditions brokers must satisfy to offer the facility, the need for **no-objection certificates**, required client agreements, funding sources and **maximum borrowing limits for brokers**, prescribed **margin requirements**, and the process for **liquidating securities if a client defaults**. The circular further requires brokers to maintain records, disclose exposure to margin trading, provide for arbitration, and handle the use of the **Investor Protection Fund** and **Trade/Settlement Guarantee Fund** in the manner specified.

The document also sets out a separate framework for **market makers**, including the criteria for selecting scrips for market making, whether market makers have exclusivity, how many market makers may be appointed per share, the qualifications for registration, and the specific obligations and rights of a market maker. It addresses **voluntary and compulsory de-registration**, information dissemination requirements, the number of shares each market maker must support, and risk-containment/monitoring measures. In addition, it includes provisions for **negotiated deals** and **odd-lot trading and settlement** in dematerialised securities, indicating that exchanges must ensure these transaction types are handled under the prescribed special procedures rather than under ordinary continuous trading rules.

For compliance purposes, the document should be read as an exchange-level operating manual covering the cash market trading infrastructure: exchanges must ensure their rules, surveillance, settlement processes, broker onboarding, disclosure controls, and risk-management arrangements align with the circular’s requirements, and because it is a master circular, it is intended to capture and supersede the scattered prior circulars on these topics as of its cutoff date.

It also sets out the framework for arbitration in recognised stock exchanges, meaning disputes arising within the exchange ecosystem must be handled through the prescribed exchange arbitration mechanism rather than ad hoc arrangements.

Because this is a “Master Circular,” it is intended to bring together and operationalize existing SEBI directions on these subjects as of the date of issue, so compliance should focus on ensuring that internal exchange policies, subsidiary oversight, governance structures, and dispute-resolution procedures align with the circular’s consolidated requirements. rows.title: Master Circular on Anti Money Laundering and Combating Financing of Terrorism (AML and CFT) Standards-PDF
rows.summary:
This SEBI master circular, issued on 19 December 2008, consolidates all anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) requirements applicable to SEBI-registered intermediaries up to 15 December 2008. It applies to all intermediaries registered under section 12 of the SEBI Act, 1992—specifically including stock brokers, sub-brokers, share transfer agents, bankers to an issue, trustees to a trust deed, registrars to an issue, merchant bankers, underwriters, portfolio managers, investment advisers, depository participants, and other securities-market intermediaries—and, to the extent local law permits, to their foreign branches and subsidiaries, especially those in jurisdictions that do not or insufficiently apply FATF recommendations. Where host-country law conflicts with SEBI’s standards, the foreign branch/subsidiary must apply the stricter of the two regimes; if local law prevents implementation, that fact must be reported to SEBI.

The circular restates the core transaction-reporting obligations under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), which came into force on 1 July 2005. Intermediaries must maintain records of: all cash transactions above Rs. 10 lakhs (or equivalent in foreign currency); all series of cash transactions that are individually below Rs. 10 lakhs but are integrally connected and occur within one calendar month; and all suspicious transactions, whether or not they involve cash. The document also confirms that the earlier SEBI AML guidelines from 18 January 2006 and the detailed procedure/reporting circular from 20 March 2006 remain the framework being consolidated here.

The circular requires intermediaries to maintain a proper AML policy framework tailored to their business and to put in place client disclosures beyond the minimum where needed to address money laundering and suspicious-transaction risks. Each intermediary must designate a “Principal Officer” responsible for ensuring compliance with PMLA obligations, and the name, designation, and full address including email address of that officer must be communicated immediately to the Director, FIU, at the specified New Delhi address. The circular is issued under SEBI’s powers under section 11(1) of the SEBI Act and Rule 7 of the PMLA record-keeping rules, so it is not merely advisory: it is intended to impose enforceable compliance obligations on securities-market intermediaries.

rows.title: Request for informal guidance by way of an interpretative letter on applicability of Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 by Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited
rows.desc: Page 1 of 5 GENERAL MANAGER DEPARTMENT OF DEBT AND HYBRID SECURITIES POLICY AND DEVELOPMENT – 1 SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS-RACPOD1/P/OW/2025/0000025190/1 September 23, 2025 To, Ms. Rashmi Jain, Company Secretary and Compliance Officer, Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited, E Block, Valtas Premises, TB Kadam Marg, Chichpokli, Mumbai-400 033 Ma’am, Subject: Request for informal guidance by way of an interpretative letter on applicability of Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 by Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited 1. This has reference to your letter dated June 09, 2025, seeking an interpretative letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003. 2. Vide the said letter it has been inter-alia stated that Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited is a public limited company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Sons Private Limited, having only Non-Convertible debentures (‘NCDs’) listed on BSE; with no other listed specified securities. Further, based on your audited financial statements, the value of outstanding listed NCDs as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores. Page 2 of 5 3. In view of the above, you have sought an interpretive letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 from SEBI on the following: 3.1. Query 1: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the Company were Rs.535 Crores. Hence, would the company be classified as a HVDLE w.e.f April 01, 2025? 3.2. Query 2: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the company were Rs.535 crores. Hence, would the company be under statutory obligations to comply with Regulation 3(3) of SEBI Listing Regulations which mandates the company to comply with the provision of Chapter IV of the SEBI Listing Regulations or considering that regulation 15(1A) restricts its applicability to only listed entities which have listed its non-convertible debt securities and has an outstanding value of listed non-convertible debt securities of Rupees One Thousand Crore and above, the same is not applicable to the Company. 3.3. Query 3: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the Company were Rs.535 Crores. Hence, would the Company be under statutory obligations to comply with the provisions of Chapter VA of SEBI Listing Regulations? The company has not listed any new debt securities on or after April 01, 2025. If the company is classified as HVDLE, obtaining prior No Objection Certificate from the Debenture Trustee will not be applicable. However, does the company require to obtain prior approval of shareholders for its Material Related Party Transactions or subsequent modification? In light of the current scenario, where the company remain a wholly owned subsidiary, how can the necessary approval be obtained considering that all shareholders are related parties? Page 3 of 5 4. Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered. Without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our response on the queries raised in your communications, are as under: 4.1. In regards to query 1, the following is informed: Since the outstanding value of listed NCDs of the applicant as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores, which is less than the specified threshold of Rs.1000 crore, as specified under Regulations 15(1A) and 62C(1) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI (LODR) Regulations”), the applicant is not classified as HVDLE on March 31, 2025, under Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations. However, in case the value of the outstanding listed NCDs becomes equal to or greater than the specified threshold of Rs.1000 crores during the financial year, it shall ensure compliance with the relevant provisions within six months from the date of such trigger. 4.2. In regards to query 2, the following is informed: i. In terms of the amendment notification dated March 28, 2025, Chapter VA has been inserted in the SEBI (LODR) Regulations for entities that has listed only NCDs, with an outstanding value of Rs. 1000 Crore and above and does not have any listed specified securities. Such ‘high value debt listed entities’ shall be determined on the basis of value of principal outstanding of listed debt securities as on March 31, 2025. Accordingly, Chapter IV of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations is not applicable to the applicant. ii. rows.title: Informal Guidance request received from Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited  in relation to provisions for extension of the tenure of the close ended AIFs under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012
rows.desc: Page 1 of 4 DEPUTY GENERAL MANAGER ALTERNATIVE INVESTMENT FUND AND FOREIGN PORTFOLIO INVESTOR DEPARTMENT DIVISION OF POLICY AND DEVELOPMENT AFD/PoD/OW/2025/18380 July 09, 2025 Shri. K. Rajagopal Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited, Sundaram Towers, 1 st and 2 nd floor 46, Whites Road, Royapettah, Chennai, 600014 Dear Sir, Sub: Request for Informal Guidance by way of interpretive letter under the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 in connection with the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 (“AIF Regulations”) Ref: Your letter dated April 23, 2025 1. In the context of your letter under reference, you have, inter alia, stated that Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited (‘the Applicant’) is a SEBI registered Portfolio Manager bearing registration no. INP000006271 and also the Investment Manager for Sundaram Alternative Investment Trust, a Category III Alternative Investment Fund (“AIF”) having registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291 and Sundaram Category II AIF having registration no. IN/AIF2/17- 18/0340, and have sought an interpretive letter under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 (“Informal Guidance Scheme”) from SEBI in respect of the following query – i. Please clarify whether during the extended period, the close-ended Alternative Investment Fund is permitted only to liquidate its existing portfolio investments or allowed to make investments in portfolio companies. Page 2 of 4 2. Our Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the issues raised in your letter are as under: 2.1. In terms of Regulation 13(5) of AIF Regulations, extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund: Provided that a large value fund for accredited investors may be permitted to extend its tenure up to five years subject to the approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the large value fund for accredited investors: Provided further that the extension in tenure of any existing scheme of a large value fund for accredited investors shall be subject to such conditions as may be specified by the Board from time to time. 2.2. In terms of Regulation 13 (6), in the absence of consent of unit holders under Regulation 13 (5) or upon expiry of the extended tenure, the Alternative Investment Fund or the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall be wound up in accordance with Regulation 29 of these regulations. 2.3. Under the section ‘Winding up’, Regulations 29 (7), 29 (10), and 29B (4) of the AIF Regulations, prescribe the following: Regulation 29 (7) Within the liquidation period, the assets shall be liquidated, and the proceeds accruing to investors in the Alternative Investment Fund or the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall be distributed to them after satisfying all liabilities. [As Per Regulation 2 (pb) of SEBI AIF Regulations 2012, “liquidation period” means a period of one year following the expiry of tenure or extended tenure of the scheme of an Alternative Investment Fund.] Regulation 29 (10) Page 3 of 4 If the scheme of an Alternative Investment Fund enters into a dissolution period as provided under regulation 29B and the unliquidated investments of the scheme are not sold by the expiry of the dissolution period, such investments shall be mandatorily distributed in-specie to the investors, in the manner as may be specified by the Board. [As per Regulation 2 (ia) of SEBI AIF Regulations 2012, “dissolution period” means the period following the expiry of the liquidation period of the scheme for the purpose of liquidating the unliquidated investments of the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund. Regulation 29B (4) The scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall not accept any fresh commitment from any investor and shall not make any new investment during the dissolution period. 2.4. In view of the aforesaid provisions under Regulation 29 providing for winding up of a scheme, it is construed that the AIF shall take steps to close down the existing investments, and shall distribute the proceeds to the investors or distribute the investment in-specie to the investors, as the case may be. The liquidation period and dissolution period form part of winding up of the scheme of an AIF. Thus, AIFs / Scheme of an AIF cannot make any fresh investments during liquidation period and dissolution period. 2.5. Further, AIF Regulations do not expressly prohibit an AIF from making investments in the extended tenure. As per Regulation 13 (6), the winding of a scheme is triggered upon the expiry of extended tenure. Therefore, the extended period is not part of the winding-up of the scheme of an
rows.summary: SEBI received a request to clarify whether extended-term close-ended AIFs may only wind down existing holdings or also make new investments.

rows.title: Informal guidance application received from InfoBeans Technologies Limited seeking interpretation of Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: Page 1 of 5 Deputy General Manager Corporation Finance Department Policy and Development – 2 rajkd@sebi.gov.in 022-26449253 No.: SEBI/HO/CFD/PoD2/OW/P/2025/13133/1 May 14, 2025 To InfoBeans Technologies Limited SEZ Unit, Crystal IT Park, STP-1, 2 nd Floor, Ring Road, Indore, Madhya Pradesh - 452001. Madam, Kind attention: Ms. Surbhi Jain, Company Secretary and Compliance Officer Sub: Request for Informal guidance by way of an interpretive letter under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 received from InfoBeans Technologies Limited (“Company”) seeking interpretation of the provisions of regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 1. This is with reference to your letter dated February 25, 2025 read with clarification dated March 21, 2025 (“Application”) seeking interpretative letter under SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme 2003 in respect of the term “material pecuniary relationship” used in regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“LODR Regulations”) in the context of an Independent Director. 2. The following information is gathered from your Application: a. InfoBeans Technologies Limited (“Company” / “Applicant”) is an entity having its registered office at Indore, Madhya Pradesh. The shares of the Company are listed on National Stock Exchange of India Limited and BSE Limited. Page 2 of 5 b. The Company has appointed an Independent Director and pays sitting fees/commission as per the permissible limit under the Companies Act. Subsequently, the Company intends to engage the same individual (Ms. Opal Perry) as a consultant to its US-based subsidiary, InfoBeans INC. As a consultant, the individual will receive compensation from InfoBeans INC for services rendered. c. Ms. Opal’s responsibilities in the US subsidiary will be advisory in nature, focusing on strategic guidance, risk management, and business development. She will not have executive authority or direct involvement in the day-to-day operations. d. The aggregate consultancy fees payable to the Independent Director, excluding sitting fees/commission, will not exceed 10% of the director's total annual income. e. The US subsidiary's company structure does not formally define designation as “Independent Director”. Despite this, you have stated that you will ensure compliance with the Companies Act limits regarding her pecuniary relationship and total income. f. In this background, you have requested for clarification on the expression “material pecuniary relationship” mentioned in Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the LODR Regulations in the context of an Independent Director. 3. In view of the above facts and circumstances, you have sought confirmation that the appointment of Ms. Opal in the US subsidiary, as described above, and the proposed consultancy arrangement with InfoBeans INC, would not conflict with SEBI’s regulatory framework concerning Independent Directors under the LODR Regulations. 4. With respect to your query, we have considered the submissions made by you in your Application and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the queries are given below: Page 3 of 5 4.1. The term “independent director” has been defined under Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the LODR Regulations inter-alia as a non-executive director who does not have any material pecuniary relationship with the listed entity and its related entities. The provision is reproduced for reference as under- “Definitions. 16. (1) For the purpose of this chapter, unless the context otherwise requires – (a)... (b) “independent director" means a non-executive director, other than a nominee director of the listed entity: (i)... (ii).... (iii).... (iv) who, apart from receiving director's remuneration, has or had no material pecuniary relationship with the listed entity, its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or their promoters, or directors, during the three immediately preceding financial years or during the current financial year;” It may be noted that no quantitative limits have been specified in the regulations for determining whether a pecuniary relationship between an independent director and listed entity, its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or their promoters, or directors is ‘material’ or not. 4.2. However, regulation 16(1)(b) specifies various parameters to determine the independence of a director. For example, such director should not be a promoter of the listed entity or its holdings or subsidiary or associate companies and not be related to such promoter, shall not hold the position of key managerial personnel in such entities, shall not be a non-independent director of another company on the board of which any non-independent director of the listed entity is an independent director, shall neither himself nor his relatives be a material supplie
rows.summary: SEBI received InfoBeans’ request for an interpretive ruling on whether a proposed independent director has a “material pecuniary relationship” under LODR rules.

This consultation paper proposes adding two **optional** faster-settlement alternatives in Indian securities markets — **optional T+0 settlement** and **optional instant settlement** — while keeping the existing **T+1 settlement cycle** in place. The paper is framed as a request for public comments and is not itself a final rule, but it signals a potential change in market infrastructure and post-trade operations for participants in Indian securities markets.

For a compliance team, the key point is that the proposal would create a settlement framework with **multiple settlement choices** rather than a single mandatory cycle. Under the proposed structure, trades could continue to settle on **T+1** as the standard, but market participants may also be offered the ability to settle on the **same day (T+0)** or **immediately after execution (instant settlement)**, depending on the final design and operational eligibility criteria to be set later. This would have implications for trading, clearing, funding, custody, risk controls, internal cut-offs, client disclosures, operational readiness, and reconciliation processes, because firms would need to be able to process and meet obligations on a much shorter timeline for any trades executed under the optional accelerated modes.

The document title provided does not include the detailed implementation mechanics, thresholds, dates, or specific eligibility rules, so no final effective date, phase-in schedule, numerical limits, or entity-specific compliance obligations can be confirmed from the excerpt alone. What is clear is that the consultation is aimed at **Indian securities market participants** and is intended to gather views before any formal introduction of these optional settlement modes. A compliance team should therefore treat this as an early-stage policy proposal that could require significant operational and legal review if adopted, especially around whether the firm’s systems, contractual terms, client onboarding, and settlement funding arrangements can support optional same-day or instant settlement.

rows.title: Consultation Paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting norms under SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021  Addendum- Executive Summary
rows.summary:
This SEBI addendum is not itself a final rule change, but an executive summary of a consultation paper issued on 14 August 2023 proposing revisions to the voluntary delisting framework under the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021. For compliance teams, the key proposed change is to the counter-offer trigger in reverse book building (RBB): under current regulations, a counter-offer is allowed only if the acquirer’s existing shareholding plus shares tendered by public shareholders reaches at least 90% of paid-up capital; the proposal would lower that trigger so a counter-offer could be made when the cumulative holding/tendered shares are below 90% but at or above 75% of paid-up capital. If that counter-offer route is used after the 90% threshold is not reached, the proposed floor price for the counter-offer would be the volume-weighted average price of the shares tendered by willing shareholders in the delisting offer.

The consultation paper also proposes to expand the floor-price methodology by adding “Adjusted Book Value” as an additional factor, and it states this would apply to both frequently traded and infrequently traded shares. Another major proposal is to allow delisting at a fixed price as an alternative to the current RBB-only exit-price discovery mechanism, but only for companies whose shares are frequently traded. In parallel, the reference date for calculating the floor price would move from the date of board approval to the date of the initial public announcement; for delisting of a subsidiary’s equity shares under a scheme of arrangement under Regulation 37, the reference date would instead be the date prior intimation is given to the stock exchanges.

The paper also proposes a special delisting framework for investment holding companies (IHCs) through a scheme of arrangement involving selective capital reduction under Section 66 of the Companies Act. Under this mechanism, underlying shares that the IHC holds in other listed companies would be transferred to public shareholders in proportion to their holdings in the IHC, while public shareholders would receive cash for the IHC’s investments in unlisted companies and other assets. This alternative to RBB would be available only to listed IHCs in which at least 75% of total value consists of investments in other listed companies. As this is only an executive summary, the document does not set final operative deadlines or implementation dates beyond the consultation-paper publication date; firms should treat these as proposed changes pending SEBI’s finalization.

This would likely increase ongoing disclosure, listing-compliance, and exchange-reporting obligations for listed companies accessing the debt market, and compliance teams should assess whether current issuance structures, timelines, and trustee/listing coordination processes would need to be updated.

rows.title: Bharat Ka Share Bazaar @ INDIA INTERNATIONAL TRADE FAIR – 2025
rows.desc: @ INDIA INTERNATIONAL TRADE FAIR – 2025 The ‘India International Trade Fair’ (IITF) is one of the largest trade fairs in the world, will be held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi from November 14 to 27, 2025. This year’s theme, ‘Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat’, highlights India’s cultural diversity and development. The IITF is a platform that has been used by various Regulators in the financial sector and other State and Government Institutions to spread awareness about their policies and programs among the public. In order to spread awareness, SEBI along with other securities market institutions has been setting up pavilion “ ” for last 10 years. Considering the huge success of previous years’ events, SEBI along with BSE, NSE, MCX, NCDEX, AMFI, CDSL, NSDL, NISM, CAMS and Kfintech has taken part in the 44 th IITF 2025, at Hall No-3, Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Join us at IITF 2025! Visit SEBI Pavilion “ ” –  Participate in our daily quiz, test your Knowledge and win exciting prizes.  Protect yourself from cyber investment fraud related to securities market through our initiatives like “SEBI Check”, Document Identification Verification System, etc.  Learn about securities market and get insights from the experts.  Experiential learning through “ (Securities transaction Simulation)”  On the spot KYC updation, nomination updation and other investor related services at our Investor Assistance Centre.  Update yourself about various cyber investment frauds related to securities market and their prevention through interactive activities i.e. “Nukkad Natak”, “Muppet shows” etc. Don’t miss this opportunity towards Investor education and awareness. Open to all! Block your Dates!
rows.summary: SEBI and market institutions will use IITF 2025 to educate the public on securities investing, investor services, and fraud prevention.

rows.title: MITRA - Gateway to unclaimed Mutual Funds
rows.desc: Convenience Zero Hassles Zero Hassles We value your time as much as you do! Submit your service requests with zero hassles with our seamless user experience Easy Access ONE to All ONE to All One service request is now enough to add, modify information across all your Mutual Fund folios Comprehensive All Mutual Funds All Mutual Funds MFCentral is a unified services gateway for all your mutual funds Safe Highly Secure Highly Secure MFCentral is a highly secure platform with multiple layers of protection & data encryption to perform your MF transactions Introducing India’s First All-in-one Investment Management Platform to Transform the Mutual Fund Industry MFCentral is the investor services hub conceived by KFintech & CAMS powering a new era of collaboration by providing convenience to transact across all folios of an investor with unparalleled user experience. Leveraging best in class technology, MFCentral brings ease, convenience and speed to your service requirements across all the Mutual Funds. View your Mutual Fund portfolio like a PRO! Now view your portfolio across all the Mutual Funds on a single platform! Slice and dice your assets based on asset class, fund house, returns, scheme level holdings and performance. View Now Managing your service requests can't get any SIMPLER! Out with paper, in with digital. Explore a range of services such as bank mandate change to updating your personal contact details to change in IDCW and more. Get the change done across all your folios with just a single request! Get Started Quick Links Easy access for seamless experience Update PAN Details Apply for PAN Transmission Request Transfer of units MITRA What’s New Positive Pay System (PPS) for cheques Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had announced introduction of Positive Pay System in Sept. 2020 to introduce an additional layer security for cheques above of Rs.50,000. Banks have indicated enforcement of PPS from 1st September 2021. Investors are advised to take note about PPS requirement for their MF Investment cheque(s) to avoid rejection during clearing process. Realization Based NAV (as per SEBI Circular SEBI/HO/IMD/DF2/CIR/P/2020/253) Effective 1st February 2021, closing NAV of the day when fund is available for utilization shall be applicable for purchase of mutual fund units (including for systematic transactions registered prior to 1st February 2021 also) irrespective of scheme category or investment amount. Dividend plan/option in now called Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal Plan (IDCW) As per SEBI communication dated October 05, 2020 on ‘Review of Dividend option(s) / Plan(s) in case of Mutual Fund Schemes’, Dividend Option /Plan of all existing and proposed schemes of Mutual Funds will be named / renamed and all schemes having Dividend Option / Plan will reflect as IDCW in all statements and transaction description. Entire expanse of Mutual Fund universe

rows.title: Depository Participants
rows.desc: Page 1 of 4 Rights and Obligations of Beneficial Owner and Depository Participant as prescribed by SEBI and Depositories General Clause 1. The Beneficial Owner and the Depository participant (DP) shall be bound by the provisions of the Depositories Act, 1996, SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996, Rules and Regulations of Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Circulars/Notifications/Guidelines issued there under, Bye Laws and Business Rules/Operating Instructions issued by the Depositories and relevant notifications of Government Authorities as may be in force from time to time. 2. The DP shall open/activate demat account of a beneficial owner in the depository system only after receipt of complete Account opening form, KYC and supporting documents as specified by SEBI from time to time. Beneficial Owner information 3. The DP shall maintain all the details of the beneficial owner(s) as mentioned in the account opening form, supporting documents submitted by them and/or any other information pertaining to the beneficial owner confidentially and shall not disclose the same to any person except as required by any statutory, legal or regulatory authority in this regard. 4. The Beneficial Owner shall immediately notify the DP in writing, if there is any change in details provided in the account opening form as submitted to the DP at the time of opening the demat account or furnished to the DP from time to time. Fees/Charges/Tariff 5. The Beneficial Owner shall pay such charges to the DP for the purpose of holding and transfer of securities in dematerialized form and for availing depository services as may be agreed to from time to time between the DP and the Beneficial Owner as set out in the Tariff Sheet provided by the DP. It may be informed to the Beneficial Owner that "no charges are payable for opening of demat accounts” 6. In case of Basic Services Demat Accounts, the DP shall adhere to the charge structure as laid down under the relevant SEBI and/or Depository circulars/directions/notifications issued from time to time. 7. The DP shall not increase any charges/tariff agreed upon unless it has given a notice in writing of not less than thirty days to the Beneficial Owner regarding the same. Dematerialization 8. The Beneficial Owner shall have the right to get the securities, which have been admitted on the Depositories, dematerialized in the form and manner laid down under the Bye Laws, Business Rules and Operating Instructions of the depositories. Separate Accounts Page 2 of 4 9. The DP shall open separate accounts in the name of each of the beneficial owners and securities of each beneficial owner shall be segregated and shall not be mixed up with the securities of other beneficial owners and/or DP’s own securities held in dematerialized form. 10. The DP shall not facilitate the Beneficial Owner to create or permit any pledge and /or hypothecation or any other interest or encumbrance over all or any of such securities submitted for dematerialization and/or held in demat account except in the form and manner prescribed in the Depositories Act, 1996, SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996 and Bye-Laws/Operating Instructions/Business Rules of the Depositories. Transfer of Securities 11. The DP shall effect transfer to and from the demat accounts of the Beneficial Owner only on the basis of an order, instruction, direction or mandate duly authorized by the Beneficial Owner and the DP shall maintain the original documents and the audit trail of such authorizations. 12. The Beneficial Owner reserves the right to give standing instructions with regard to the crediting of securities in his demat account and the DP shall act according to such instructions. Statement of account 13. The DP shall provide statements of accounts to the beneficial owner in such form and manner and at such time as agreed with the Beneficial Owner and as specified by SEBI/depository in this regard. 14. However, if there is no transaction in the demat account, or if the balance has become Nil during the year, the DP shall send one physical statement of holding annually to such BOs and shall resume sending the transaction statement as and when there is a transaction in the account. 15. The DP may provide the services of issuing the statement of demat accounts in an electronic mode if the Beneficial Owner so desires. The DP will furnish to the Beneficial Owner the statement of demat accounts under its digital signature, as governed under the Information Technology Act, 2000. However if the DP does not have the facility of providing the statement of demat account in the electronic mode, then the Participant shall be obliged to forward the statement of demat accounts in physical form. 16. In case of Basic Services Demat Accounts, the DP shall send the transaction statements as mandated by SEBI and/or Depository from time to time. Manner of Closure of Demat account 17. rows.title: Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI)
rows.desc: Proposal No Comment Rationale Level of Agreement Rationale for rejection 2 Identification of SWAGT-FIs – requirement for validation of SWAGAT-FI status for existing FPIs will increase burden on investors and lead to operational inconvenience. Request to relook at the proposal regarding providing proof. FPIs will need to prove diversification, independen ce of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind pool, absen ce of segregated portfolios, which are burdensome and wil l increase paperwork. Existing subcategory framework should be applied instead of the FPIs having to pro vide additional documents to meet the specified criteria . Disagree To reduce operational burden, the verification requirements shall be on similar lines to the existing exemption criteria under Additional Disclosure Framework, which has already been implemented by the industry. 4 No the periodicity of re-KYC should be maintained as at present. The periodicity of payment is also to be maintained as is currently practiced. The need to do a re-KYC is to be maintained for FPI s similar to other types of investors. Any material change e. g. UBO, if not reported on time will be found while conduct ing the re- KYC. The payment of yearly fees should be maintained as at the current periodicity or manner of payment. The propo sal to get payments at say a period of every 10 years woul d restrict the ability of SEBI to increase or decrease the yea rly fees. In view of retaining flexibility of being able to m anage the yearly fees far more easily it is suggested that th e current system is to be maintained. Disagree Requirements regarding material change shall continue. Proposal for removal of additional re-KYC requirement was made on the basis of a risk vs convenience assessment. There is no yearly fee requirement even today. Only the block period for fee is being increased from 3 years to 10 years, to coincide with the re-KYC requirement. 6 Many commenters were of the opinion to not facilitate single demat account for different modes of foreign investment. Foreign investors generally rely on custodian repor ts rather than depository statements for tracking and reconci ling their holdings. While consolidated custodian reports can be used for an overall view, FPI and FVCI holdings must be distinctly identifiable as required by RBI NDI Rules. A single demat account combining both routes prevent issuers and regulators from distinguishing between FPI and FVCI investments, leading to monitoring and compliance challenges. Recording unlisted FVCI investments in an FPI- tagged account would also create regulatory and rep orting issues. Maintaining separate demat accounts ensures accurate record-keeping, prevents co-mingling of se curities, facilitates data retrieval, and preserves confident iality— whereas a single account complicates segregation, s lows data collection, and increases compliance risks. Disagree Single demat account is proposed on optional basis, so investors can choose as per their convenience. Requisite clarification on operational matters shall be provided under the respective notification or Standard Operating Procedure to be issued for implementation of SWAGAT-FI framework.
rows.summary: SEBI is keeping FPI re-KYC and fee payments as-is, while easing verification rules to reduce paperwork and investor burden.

rows.title:
The Information Technology Department (ITD) of SEBI is the enabler of technology landscape in the organisation. ITD is committed to its vision of leveraging technology in partnership with every department of SEBI to achieve the following goals: 
1.	Development and implementation of Enterprise wide solutions like Portals and gateways, Network Infrastructure, Private Cloud Infrastructure, Mail and messaging solution, Data lake, Document Management system, SAP Solution etc. 
2.	Facilitating Ease of doing Business for market intermediaries by enhancing the digital interfaces between them and SEBI in respect of a large range of functions such as Regulations, Compliance and Reporting. 
3.	Developing Data Warehouse system for surveillance, inspections and supervision activities. 
4.	Driving data analytics practice at SEBI. 
5.	Ensuring deployment of strong cyber security measures and information technology (IT) resilience in the market Infrastructure to facilitate uninterrupted trading and privacy of investor data. 
6.	Undertaking IT inspections and audit for MIIs and intermediaries. 
7.	Development of framework for information interchange with various government agencies. 
8.	Facilitating innovation in markets through SEBI’s Innovation Sandbox Framework.

The Office will support SEBI operations by acting as the single point of contact for investors, receiving investor complaints centrally rather than through separate departmental channels, and forwarding each complaint to the relevant department for handling. It will also serve as the focal point for SEBI’s investor education efforts, meaning it will coordinate or lead outreach and education activities intended to inform and assist investors.

From a compliance perspective, the practical change is the creation of a centralized intake and routing mechanism for complaints, which should improve consistency in complaint capture and internal escalation. Any SEBI department receiving matters that fall within this Office’s remit would need to coordinate with it, since the Office is positioned as the main interface with investors. No specific effective date, filing deadline, numerical threshold, or rate is stated in the title, and the provided content does not include any detailed procedural requirements beyond central receipt and forwarding of complaints.

rows.title: Settlement Application
rows.summary:
This document is the online **SEBI Settlement Application** form and its filing instructions, and the key compliance requirement is that once the applicant successfully pays the **non-refundable settlement application fee online**, the applicant must **physically submit the settlement application together with all required documents, including proof of payment, to the SEBI Settlement Division within 7 calendar days** from the date of successful payment. The form specifically directs applicants to review the **SEBI Circular dated June 18, 2019** before filing, and it is designed for multiple settlement pathways, including **Summary Settlement (SS), Suo Motu (SM), Pre-SCN, Post-SCN, Post-Appeal, Post-SAT Order, and Settlement with Confidentiality (SC)**. The application requires the applicant to identify the relevant proceeding by entering items such as the **Show Cause Notice number/date, Summary Settlement Notice number/date, SAT Appeal number, and Appeal number**, depending on the application type.

For the applicant details section, the form requires entry of the **name, PAN, applicant type (Individual or Body Corporate), and proposed settlement amount**, and it expressly states that the **settlement amount cannot be less than Rs. 3 lakhs** under the Settlement Regulations. The applicant must upload **certified true copies** of supporting tax and identity documents, including **ITRs for the last 3 financial years** in PDF format up to **20 MB** and a **PAN card copy** in PDF format up to **500 KB**. It also requires correspondence details such as **GST number, state/territory, phone number (must be 10 digits), primary email address, and alternate email addresses**; the form notes that the **primary email address will be used for all communications** with the entity.

The attachments section requires certified true copies of the principal case documents, including **Form-A**, the **Summary Settlement Notice**, the **Show Cause Notice**, the **SAT Appeal**, **any orders passed**, and **any other relevant document**, with each upload limited to **PDF files up to 20 MB**. The form also includes fields for **Settlement Application UID**, **Type of Category**, and fee/payment fields such as **Application Fees (in Rs.), CGST, SGST, IGST, and Payment Status**, indicating that tax components are calculated or recorded as part of the filing process. In practical compliance terms, this means the filing is not complete upon payment alone: the applicant must ensure the online submission is followed promptly by the hard-copy package, all prescribed documents are included, the minimum settlement amount threshold is met, and the required identifiers and jurisdiction/contact details are accurately provided to avoid rejection or processing delays.

rows.title: Settlement Calculator BETA
rows.summary:
This document is a “Settlement Calculator BETA” intended to help applicants estimate an indicative settlement amount under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Settlement Proceedings Regulations, 2018, using the computation matrix in Schedule II and the factors in Regulation 10. It makes clear that the calculator is only advisory: the final settlement amount can be modified by the Internal Committee (IC), the High Powered Advisory Committee (HPAC), or the Panel of Whole Time Members (WTMs), and in some cases non-monetary settlement terms may also be imposed under Regulation 9. The settlement amount is made up of the indicative amount (IA), and the IA must not be less than ₹3 lakh for a first-time applicant or ₹7 lakh for any other applicant; a “first-time applicant” is defined as someone against whom no order has ever been passed by SEBI’s adjudicating officer or Board and who has never obtained a settlement order from SEBI as of the date of the current application.

The document requires the IA to be calculated using a proceeding conversion factor (PCF) based on the stage of the case when the application is made, and the IA is computed per count of default, either jointly or separately depending on the facts. If a person’s business has been corporatized, converted into an LLP or partnership, or merged/taken over by new management, the record of the old entity is treated as the record of the new entity; related issues such as insolvency, name changes, or changes in management/ownership are to be handled according to any SEBI guidance issued from time to time. For voluntary applications or applications seeking confidentiality, an entity can obtain a lower PCF only if, before receiving any show-cause notice, it itself informs SEBI of the default (“intimation defaults”) and cooperates in any investigation, inquiry, inspection, or audit; in that case the application is treated as if made “pre-issue of notice to show cause” for PCF purposes.

The calculator and settlement process rely on the alleged defaults described in the relevant inspection report, investigation report, report of the designated authority, show-cause notice, supplementary show-cause notice, or in the findings/order of a Designated Member, Whole Time Member, Adjudicating Officer, or Securities Appellate Tribunal, as applicable. However, the IC/HPAC/WTM panel may conclude that the facts show a different default and may seek modification of the charge(s), and it can also re-categorize alleged defaults based on the facts and circumstances. The document also gives these bodies broad discretion to accept or reject an application and to recommend a settlement amount either lower or higher than the amount produced by the calculator, but they must record reasons and act consistently with securities law and the gravity of the charges.

For body corporates, the IC/HPAC/WTM panel may require the settlement amount to be paid by officers in default, including persons in charge, so that the burden is not placed on investors holding the issuer’s securities. The same principle may be applied, mutatis mutandis, to the sponsor, manager, or trustee of a trust, the karta of a Hindu Undivided Family, and office bearers of an association of persons. Finally, if the formulae in the schedule cannot be applied or adapted because of the peculiar nature of the default or because the default is not covered by the tables in the calculator, the settlement authority has discretion to deal with the matter outside the standard formula framework.

rows.title: Adjudication Order in the matter of Fast Track Finsec Private Limited
rows.summary:
SEBI conducted an inspection of Fast Track Finsec Private Limited, a SEBI-registered merchant banker since April 5, 2018 (registration no. INM000012500), covering the period April 1, 2020 to December 31, 2021, to test compliance with the Merchant Bankers Regulations, CAPSM Regulations, SAST Regulations, ICDR Regulations, and related SEBI circulars. Based on prima facie findings, SEBI initiated adjudication on July 22, 2024 and appointed an Adjudicating Officer on March 18, 2025 under Sections 15-I, 15A(a), and 15HB of the SEBI Act and the SEBI Adjudication Rules. The show-cause notice dated April 21, 2025 alleged violations across ten areas: irregularities in the IPO of Trekkingtoes.com Limited; irregularities in five open offers/takeovers involving KD Leisures Limited, AKM Lace and Embrotex Limited, Spaceage Products Limited, Specular Marketing and Finance Limited, and Oracle Credit Limited; irregularities in periodic reports; failure to disclose track record on the company’s website; non-compliance with merchant banker certification requirements; and deficiencies in the internal code of conduct.

In its reply dated May 3, 2025, the noticee said it had already given a detailed response in a prior letter dated May 10, 2022 and asked that it be treated as reiterated. It also argued that penalties had already been imposed in related matters under Adjudicating Order No. Order/MC/RM/2021-22/14794 dated January 27, 2022 (penalty of INR 2,00,000, paid on January 28, 2022) and Order No. Order/SM/DD/2021-22/15644 dated March 28, 2022 (penalty of INR 6,00,000, paid on June 17, 2022). The noticee further pointed to an interim order dated January 24, 2022 restraining it from taking up any new merchant banking assignment in the securities market until further orders, stating that it had already remained under restraint for one year and implying that additional punishment would be duplicative. The document excerpt provided does not include SEBI’s final adjudication findings or the ultimate penalty outcome, so the key compliance point from the excerpt is that SEBI treated these matters as potentially serious violations of merchant banker, disclosure, certification, reporting, and internal-control obligations during the inspection period.

rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/251 A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 20 September 02, 2026 To All Authorised Dealer Category-I banks Madam / Sir Deposits and Accounts – Accounts of Non-resident banks Please refer to Para B.2(ii) and B.8(i) of Part B of the A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No.92, dated April 4, 2003, in terms of which AD banks were required to: a.
