For a compliance team, the key point is that these are not general principles only: they create enforceable requirements around lending governance, exposure limits, documentation, security creation, reporting, and related-party controls.

A major compliance obligation introduced in the opening provisions is that LABs must align lending and credit administration with RBI-defined terms and the scope of the directions; the document expressly applies to **Local Area Banks only**. The definitions section is important because it sets the regulatory meaning of products and exposures that will be used throughout the directions, including **bank guarantee**, **bills purchased and discounted**, and **cash credit (CC)**. In particular, a **cash credit facility** is defined as a running account backed by hypothecation/pledge of goods, book debts, standing crops, etc., with **drawing power (DP)** periodically fixed based on eligible current assets and the outstanding amount repayable on demand; this definition signals that CC account management and DP discipline are part of the regulated credit-risk framework.

The document also introduces governance architecture for credit decisions, including a **“Committee on lending to related parties”** as a Board-level committee entrusted with sanctioning loans to related parties. That means LABs must ensure related-party lending is not handled informally at management level but through the specified Board governance process. More broadly, the table of contents shows that the directions cover **Board-approved policies**, **credit risk evaluation**, **statutory and regulatory restrictions**, **unhedged foreign currency exposure (UFCE)**, **Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) requirements for borrowers**, **valuation of properties and empanelment of valuers**, **filing of security interests with CERSAI** for immovable, movable, and intangible assets, and **maintenance of cash credit/current/overdraft accounts**—so compliance is not limited to underwriting, but extends into post-sanction monitoring, collateral perfection, borrower identification, and account operation.

Because the text provided is only the introductory and preliminary portion of the full directions, it does **not yet state the numeric exposure limits, thresholds, or detailed filing deadlines** that may appear in the later chapters. However, it clearly establishes that LABs must treat credit risk management as a formal regulatory compliance function, with mandatory policy approval by the Board and adherence to RBI-prescribed restrictions across lending products and borrower categories. If you want, I can also turn this into a **chapter-by-chapter compliance checklist** once you provide the remaining text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
These Directions, issued under section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005, create the RBI’s dedicated framework for **Local Area Banks (LABs)** on **credit information reporting, dissemination, customer access, and grievance redressal**. They take effect **immediately** on issuance (unless a specific provision states otherwise), and the document is the **2025 Directions, updated as on July 1, 2026**. The core compliance objective is to standardize how LABs report borrower credit data to Credit Information Companies (CICs), protect the confidentiality and security of that data, and ensure consumers can obtain corrections and redress where credit-reporting errors occur.

For a compliance team, the main operational requirement is that LABs must become and remain compliant CIC members and must **report credit information in the prescribed formats and timelines**, keep the data **updated**, and follow RBI-prescribed guidelines for accuracy, rectification of rejected submissions, and monitoring of the **Data Quality Index (DQI)**. The Directions also require banks to use credit information reports in credit appraisal in the manner prescribed, and to follow the rules on **displaying credit information** and on **correction of credit information reports** when errors are identified. In addition, the Directions expressly extend to customer-service and grievance-handling obligations, including a framework for **compensation to customers** in appropriate cases and the applicability of the **Reserve Bank-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021** where relevant.

The document is structured to also address governance and implementation: it provides for a **Technical Working Group**, sets out **best practices**, and clarifies the effect of **repeal and savings**, interaction with other laws, and interpretive principles. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed operational clauses, the compliance implication is that affected Local Area Banks must align internal systems, vendor/process controls, customer-facing procedures, and escalation mechanisms to the RBI’s specified reporting standards and remediation requirements. If your institution is a Local Area Bank, this is a direct and ongoing compliance framework governing every stage of credit information handling—from submission to CICs, to correction and customer grievance resolution.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Debit Card: Issuance and Conduct Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Local Area Banks** and take **immediate effect** from **November 28, 2025**. They govern the general conduct, issuance, and associated controls for **debit cards, including co-branded debit cards**, and must be read together with any other RBI prudential, payment, technology, and cyber-security directions that apply to debit and co-branded cards. The RBI states that, for issuing debit cards, **prior RBI approval is not required**, but each bank must operate under a **Board-approved debit card issuance policy** and broader card-conduct framework.

A bank must maintain **Board-approved comprehensive policies and procedures** covering debit card issuance, co-branding arrangements where relevant, the standard operating procedure for **blocking, deactivating, or suspending cards at the bank’s discretion**, the **time period for completing formalities after a lost card is blocked**, and **grievance redressal plus compensation**. These policies are not optional or generic; the Directions expect the bank’s internal procedures to address the specific matters later set out in the Directions themselves.

On issuance, debit cards may be issued **only to customers holding Savings Bank or Current Accounts**. The document begins the restriction section by stating that **no bank shall issue debit cards to cash ...**, but the excerpt provided cuts off before the full restriction is visible, so the remaining wording cannot be safely reconstructed from this text alone. The definition of “debit card” includes both **physical and virtual payment instruments** linked to a savings or current account and usable for cash withdrawal, online payments, point-of-sale and QR-code transactions, fund transfers, and similar activities, subject to prescribed terms and conditions.

The Directions also define several compliance-relevant terms, including **cardholders**, **card-issuers**, **co-branded cards**, **convenience fees**, **form factors**, and **card loyalty/reward programmes**. A **co-branded card** is one issued jointly by a bank and a co-branding partner and bearing both names, while a **form factor** is any physical or virtual substitute instrument used instead of a card to carry out payment or banking transactions. A **card loyalty/reward programme** includes schemes tied to debit card usage that provide digital coupons, points, discounts, cash back, or other monetary-value benefits redeemable for the same or later transactions after accumulation.

For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that Local Area Banks must ensure **board-level approval, documented controls, and customer-eligibility restrictions** are in place immediately, and must align all debit-card issuance and conduct practices—including any co-branding and any card-blocking and grievance procedures—with the RBI’s Directions and any other applicable RBI card-security and payment regulations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set, issued on November 28, 2025 and updated as on April 01, 2026, establishes the credit-facility framework for Local Area Banks and replaces the earlier position on these matters, with the update date indicating the operative text to read as of April 1, 2026. The document is structured as a full credit administration code for local area banks and expressly covers board-approved policies, digital lending, lending against gold and silver collateral, microfinance, non-fund-based credit facilities, and credit to the real estate sector, so compliance teams should assume it applies to all such activities conducted by a Local Area Bank unless a chapter says otherwise. It also contains repeal/savings language and interpretive provisions, meaning prior inconsistent instructions on the covered topics are superseded to the extent repealed, while other applicable laws continue to apply.

A major part of the directions is the digital lending regime for bank–LSP arrangements and DLAs, which imposes conduct, customer-protection, technology, data, reporting, and loss-sharing obligations when the bank uses a lending service provider or a digital lending app. The bank must have board-approved policies and controls around these arrangements, including accountability for customer-facing conduct, data handling, reporting of credit information, and allocation of losses in default situations; compliance officers should treat the bank as remaining responsible for outsourced digital-lending activities rather than shifting compliance risk to the LSP. The chapter also covers general provisions for digital lending, so any new or renewed LSP/DLA arrangement should be checked against the RBI’s required operational, disclosure, and governance standards before launch.

For lending against gold and silver collateral, the directions impose separate restrictions and ceilings, valuation and assaying requirements, and an LTV framework that must be followed before sanction and during the life of the loan. The document signals that these loans are not to be treated as ordinary secured credit: the bank must follow prescribed collateral-handling and valuation processes, and lending limits must stay within RBI’s specified cap. Compliance teams should verify branch-level controls for acceptance, storage, valuation, renewal, and monitoring of precious-metal collateral, because these loans typically carry extra regulatory scrutiny.

The microfinance chapter defines what counts as microfinance, requires assessment of household income, and caps the total repayment obligations a household can take on. This means the bank must assess borrower household income before extending or revising such exposures and ensure that the household’s aggregate repayment obligations remain within the RBI-prescribed percentage threshold under the directions; the exact cap is not provided in the excerpt, but the requirement is clearly mandatory and household-based rather than borrower-only based. The bank therefore needs systems to aggregate all household debt obligations across lenders and product types before approving microfinance loans.

The non-fund-based credit chapter governs guarantees, e-guarantees, co-acceptances, and overseas current or capital account transaction-related guarantees, including the timing of payment when a guarantee is invoked. Compliance should note that the directions extend beyond funded loans and cover contingent liabilities and documentary/payment obligations, with specific rules on issuing, using electronic guarantees, and settling invoked guarantees in a timely manner. Finally, the real-estate chapter addresses the quantum of lending to the real estate sector, indicating that exposure sizing to that sector is regulated and must be checked against the RBI’s prescribed limits before origination or enhancement of facilities.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits Directions, 2025** (as updated **August 25, 2026**) set the deposit-interest framework for **local area banks** and replace earlier RBI directions for this topic, with the document stating that it comes into force on the date specified in the directions and applies to deposit products and related interest-payment practices covered in the text. The directions require local area banks to follow RBI-prescribed rules for **domestic rupee deposits**, **rupee deposits of non-residents**, and **foreign currency deposits**, including how interest may be set, calculated, compounded, paid, forfeited, or continued after account events such as death, renewal, premature withdrawal, or a depositor’s return to India.

For **domestic current accounts, savings deposits, and term deposits**, the directions establish the permissible interest-rate framework and associated operational rules, including periodicity of interest payment on savings accounts, treatment of overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, and the manner in which additional interest may be paid in specified cases. They also prescribe the rule for **interest payable on the domestic deposit account of a deceased depositor**, and they specifically allow banks, at their discretion, to pay interest on the **minimum credit balance in the composite cash credit account of a farmer** under the conditions stated in the directions. The document also addresses **premature withdrawal of domestic term deposits**, including the penalty or reduction in interest that may apply when a term deposit is broken before maturity.

For **rupee deposits of non-residents**, including **NRE deposits**, the directions regulate the interest rate treatment and impose specific restrictions, including a **prohibition on marking lien** on such deposits. They also set the rules for **premature withdrawal penalties** on NRE deposits and the interest payable when the **NRE term deposit account holder has died**, ensuring that banks follow RBI’s specified settlement method rather than their own ad hoc policies.

For **foreign currency deposits**, the directions govern **FCNR(B)** accounts and related foreign-currency resident accounts. They specify how interest must be **calculated on FCNR(B) deposits**, how interest is to be handled **upon renewal**, what interest is payable when the **FCNR(B) depositor dies**, and how interest is treated when an **NRI returns to India** and the FCNR(B) account is converted to a **Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) account** or resident rupee account. The directions also regulate **premature withdrawal** of foreign currency deposits and impose a penalty framework for such withdrawals, while separately addressing the **Resident Foreign Currency Accounts Scheme**.

Finally, the directions include **prohibitions and exemptions** and end with **repeal and saving provisions**, meaning earlier inconsistent instructions are superseded to the extent covered while preserving valid actions taken under the prior framework. For a compliance team, the key point is that these are operative RBI rules for local area banks’ deposit products: the bank must ensure its product terms, customer disclosures, account-opening and renewal processes, death/claim settlement procedures, non-resident account handling, and premature-withdrawal treatment are aligned with the exact RBI requirements in the directions and any applicable schedule.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025** apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and are **effective immediately upon issuance**. The Directions are issued under **section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and replace the prior LAB capital adequacy framework through a **repeal-and-saving mechanism** in Chapter IV, while preserving actions already taken under the earlier framework to the extent saved by the new Directions.

Substantively, the document sets out the full **prudential capital adequacy regime** for LABs, covering the definition of **regulatory capital**, the composition of **Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital**, deductions from capital funds, limits on Tier 2 elements, cross-holding restrictions, and capital treatment for subsidiaries. It also prescribes how LABs must calculate **risk-weighted assets (RWAs)** for **credit risk, market risk, and interest rate derivatives**, and then compute the overall capital ratio. The table of contents shows dedicated chapters for **minimum regulatory capital**, **definition of capital funds**, **Tier 1 capital**, **Tier 2 capital**, **deductions**, **limits for Tier 2 elements**, **norms on cross holdings**, and **capital for subsidiaries**, indicating that compliance teams must review both the eligibility of instruments counted as capital and the calculation methodology for exposures.

The definition section establishes key technical terms that drive the capital calculations, including **banking book**, **basis risk**, **credit risk**, **DTA/DTL** (using the meanings from the applicable accounting standards), **derivative** (as defined in **section 45U(a) of the RBI Act, 1934**), and **duration (Macaulay duration)** as a measure of price volatility and interest rate risk for fixed-income securities. Although the excerpt provided cuts off partway through the definitions, it is clear the Directions are designed to standardize the prudential treatment of balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet items for capital adequacy purposes. The document also includes an **Annex I** requiring a **reporting format for details of investments by FIIs and NRIs in Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares qualifying as Tier 1 Capital**, which indicates a specific ongoing reporting obligation where such instruments are issued or held.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that LABs must ensure their capital instruments, deductions, and risk-weighted asset calculations conform to the new RBI framework immediately, with particular attention to any **eligibility conditions for Tier 1/Tier 2 instruments, deduction requirements, exposure treatment, and subsidiary capital rules**. Because the Directions explicitly cover **market risk** and **interest rate derivative** capital charges in addition to credit risk, banks with trading activity or derivative positions must verify that those positions are captured correctly in capital computations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on January 22, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and takes effect **immediately** upon issuance. It sets out the framework for how LABs must meet and report **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** requirements, and it requires CRR maintenance to be reported through **statutory return Form A** and SLR maintenance through **statutory return Form VIII**. The directions are issued under the RBI’s authority under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, along with **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**.

The document defines the key measurement concepts that compliance teams will need to apply. **Aggregate deposits** means the total of **demand deposits and time deposits**. For savings bank accounts, banks must split balances into demand and time liabilities using the specified half-yearly methodology: as of the close of business on **March 31** and **September 30**, the bank must calculate the proportion of savings balances treated as demand vs. time liability under Regulation 7 of the RBI Scheduled Banks’ Regulations, 1951; the **average of the minimum balances maintained in each account during the half-year** is treated as the **time liability** portion, and the remainder of the average actual balances during that half-year is the **demand liability** portion. That ratio then applies to all reporting fortnights in the **next half-year**.

The directions also specify what counts as **approved securities / SLR securities**. These include **Government of India dated securities** issued under the market borrowing programme and Market Stabilization Scheme, **Government of India Treasury Bills**, **State Development Loans (SDLs)** issued by state governments under the market borrowing programme, and any other instrument later notified by RBI. For **Form A reporting**, banks must report the **total investment in approved securities as per the investment book, including encumbered securities**. However, for **SLR compliance**, only the **unencumbered portion** of investments in approved securities qualifies as the specified SLR asset.

The excerpt also begins to clarify an important exception: certain securities that are **lodged with another institution** are treated as **not encumbered for SLR purposes** and therefore continue to qualify as SLR assets, though the text provided cuts off before listing all such cases. A compliance team should therefore note that this instrument is not merely definitional—it establishes the reporting basis, the apportionment methodology for savings deposits, and the distinction between investment-book reporting and eligible SLR assets, all of which affect regulatory returns and liquidity compliance for LABs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Governance) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and take **immediate effect**. They apply to **all Local Area Banks** and establish the governance framework banks must follow for board composition, director appointments, leadership roles, board functioning, board committees, remuneration governance, and RBI approvals/reporting.

The directions define key governance terms used throughout the framework, including **Chairperson** (the bank’s part-time chairman), **Clawback** (a contractual right requiring return of previously paid or vested remuneration in specified circumstances), **Malus** (the ability to prevent vesting of deferred remuneration before vesting occurs), **Retention period** (the post-vesting period during which awarded variable-pay instruments cannot be sold or accessed), **Independent Director** (as per **Section 149(6) of the Companies Act, 2013**), and **Substantial interest** (as per **Section 5(ne) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**). Where the Directions do not define a term, the meaning from the **RBI Act, 1934**, **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Companies Act, 2013**, and related rules applies.

Although the excerpt provided stops before the substantive chapters, the table of contents shows that the Directions impose binding rules on: the **constitution of the board and appointment of directors**; the appointment and roles of the **MD&CEO, part-time Chairman, and whole-time directors**; the **role and responsibilities of the board and individual directors**; a **calendar of reviews and board meeting procedures**; mandatory board committees, specifically a **Nomination and Remuneration Committee** and an **Audit Committee of the Board**; and detailed rules on **remuneration** for **non-executive directors, whole-time directors, MD&CEO, material risk takers, and control function staff**. The Directions also include a chapter on **regulatory approvals and reporting**, indicating that certain governance actions will require RBI approval or notification and associated reporting obligations.

For compliance purposes, the immediate operational implication is that every Local Area Bank must review its existing board structure, committee composition, leadership appointments, meeting procedures, and remuneration policies against the new RBI framework as soon as possible. The document also indicates that **Annexes I–VI** contain supporting requirements or formats, which likely include the detailed standards and reporting templates that banks will need to implement to remain compliant.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025** apply only to **Local Area Banks** and become **effective on January 1, 2026**. The directions define and regulate three digital channel types: **internet banking** (web-browser based, excluding mobile apps), **mobile banking** (mobile apps, USSD, and SMS), and broader **digital banking channels** accessed through customer electronic devices for automated financial/banking transactions. They also distinguish between **“view only” banking**, which permits only non-liability-changing functions such as balance enquiry, balance viewing, and statement downloads, and **“transactional” banking**, which includes fund movement and other transactions that affect the customer’s assets or liabilities.

For **view only banking**, a Local Area Bank is eligible only if it has **implemented Core Banking Solution (CBS)** and its public-facing IT infrastructure is **enabled for IPv6 traffic**. If a bank starts a view-only digital channel after the directions take effect, it must **inform the Reserve Bank’s Department of Regulation via the PRAVAAH portal within 30 days of the board-approved decision to launch**, and it must submit the **Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy (GAICA) Report** referenced in the directions; the launch remains subject to supervisory scrutiny. The document also makes clear that banks offering only view-only access **cannot provide loans, fund transfers, or other services that create customer liability or move funds**, although they may provide **downloadable forms** for those services.

For **transactional banking**, the directions require that banks obtain **prior approval** before offering such facilities; the excerpt provided cuts off mid-sentence, so the exact approval pathway and any further conditions are not visible here. More generally, all Local Area Banks must maintain **comprehensive policies for all digital banking channels**, explicitly covering compliance with **statutory and regulatory requirements** as well as **liquidity and operational risk management** in the digital banking environment. The document also states that any term not defined in the directions takes its meaning from the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, related rules/regulations, RBI glossaries, or commercial usage, as applicable.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** establish the operating framework for how **local area banks** may open and report branches and other customer touchpoints, and they appear to replace earlier branch-authorisation instructions under the RBI’s banking regulation powers. The directions are issued on **November 28, 2025**, and they apply to the entities covered under the document’s applicability section—i.e., **local area banks**—for all matters relating to **banking outlets, branches, offices, customer service points, ATMs, cash deposit machines, bunch note acceptor machines, business facilitator/business correspondent arrangements, doorstep banking, and reporting**. The RBI also reserves the right to issue clarifications, and its interpretation of any provision is stated to be **final and binding**.

At a high level, the document requires each local area bank’s **Board of Directors** to approve a formal policy governing branch/banking-outlet authorisation and related distribution arrangements, and to assign clear responsibility for oversight and compliance. The board-level policy is expected to cover where outlets may be opened, how approvals and internal controls are handled, and how the bank will manage alternatives to full branches, including **off-site/mobile ATMs, CDMs, and BNAMs**. Compliance teams should treat this as a governance requirement: the bank cannot rely on ad hoc expansion decisions, but must maintain a board-approved framework and evidence that senior management is implementing it.

The directions also set out the rules for **opening banking outlets**, including the conditions under which the bank may establish branches or comparable customer-access points and the reporting/authorisation process that follows. The document separately addresses **off-site and mobile ATMs, CDMs, and BNAMs**, indicating that these devices are regulated as part of the outlet network and not merely as generic equipment deployments. Where the bank uses these channels, it must follow the RBI’s prescribed authorisation and reporting expectations rather than treating them as operational exceptions.

A substantial portion of the document deals with the **Business Facilitator / Business Correspondent (BF/BC) model**. The RBI distinguishes between business facilitators and business correspondents and provides separate guidance for engaging them, implying different permissible activities and control requirements depending on the role assigned. For any BC arrangement, the bank will need documented onboarding, monitoring, and oversight processes, because the model is treated as a regulated extension of the bank’s distribution and service network rather than a purely outsourced service. This is especially important for compliance teams because conduct, customer service, and operational-risk controls will need to be extended to these third-party arrangements.

The directions also include a chapter on **doorstep banking**, covering eligibility, services to be offered, delivery modalities, the delivery process, risk management, transparency, other conditions, and grievance redressal. This means a bank that offers doorstep banking must define exactly who can receive the service, what services are permitted, how requests are handled, and how the bank will mitigate fraud, error, and service-quality risk. The document also explicitly requires a customer grievance mechanism for doorstep banking, so complaints and failures in delivery are not optional operational issues but part of the compliance framework.

Finally, the directions require **information reporting** on banking outlets, branches, offices, customer service points, and related infrastructure, which means the bank must keep its internal records and regulatory submissions aligned with the RBI’s prescribed reporting format and timing. The chapter on **repeal and savings** indicates that prior inconsistent branch-authorisation provisions are being superseded, while other applicable laws remain in force. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that branch expansion, alternative delivery channels, third-party customer service models, and related reporting all need to be reviewed against this 2025 framework, with board approval, internal controls, and reporting processes updated accordingly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** take effect **immediately** and apply to **Local Area Banks**. The directions are issued under **Section 44A and Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they establish the process for voluntary amalgamations involving local area banks.

The scope is broad enough to cover: **(i)** amalgamation of **two banks**, **(ii)** amalgamation of **a bank with a banking company** as defined under **Section 5(c) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **excluding foreign banks**, or vice versa, and **(iii)** amalgamation of an **NBFC with a bank, or vice versa**. For purposes of the directions, the “**amalgamated entity**” is the entity transferring its business, the “**amalgamating entity**” is the entity acquiring that business, “**amalgamation**” includes any merger under the relevant statutes/regulations or equivalent scheme terminology, and “**Tribunal**” means the **National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)** under the Companies Act, 2013. Any undefined terms take their meaning from the **RBI Act, 1934**, the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, other applicable statutory modifications/re-enactments, or RBI’s glossary/commercial usage.

At the board level, an amalgamation must be approved by a **two-thirds majority of the total number of board members** of **both** the amalgamating and amalgamated banks; this is not limited to those present and voting. Before granting approval, the banks must ensure that **Deeds of Covenants** required under the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Governance) Directions, 2025** have been obtained from **all independent and non-executive directors** participating in the meeting. The directions also state that the boards must give “particular consideration” to further matters in the approval process, indicating that board deliberation is not purely formal but must satisfy RBI’s substantive expectations.

The document also creates a separate layer of **shareholder approval**, followed by **RBI approval or sanction** under a subsequent chapter, and then rules on the **entitlement of dissenting shareholders** and **buying/selling of shares by promoters**. In addition, the directions contain **repeal and saving provisions**, clarify that the directions do **not bar application of other laws**, and include interpretive provisions. For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that any Local Area Bank contemplating a voluntary amalgamation must clear the prescribed **board supermajority threshold**, ensure the **governance-related covenant documentation** is in place for independent and non-executive directors, and then proceed through the shareholder and RBI approval process under the framework established by these immediate-effect directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **“Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights) Directions, 2025”**, applicable specifically to **Local Area Banks**. The Directions are issued under **Sections 12, 12B, and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and must be read together with the RBI’s separate **Guidelines on Acquisition and Holding of Shares or Voting Rights in Banking Companies**. They take effect **on the day they are placed on the RBI’s official website**.

Substantively, the document’s purpose is to ensure that the **ownership and control of banking companies remain sufficiently diversified** and that **major shareholders are “fit and proper” on an ongoing basis**. For compliance teams, this means acquisition and holding of shares or voting rights in Local Area Banks are no longer just a one-time approval issue; the framework is designed around both **prior approval for acquisitions** and **continuous monitoring after acquisition**. The definition of **“acquisition”** is broad and covers obtaining, or agreeing to obtain, shares or voting rights in a banking company **directly or indirectly**.

The document establishes a structure in which applicants seeking to acquire shares or voting rights must satisfy **fit-and-proper criteria** and follow a **prior approval procedure** before acquisition, and banks must maintain arrangements for **continuous monitoring** of shareholders after the transaction. It also introduces ongoing compliance expectations around **due diligence**, **detecting violations of Section 12B(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and **reporting requirements** if issues arise. The annexes indicate that the Directions also set out operational specifics such as **limits on shareholding**, a **lock-in requirement**, and a **ceiling on voting rights**, which are key thresholds that compliance officers should review against any contemplated or existing shareholder position.

The document also contains a **repeal-and-saving framework**, meaning prior provisions are being superseded while preserving certain past actions or rights where applicable, and it states that application of other laws is **not barred**. Because the excerpt provided ends at the start of the definitions section, the full operational thresholds, procedural forms, and any exact percentage limits or filing timelines are not visible in the text provided here; however, the Directions clearly signal that Local Area Banks must implement controls to screen proposed shareholders, monitor ownership changes continuously, and ensure compliance with RBI’s ownership/voting-right restrictions and reporting obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend) Directions, 2026** apply specifically to **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and take effect from **FY 2026–27**. They were issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and require RRBs to follow new prudential conditions before declaring any dividend, including interim dividend on equity shares. The core policy change is that dividend distribution is no longer just a board discretion issue; it is tied to regulatory capital strength, asset quality, and supervisory review outcomes.

Before approving a dividend, the **Board of Directors** must consider four specific factors: the **divergence in asset classification and provisioning for NPAs** identified in **NABARD supervisory findings** (including the trend in such divergence), the **auditor’s report** for the year in which the dividend is proposed, including any **modified opinion or Emphasis of Matter**, the bank’s **current and projected capital position** relative to the applicable regulatory capital requirement, and the bank’s **long-term growth plans**. This means the board is expected to formally review not just profitability, but also supervisory concerns, audit qualifications, and forward-looking capital adequacy before any distribution decision.

To be eligible to declare a dividend, the bank must have been **compliant with the applicable regulatory capital requirement at the end of the previous financial year** and must **remain compliant at the end of the financial year in which the dividend is proposed**. The directions define **“Adjusted Profit After Tax (PAT)”** as the financial year’s PAT **minus 50% of Net NPA as on March 31 of the financial year for which the dividend is to be paid**, which is a key metric for evaluating dividend capacity. “Dividend” expressly includes **interim dividend**, and “extraordinary profit/income” has the meaning used under the applicable Accounting Standards.

The document also restricts what profits can be used for dividend payment and requires a reporting system to the RBI/NABARD framework, with a specific **restriction on payment of dividend** if prudential conditions are not met. It further provides for **penal consequences for non-compliance**, signaling that breaches may attract supervisory or regulatory action beyond simply disallowing the dividend. Finally, the Directions include **repeal and saving provisions** and confirm that **other applicable laws are not barred**, meaning the dividend decision must comply with these Directions as well as any other relevant statutory or regulatory requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Regional Rural Banks – Miscellaneous” Directions, 2025, issued on November 28, 2025 as DOR/2025-26/268, consolidate and update a wide range of compliance, governance, operational, conduct, tax, HR, and reporting obligations for regional rural banks (RRBs). The directions apply to RRBs and require board-level oversight in several areas, including board-approved policies and periodic board review of compliance-sensitive matters. They also introduce or restate detailed obligations around the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF), including rules for credits to the fund, refunds and interest, registration, transfer and claim procedures, returns, notes to accounts disclosure, audit, record preservation, information submission, contact details, and interpretation of the scheme.  

On deposit and customer-service related compliance, RRBs must conduct camps and campaigns for periodic KYC updation, indicating an ongoing customer due-diligence and outreach requirement rather than a one-time exercise. In the regulatory and legal compliance area, the directions require adherence to legal compliance obligations, compliance with court directives, and registration-related requirements under the FATCA intergovernmental agreement with the United States. The document also imposes conduct prohibitions: RRBs are barred from accepting deposits at the instance of private financiers or unincorporated bodies, and they are prohibited from associating with prize chit schemes or selling lottery tickets.  

The directions further address tax and accounting matters by requiring RRBs to furnish information when demanded by Income Tax Authorities. On the people-side, RRBs must implement training and awareness programs and meet specified certification requirements for staff, and on the administrative side they must follow mandatory leave requirements, maintain business continuity planning (BCP), and submit statements of immovable property. The table of contents also shows a repeal chapter, indicating that prior related directions are being superseded or replaced by this 2025 instrument, so compliance teams should treat it as a comprehensive updated framework and review the final text for any transitional provisions, effective dates, or detailed procedural deadlines tied to each chapter.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
These RBI Directions consolidate and replace the Reserve Bank’s customer-service and conduct instructions for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) into a single framework titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025**. They apply **only to Regional Rural Banks**, and they came into effect **immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025**, unless a specific provision states a different date. The stated purpose is to standardize RBI requirements on customer service, fair conduct, and related protections across RRBs under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

For compliance purposes, the document is broad and operational: it covers how RRBs must structure their **institutional framework**, provide **customer service in branches**, handle **customer guidance and protection**, support **financial inclusion and accessibility**, process **payments and remittances**, manage **deposit accounts and other liabilities**, and conduct **responsible lending**. It also includes detailed appendices and mandatory formats for notices, claim processing, indemnities, affidavits, locker inventories, safe-custody inventories, and the **Key Facts Statement (KFS)** that must be used in lending disclosures. Because the directions are a consolidation of prior RBI instructions, RRBs will need to treat them as the primary reference point for policies, branch processes, disclosures, complaint handling, account operations, and lending documentation.

The document also defines key terms that are central to compliance, including **accounts with survivorship clauses** (such as “either or survivor,” “anyone or survivor,” “former or survivor,” or “latter or survivor”), **apostille** authentication, and **APR (Annual Percentage Rate)**, which is defined as the full annual cost of credit including interest and all associated charges. This matters because the later chapters and annexures rely on these definitions for account-settlement, disclosure, and consumer-protection obligations. The table of contents shows substantial prescriptive requirements across 10 chapters, indicating that compliance officers should expect detailed rules on branch notice requirements, customer communication standards, accessible service delivery, liability/deposit account procedures, and lending conduct, with annexed forms serving as mandatory or prescribed templates.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Regional Rural Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, with an updated text date of **December 29, 2025**. These directions are aimed at **regional rural banks (RRBs)** and are intended to prevent their misuse for **money laundering and terrorist financing**, in line with India’s obligations under the **FATF** framework and the domestic legal regime under the **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002** and the **Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**.

The document is a comprehensive KYC/AML/CFT framework for RRBs, covering **customer acceptance, customer identification, customer due diligence, beneficial ownership, ongoing monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND)**. It replaces/updates prior KYC instructions for this sector through a formal regulatory framework that applies to RRBs and governs how they onboard and monitor customers, including individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and arrangements involving beneficial owners. The directions also address **enhanced due diligence** for higher-risk relationships and **simplified due diligence** where lower risk permits, meaning banks must calibrate the depth of checks to the customer’s risk profile rather than applying a one-size-fits-all process.

The structure of the document shows that compliance obligations are not limited to opening accounts; they extend through the entire customer lifecycle. RRBs must establish board-approved policies and internal controls, define risk management procedures, implement a customer identification procedure at onboarding, and maintain **ongoing due diligence** after account opening. The directions also require detailed **record management** and **reporting obligations** to FIU-IND, meaning banks must keep KYC and transaction records in a usable form and file required regulatory reports whenever triggered by the AML/CFT rules.

Because the chapter list includes specific sections on **legal entities**, **beneficial ownership**, and **international-agency communications**, the document clearly requires RRBs to look through formal account holders to determine who ultimately owns or controls them, and to comply with any directions or freezing/other measures arising from **international sanctions or communications from competent agencies**. The later chapters on **other instructions** and **repeal and savings** indicate that the 2025 directions are meant to be a consolidated set of operative requirements, with prior inconsistent instructions repealed or superseded while preserving actions already taken under earlier rules where applicable.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these directions establish the current RBI KYC standard specifically for RRBs and create an ongoing obligation to maintain a documented, risk-based AML/CFT program from onboarding through periodic review, monitoring, and reporting. The document is effective from its issuance framework in **2025**, and the “updated as on December 29, 2025” note means the version provided should be treated as the current consolidated text for compliance implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025**, under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and they **came into force immediately** on issuance. These Directions apply to **all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** as defined in Section 5(ja) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The document replaces the prior framework for how RRB financial statements are to be prepared and disclosed, and it is updated as of **April 1, 2026**.

At the core, the Directions require each RRB to prepare its **balance sheet and profit and loss account** for every year/period in the **Forms in the Third Schedule of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, as required by Section 29; the Government’s specified forms under notification **S.O. 240(E) dated March 26, 1992** are reproduced in Annex I. Banks must comply strictly with the **Accounting Standards notified under the Companies Act, 2013** and follow the detailed instructions for compilation and disclosure set out in the Directions, including the specific guidance on selected accounting-standard issues.

The document also imposes detailed **notes, presentation, and disclosure requirements** in the financial statements, including a dedicated chapter on **notes to accounts** and disclosure obligations. It separately addresses several operational/accounting matters that affect reported figures and disclosures: **inter-branch account provisioning for net debit balances**, **reconciliation of Nostro accounts and treatment of outstanding entries**, **transfer to or appropriation from reserve funds**, **provisioning for fraud**, **unreconciled balances**, **deferred tax liability on Special Reserve created under Section 36(1)(viii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961**, and restrictions against **window dressing**. These provisions mean RRBs must not only use the prescribed formats, but also implement specific internal accounting treatments and reconciliation/provisioning processes that feed into the published statements.

Finally, the Directions include a **repeal and saving** framework and a clause confirming that **other applicable laws are not barred**, with interpretive provisions to govern application. For compliance teams, the practical effect is that all RRB financial reporting must be aligned to the RBI’s mandated presentation, note-disclosure, provisioning, and reconciliation rules immediately, with special attention to any disclosures or accounting treatments that affect reserve movements, fraud provisioning, inter-branch/Nostro items, deferred tax on special reserves, and the prohibition on obscuring the bank’s true financial position.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
These Directions, issued by the Reserve Bank of India on November 28, 2025, take immediate effect and apply to all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs). They establish the RBI’s framework for identifying and treating wilful defaulters and large defaulters, and they also state that the restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters and the reporting provisions for large defaulters apply to all entities regulated by the RBI, even where an entity would not otherwise fall within the document’s definition of “lender.” The stated purpose is to ensure a non-discriminatory, transparent process consistent with natural justice, and to support credit-information sharing so that lenders are cautioned and further institutional finance is withheld from wilful defaulters.

The document defines key terms that compliance teams need to operationalize. A “borrower” is any person or entity that has taken a credit facility from an RRB, and “credit facility” includes both fund-based and non-fund-based exposures, including off-balance-sheet items such as derivatives, guarantees, and letters of credit. “Default” has the same meaning as in the RBI’s 2025 Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, and “diversion of funds” is defined broadly to include, among other things, using short-term working capital for long-term purposes contrary to sanction terms, using borrowed funds to create assets other than those for which the facility was sanctioned, transferring funds to subsidiaries/group companies without approval, routing funds through other lenders without prior written permission, investing borrowed funds in other entities’ equity or debt without approval, and any unexplained shortfall between amounts drawn and amounts deployed. The definition of “director” specifically captures directors of a company that was classified as a large or wilful defaulter if they were associated with the company when the acts or omissions leading to default occurred, and “DIN” is defined by reference to the Companies Act, 2013.

For governance, the Directions require RRBs to operate through an identification committee for determining wilful default, and the board is assigned a formal role in the process. The document’s structure shows separate chapters for the board’s functions, treatment of wilful defaulters, and reporting of both wilful defaulters and large defaulters, indicating that classification is not merely an internal credit decision but a regulated process with review, reporting, and escalation steps. The treatment framework is intended to ensure that once wilful default is established, lenders do not extend further institutional finance to the concerned borrower, and the information is disseminated through credit-reporting channels so other lenders are alerted.

The document also contains dedicated reporting obligations for wilful defaulters and large defaulters, with prescribed annexed formats for submission of the list of large defaulters and the data on wilful default cases. Although the excerpt does not show the detailed numerical thresholds or the specific periodicity of submission, it clearly requires formal reporting in standardized formats, which means RRBs must maintain systems to identify, document, and transmit the required case data accurately and on time. The directions further indicate preventive measures and auditor involvement, so compliance should expect controls around credit origination, monitoring of end-use of funds, and audit review to detect diversion, misuse, or other conduct that can trigger wilful-default classification. Finally, the directions repeal or modify prior provisions to the extent addressed in Chapter VI, so RRB compliance teams should treat this as the operative 2025 regime and align internal policies, board oversight, committee procedures, and reporting workflows accordingly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025** (as updated through **July 1, 2026**) establish the framework RRBs must follow for **early identification, reporting, and time-bound resolution of stressed assets**, and they also **rationalize rules for compromise settlements and technical write-offs**. The document makes clear that, in addition to general stressed-asset resolution, it addresses **state government Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)** that may waive or sacrifice debt obligations for targeted borrower groups against fiscal support, because such schemes can weaken credit discipline, create moral hazard, and create prudential issues such as delayed recoveries, mismatches between claims submitted by RRBs and amounts accepted by governments, and mandatory fresh-credit conditions. It further states that the RBI has provided **broad principles for RRB participation in DRS** and a **model operating procedure** for use by state governments when designing and implementing such schemes.

For compliance purposes, the Directions apply to **Regional Rural Banks** and require them to operate under **board-approved policies** for stress recognition and resolution, with reporting and disclosure obligations built around early detection of asset stress. The document is structured to cover: general requirements; prudential norms for restructuring; special cases such as **compromise settlements and technical write-offs**; a dedicated chapter for **accounts impacted by natural calamities**; **government debt relief schemes**; and **special trade relief measures**. It also contains a chapter on **repeal and saving**, clarifies that application of other laws is not barred, and provides interpretive provisions.

A key compliance takeaway is that the Directions are intended not only to permit resolution but to ensure that any resolution activity is **consistent, timely, and prudentially sound**. RRBs are expected to maintain formal internal governance over these processes, including procedures for identifying stress early, reporting it appropriately, and applying the specific treatment required under restructuring or special-resolution scenarios. The text also signals that the RBI has attempted to standardize how compromise settlements and technical write-offs are handled so that banks do not treat them inconsistently or in a way that undermines recovery discipline.

Where natural calamities or government-sponsored relief schemes are involved, the document anticipates a more coordinated process with local banking committees and prescribed reporting. In practical terms, compliance teams should treat the Directions as a comprehensive operating rulebook for how RRBs must classify, report, restructure, compromise, write off, and otherwise resolve stressed exposures, while also managing exposure to state-led debt relief initiatives in a way that preserves prudential discipline.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction applies specifically to all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and it came into force immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025. It sets the prudential rules RRBs must use for income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning on advances, with the stated purpose of increasing consistency and transparency in reported accounts. The directions are not standalone for restructured borrowers: RRBs must also follow the RBI’s separate “Regional Rural Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets” Directions, 2025 for restructured accounts, in addition to these IRAC rules.

The document reorganizes RRB compliance around five core areas: general instructions, disclosure requirements, asset classification, provisioning, and income recognition, plus repeal/savings and interpretation provisions. On asset classification, the directions establish the norms by which loan and advance accounts are to be treated as standard or non-performing, including specific rules for special situations, valuation of security, categories of NPAs, and the process for upgrading accounts once they become non-performing. The text also introduces automation requirements for the IRAC process, meaning banks are expected to mechanize income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning workflows rather than rely solely on manual processes.

On provisioning, the directions prescribe mandatory provisioning norms for RRB exposures and add an extra provisioning layer where a resolution plan has been implemented under Chapter IV-A of the RBI’s separate stressed-asset resolution directions. This means that if a stressed asset is resolved under the RBI resolution framework, the bank must still apply whatever additional specific provisioning these IRAC directions require on top of the normal provision treatment. The document also contains separate income recognition rules, which control when interest and other income can be booked on advances, tying income recognition to the classification status of the asset.

The document is labeled “updated as on July 01, 2026,” so a compliance team should treat that as the operative consolidated version and check the full text for any amendments reflected in the update. Although the excerpt provided here includes the chapter structure and foundational applicability, it does not show the later detailed thresholds, time periods, provisioning percentages, or NPA recognition cutoffs; those would need to be read from the full instrument to operationalize compliance controls. What is clear from the text shown is that the Directions are mandatory for all RRBs, apply immediately, supersede prior RRB-specific IRAC directions to the extent repealed, and require alignment with RBI’s stressed-asset resolution framework wherever restructuring occurs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025** under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and they **take effect from the date of issue, November 28, 2025**. The directions apply specifically to **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and set out a comprehensive ALM framework covering governance, liquidity risk, currency risk, interest rate risk, monitoring, and reporting. The RBI states that these requirements are being issued in the public interest and are intended to standardize how RRBs manage balance-sheet risks.

For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that the **Board of each RRB retains overall responsibility for ALM**, including approving ALM policies, setting risk limits, reviewing risk positions, and ensuring the institution has adequate systems and controls. The directions require the bank to maintain **robust ALM information systems**, an ALM organizational structure with clearly assigned responsibilities, and a formal ALM process to identify, measure, monitor, and manage liquidity and market-related risks. Compliance teams should expect the rules to require periodic board-level review and documented policy approval rather than relying on ad hoc treasury or finance practices.

On **liquidity risk**, RRBs must manage mismatches across maturity buckets using a **maturity ladder approach**, supported by prescribed statements and behavioral assumptions for assets and liabilities whose contractual maturities do not reflect actual repayment/withdrawal behavior. The framework also requires a **Statement of Dynamic Liquidity** and references the use of the **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)** and **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** as part of liquidity management. In practice, this means the bank must continuously monitor near-term funding gaps, incorporate behavioral pattern analysis for deposits, loans, and other balance-sheet items, and maintain the ability to prepare the required RBI-format statements.

For **currency risk**, the directions require RRBs to manage foreign exchange exposures if they undertake such activities, though the document excerpt does not provide the detailed limits in the visible text. For **interest rate risk (IRR)**, the directions require both **traditional gap analysis** and an **Interest Rate Sensitivity Statement**, again using behavioral assumptions where contractual repricing does not capture economic reality. The annexes listed in the document include the prescribed formats for the **Structural Liquidity Statement**, **Short-term Dynamic Liquidity Statement**, **Interest Rate Sensitivity Statement**, **Maturity Profile – Liquidity**, and **Interest Rate Sensitivity**, so compliance teams should treat those annexed formats as mandatory reporting templates.

The directions also establish a formal **monitoring and reporting** obligation: the bank must prepare, review, and submit the relevant statements in the manner and frequency prescribed by RBI, with internal review before submission. Chapter VIII provides **repeal and saving** provisions, meaning prior inconsistent directions on the same subject are superseded to the extent covered, while other applicable laws are not barred unless expressly overridden. For a compliance officer, the practical action item is to confirm that the RRB’s ALM policy, board approvals, risk limits, internal reporting calendar, behavioral assumption methodology, and prescribed statement formats are aligned with these 2025 directions as of **November 28, 2025**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Regional Rural Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio” Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated as of **May 18, 2026**) set the regulatory framework for how **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** must approve, classify, value, trade, and control their investment portfolios. The document is organized as binding directions covering the board’s responsibilities, investment policy requirements, classification into **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Held for Trading (HFT)**, and **Available for Sale (AFS)** buckets, valuation and market-value rules, and the operational rules for Government securities and non-SLR securities.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the directions require each RRB to have a formal **investment policy approved by its Board**, with clearly defined authority limits, procedures, and internal controls over investment decisions, shifting between accounting buckets, and reporting. The **Board** is responsible for oversight of the investment function, while the **Sponsor Bank** has a defined role in support and operational guidance. The rules also prescribe how securities may be shifted between categories: movements **to/from HTM** are restricted and subject to RBI conditions, and transfers **between AFS and HFT** are also controlled, meaning banks cannot reclassify holdings freely to manage reported gains/losses.

The directions distinguish between **government securities** and **non-SLR securities** and set separate operational requirements for each. For Government securities, RRBs must use the prescribed market infrastructure and settlement mechanisms, including access to **NDS-OM**, maintenance of **SGL** accounts, use of **gilt accounts**, and compliance with the RBI’s settlement procedures for outright purchases, sales, and **repo/reverse repo** transactions. For **non-SLR securities**, the directions impose prudential limits and governance controls, including explicit Board responsibility, disclosure expectations, and operational rules for instruments such as **corporate bonds**, **commercial paper (CP)**, and **certificates of deposit (CDs)**, as well as rules for trading and settlement in corporate bond markets.

Valuation and market-value recognition are also central. The document sets out separate valuation treatment for **HTM** versus **HFT/AFS**, and distinguishes among **quoted securities**, **unquoted SLR securities**, and **unquoted non-SLR securities**, indicating that banks must mark securities according to the applicable RBI-prescribed market value rules rather than holding them at arbitrary book values. Compliance teams should treat this as a control-heavy framework: the directions require documented classification, periodic valuation, board-approved investment policy, operational segregation of categories, proper settlement and recordkeeping, and adherence to prudential limits and disclosure rules whenever the RRB invests in government or corporate instruments. If you want, I can also turn this into a **compliance checklist** or a **“what changed / action items” memo** for internal distribution.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on Interest Rates on Advances apply to all Regional Rural Banks and take effect immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025. They are issued under Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and replace the prior framework for these institutions’ lending-rate practices by setting updated general requirements rather than fixed lending-rate caps.

For all advances, the bank must charge interest on a monthly-rest basis, meaning interest is calculated/charged monthly. The main exception is agricultural advances: the monthly-rest rule does not apply to agricultural loans, and banks must continue their existing practice for charging or compounding interest on crop-production-linked agricultural advances. For short-duration crops and allied agricultural activities, banks may align due dates with borrower cash-flow patterns and the harvesting/marketing season, but if a loan or installment becomes overdue, interest may be compounded in relation to that overdue amount.

The Directions emphasize that, although interest rates are deregulated, banks must not levy usurious rates or charges. Each bank’s Board must establish internal principles and procedures to ensure that excessive interest, processing fees, and other charges are not imposed on loans and advances. For small-value loans, especially personal loans and similar products, the bank’s lending-rate framework should include a prior-approval process that considers the borrower’s cash flows, a reasonable risk premium tied to internal borrower ratings, and the presence, absence, and value of security; the total borrower cost must be justifiable against the bank’s cost of funds and expected return. Banks are also expected to set an appropriate ceiling on interest and related charges for such loans and publicize that ceiling suitably.

For microfinance loans, each bank must have a Board-approved pricing policy. That policy must include a documented interest-rate model or approach for determining the all-inclusive rate, a clear breakdown of the rate components such as cost of funds, risk premium, and margin, the permissible range or spread for each component by borrower category, and a ceiling on the interest rate plus all other applicable charges. The overall requirement is that microfinance interest rates and fees must not be usurious, so compliance teams should ensure policies, pricing models, approval workflows, and published borrower-facing disclosures align with these Board-approved limits and the monthly-rest/agricultural carve-out rules.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
This RBI direction is a new, self-contained framework for **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** on the **transfer and distribution of credit risk**, issued under sections **21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. It is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025** and becomes effective **on the day it is placed on the RBI’s official website**. The document makes clear that it applies to **RRBs only**; the generic “bank” reference in the directions is to RRBs, and the framework is intended to govern multiple credit-risk transfer routes such as loan transfers, inter-bank participations, and borrower-account transfers only to the extent specifically permitted in the directions.

For **Part A (Transfer of Loan Exposures)**, the RBI substantially limits what RRBs may do. RRBs may **acquire loans only from a transferor that is specified as a lender in paragraph 12(4)** unless a specific exception applies. More importantly, **RRBs are permitted to act only as transferors of stressed loans under Chapter III of Part A**; they are **not permitted to be transferors or transferees in any other type of loan transfer**. The directions also prohibit any loan transfer or acquisition outside the permitted framework, while carving out no-prejudice references for **Master Direction – External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations dated March 26, 2019**, guarantees, and other products expressly permitted under RBI guidelines.

The directions apply broadly to **all loan transfers undertaken by the bank, including transfers by novation or assignment**. Where a loan transfer occurs, the **legal ownership of the loan must be mandatorily transferred to the transferee to the extent of the economic interest transferred**, so compliance teams must ensure that documentation and transaction structure reflect a true transfer of legal title aligned with the economic interest sold or assigned. The text also specifies that Part A applies to banks as **transferors**, unless another category of entity is expressly brought in as a **transferee** by a specific permission; this means RRBs cannot assume general transferee rights in the broader loan transfer market. The document then begins defining terms for this part, including **“credit enhancement”** as a contractual arrangement that provides added protection to other parties in a transaction, but the excerpt provided does not yet include the full definition set or the detailed mechanics of stressed-loan transfers, inter-bank participations, or borrower-initiated account transfers.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** are **effective immediately upon issuance** and apply to **all Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**. The directions are issued under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen prudential management of concentration risk on the asset side of RRB balance sheets, particularly exposures to a **single borrower, group borrower, or specific sectors**.

A key definitional change is the use of **“owned funds”** as the reference base for exposure limits. Owned funds include **paid-up capital, statutory reserve, other free reserves not in the nature of outside liabilities, and the credit balance in the profit and loss account**; for exposure-limit computation, they also include **share capital deposit/additional share capital received under restructuring programmes** and **contributions from the Central Government and sponsor banks**, even where the State Government’s contribution is still pending, but **only on a notional basis for advances/investments exposure calculation**. Owned funds expressly exclude **accumulated losses, shortfalls in provisions, all provisions for actual diminution in value or identifiable losses in specific assets** (including **provisions for bad and doubtful debts/NPAs, investment depreciation fund, bad and doubtful debt reserve, special bad and doubtful debt reserve, overdue interest reserve, etc.**), and **revaluation reserves**.

The directions also define **“exposure”** broadly to cover both **credit and investment exposures**. For credit exposure, RRBs must use the **sanctioned limit or the outstanding amount, whichever is higher**, except for **fully drawn term loans with no re-drawal scope**, where the **outstanding balance** may be used. **Non-fund-based exposures** must be counted at **100% of the non-fund-based credit limit or outstanding amount, whichever is higher**. This means compliance teams must ensure exposure aggregation captures both funded and non-funded commitments and investment positions when testing limits.

On **group borrowers**, the document notes that because such borrowers may require substantially larger credit facilities, **RRBs may not finance them**; however, if an RRB does extend finance directly to a group borrower, it must establish a **framework to identify group borrowers** using information available to it, with the guiding principle being **commonality of management and effective control**. In practice, this creates an obligation for RRBs to maintain internal identification and control procedures for connected counterparties where such lending is undertaken. The remaining operative provisions continue beyond the excerpt, but based on the text provided, the immediate compliance impacts are the new risk-management directions, the clarified owned-funds base, the broad exposure measurement rules, and the requirement for a group-borrower identification framework where relevant.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI circular introduces the **Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025**, issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and it is stated to have **come into effect immediately upon issuance**; the version provided is **updated as on July 01, 2026**. It applies specifically to **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** and is intended to strengthen credit risk management through both prudential requirements and prohibitions/restrictions on certain activities. The document confirms that RBI can require compliance on the basis of its powers under **Sections 20, 21 and 35A** and other enabling provisions, so the directions are mandatory for all covered RRBs.

The excerpt provided contains the opening framework and definitions that will govern the operative chapters that follow. It defines key credit products and exposures such as **bank guarantees** (including financial, performance, and deferred payment guarantees), **bills purchased and discounted** (including inland and foreign bills, and distinguishing sight bill purchase from usance bill discounting), and **cash credit (CC)** as a running-account facility against hypothecation/pledge of goods, book debts, standing crops, etc. These definitions matter because later restrictions, valuation rules, security-filing requirements, and loan-system rules will apply based on how the exposure is classified.

The table of contents shows the substantive compliance areas covered by the Directions: **Board Approved Policies**, **Credit Risk Evaluation**, **Statutory Restrictions**, **Regulatory Restrictions**, **Valuation of Properties / empanelment of valuers**, **filing of security interests in CERSAI** for immovable, movable, and intangible assets, **maintenance of cash credit/current/overdraft accounts**, and the **loan system for delivery of bank credit**. There is also a **deleted Chapter VI** and a **miscellaneous** chapter, followed by **repeal and other provisions**.
