For compliance purposes, the most important immediate takeaway is that **UCBs’ permissible role is narrow and must be checked transaction-by-transaction**: if the transaction is not a stressed-loan transfer permitted under Part A, Chapter III, the UCB should assume it is outside scope and therefore not allowed. Because the Directions are stated as a **comprehensive and self-contained framework**, banks should expect operational, legal, and documentation controls to align precisely with the prescribed transfer mechanics, ownership transfer requirement, and the limited set of permissible counterparties and transaction types.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** consolidate the prudential rules that limit concentration risk for **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, including limits on exposures to single borrowers, connected borrower groups, unsecured advances, inter-bank exposures, and large/small value lending. The directions were issued under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (Sections **21, 35A, and 56**) and **take effect immediately upon issuance** on **November 28, 2025**. They apply to all **Urban Co-operative Banks**, defined as **Primary Co-operative Banks** under **Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act.

For exposure measurement, the document defines **“credit exposure”** broadly to include **funded and non-funded credit limits**, underwriting and similar commitments, equipment leasing and hire purchase financing, and ad hoc contingency limits. For limit calculation, the **sanctioned amount or outstanding amount, whichever is higher, must be counted**; however, for **fully drawn term loans with no scope for re-drawal**, a UCB may use the **outstanding** amount instead. For **non-funded credit limits**, **100% of the limit or outstanding, whichever is higher**, must be included. The directions also state that a UCB’s share in **consortium / multiple banking / syndication** arrangements is governed by the **single borrower / group exposure** rules, and loans secured against the UCB’s **own term deposits** are excluded from credit exposure. “Exposure” is defined to include both **credit exposure** and **investment exposure in non-SLR securities** under the separate RBI investment portfolio directions, and **Tier-I capital as of March 31 of the preceding financial year** is the capital base used to fix exposure limits.

The document also sets the approach for identifying **“groups”** of connected borrowers: the UCB itself determines group membership based on its knowledge of the customer base, with the guiding principle being **commonality of management and effective control**. It specifically provides that **different firms with one or more common partners engaged in the same line of business** (such as manufacturing, processing, or trading) are to be treated as a **connected group**, and entities under **common ownership** are treated as a **single party**. In compliance terms, UCBs will need to ensure their credit and investment systems, borrower-group mapping, and exposure monitoring are aligned to these definitions so that all relevant funded, non-funded, and investment positions are captured consistently against the applicable prudential exposure limits.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set, issued on November 28, 2025 and effective immediately upon issuance, establishes the credit-risk management framework that applies to all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs), meaning primary co-operative banks as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The circular is expressly grounded in the RBI’s powers under sections 20, 21, and 35A read with section 56, and it is designed to strengthen prudential control over UCB credit exposures because credit risk can affect other risk categories and has systemic implications across sectors, borrower types, and products.

At a high level, the directions consolidate and reinforce RBI’s requirements on credit-risk governance, statutory and regulatory restrictions, credit administration, borrower identification, property valuation, CERSAI filing, account conduct, and loan structuring. The document includes multiple chapters covering board-approved policies, credit risk evaluation, statutory restrictions, regulatory restrictions, credit administration, Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) requirements for borrowers, empanelment of valuers, filing of security interests in CERSAI for immovable, movable, and intangible assets, maintenance of cash credit/current account/overdraft accounts, and the loan system for delivery of bank credit. The directions also state that they update and replace prior RBI guidance for these matters through a repeal-and-savings framework in the final chapter.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that UCBs must align their lending and credit-control processes to the RBI’s specified prudential tools and prohibitions, not merely internal policy preferences. The directions emphasize that certain activities may be statutorily restricted or prohibited, and that credit-risk management must be governed by board-approved policies and formal administration controls. UCBs should therefore expect mandatory internal policy revision, board approval, operational procedures for borrower screening and monitoring, and documentation controls across the full credit lifecycle.

The document’s defined terms show that it governs standard lending instruments such as bank guarantees, bills purchased and discounted, and cash credit facilities. In the cash credit context, the text begins to define the facility as a running account with drawing power periodically determined against security such as hypothecation or pledge of goods, book debts, and standing crops, indicating that account conduct and limit monitoring are part of the regulated credit-risk framework. Because the contents list also specifically calls out LEI compliance, property valuation controls, and CERSAI filing, compliance teams should assume the directions require tighter borrower/entity identification, independent valuation discipline for secured lending, and timely registration of security interests for covered assets.

From a governance and implementation standpoint, the directions take effect immediately and therefore require UCBs to have already moved toward compliance as of issuance, with the updated-as-on July 1, 2026 version reflecting any subsequent amendments or clarifications. A compliance officer should treat the document as a mandatory operating framework for UCB lending, requiring review of all credit policies, lending templates, account-monitoring procedures, and secured-transaction filings to ensure they conform to the RBI’s direction-by-direction standards.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** (updated as of **July 1, 2026**) create a standardized, mandatory framework for how Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) report, correct, disseminate, and protect credit information. The stated policy objectives are to ensure credit data is reported and shared in a uniform way, to protect the confidentiality and security of sensitive credit information, and to give consumers a process to access their credit information and pursue grievances related to credit reporting. The Directions are issued under **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulations) Act, 2005 (CICRA)** and, unless a provision specifies otherwise, **take immediate effect**. They apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks** (the document begins defining them as the regulated entities covered), and the obligations are framed around their role as credit information reporters and users.

At a high level, the Directions require UCBs to become and remain members of credit information companies (CICs), and to report credit information in the formats and timelines prescribed by RBI. The reporting framework covers the **data formats** to be used, **reporting timelines and updation obligations**, detailed **reporting guidelines**, and procedures for handling **rejected data**, including **rectification of rejected data and review of the Data Quality Index (DQI)**. The Directions also require a process for **correction of Credit Information Reports (CIRs)** where errors are identified, and they set out how UCBs may use credit information reports in **credit appraisal**. There are also rules on the **display of information** and on how these Directions interact with other RBI Department of Regulation instructions.

The document additionally imposes governance and technical coordination obligations. It establishes a **Technical Working Group** chapter, indicating formal mechanisms for ongoing technical coordination and implementation support around credit reporting requirements. For customer-facing compliance, the Directions create explicit requirements on **customer service and grievance redressal**, including a strengthened customer service framework, a **compensation framework for customers**, and reference to the **Reserve Bank-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021** for complaint escalation and resolution. The overall compliance expectation is that UCBs must not only report accurate credit data on time, but also maintain reliable internal processes for data quality, error correction, customer access, and complaint handling.

Finally, the Directions include a chapter on **best practices** and a chapter on **repeal and other provisions**, including **repeal and saving**, confirmation that application of other laws is not barred, and interpretive provisions. While the excerpt does not show specific numeric thresholds, fee amounts, or time limits, it makes clear that compliance officers must treat this as a comprehensive regulatory framework covering membership in CICs, data reporting and update cycles, error remediation, consumer transparency, and compensation/grievance processes. Since the text notes an updated version as of **July 1, 2026**, compliance teams should verify any amendments reflected in the updated text when implementing procedures and controls.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025” apply to Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs), meaning Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The Directions take effect immediately as of November 28, 2025, and they govern the general and conduct requirements for credit cards, debit cards, and co-branded debit cards; they expressly exclude co-branding credit cards from this document’s scope, while still requiring banks to read these Directions together with any applicable prudential, payment, technology, and cyber-security instructions issued by RBI. RBI states that these Directions are issued under section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 read with section 56, and all other enabling provisions, as a public-interest measure.

The document sets out key card-related definitions that matter for product design and compliance. It defines, among other things, add-on credit cards as supplementary cards issued to persons with a predefined relationship to the primary cardholder and within the primary cardholder’s credit limit and liability; annual percentage rate as the total annual cost of credit including interest and all other charges; charge cards as cards requiring full payment of the billed amount on the due date with no revolving credit; co-branded cards as jointly issued cards bearing both entities’ names; convenience fees as fixed or pro-rata charges for card use where cards are not ordinarily accepted as a payment method; corporate credit cards as cards issued to employees of a corporate employer with liability potentially resting with the corporate, the employee, or both depending on product design; and credit cards as physical or virtual instruments with a pre-approved revolving credit limit that may be used for purchases and cash advances, subject to prescribed terms. The definitions also introduce reward/loyalty programmes as card-linked schemes offering coupons, points, discounts, cashbacks, or other monetary-value benefits that can be redeemed on current or future transactions.

From a compliance perspective, the document is not merely descriptive; it is the framework for how UCBs must issue and conduct card business going forward. UCBs offering credit or debit cards must align their card issuance, conduct, and associated customer treatment with these Directions, including any product rules, billing practices, liability allocation, and fee structures that are addressed in the later chapters of the instrument. Because the Directions are immediately effective, affected banks should treat them as an operational requirement now, and ensure that card products, customer disclosures, back-office processes, and third-party/co-brand arrangements are reviewed for conformity. The excerpt provided ends partway through the definitions section, so additional substantive obligations likely appear in later chapters, but based on the text shown, the immediate compliance impact is that UCBs must treat these Directions as binding now and map all card products and arrangements to the RBI-defined terms and scope.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated through **July 15, 2026**) set a comprehensive prudential and conduct framework for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** across multiple lending products and credit-related activities. The document applies to UCBs and covers board-approved lending policies, digital lending through lending service providers, gold and silver-backed loans, microfinance, project finance, non-fund-based credit facilities such as guarantees and co-acceptances, and housing finance. A compliance team should treat this as a consolidated source of operational, disclosure, underwriting, technology, monitoring, and customer-protection requirements, with the specific obligations varying by product line.

A major part of the directions is the **digital lending** framework. UCBs entering into arrangements with **lending service providers (LSPs)** must meet general requirements on governance and customer protection, including technology and data controls, credit-information reporting, and rules on default-loss sharing arrangements. The directions also impose requirements on digital lending applications (DLAs), and compliance teams should ensure that any outsourced or platform-based lending activity is subject to board-approved oversight, transparent customer treatment, appropriate data handling, and reporting discipline. Where loss-sharing structures are used in case of borrower default, they must comply with the specified RBI conditions rather than being left to private contract alone.

For **lending against gold and silver collateral**, the document introduces or consolidates restrictions, ceilings, valuation/assaying standards, and **loan-to-value (LTV)** limits, together with other operational safeguards. UCBs must follow RBI-prescribed procedures for the valuation and assaying of pledged precious metal, and lending must stay within the applicable LTV ratio and any product-specific ceilings. Compliance officers should pay close attention to whether their bank is lending to retail borrowers, traders, or other eligible categories, because the chapter contains separate restrictions and operational rules depending on the collateral and purpose.

The **microfinance** chapter sets out the RBI’s definition of microfinance and requires banks to assess **household income** before extending such loans. It also caps the **aggregate repayment obligations of a household** as a share of household income, so lending decisions must test the borrower’s total debt service burden across all lenders, not just the UCB’s own exposure. This means underwriting processes need to capture reliable household-income information and existing repayment obligations, with lending systems and staff training aligned to the household-level affordability test. The chapter also contains other operational requirements that must be built into product design and monitoring.

For **project finance**, the directions distinguish phases of a project and impose prudential conditions both at **sanction** and at **disbursement/monitoring** stages. This is intended to ensure that funding is tied to project readiness, implementation progress, and ongoing oversight, rather than being disbursed loosely against incomplete documentation or weak milestones. Compliance teams should expect detailed requirements around credit appraisal, stage-wise disbursement, and monitoring of project execution, including documentation and control expectations for construction or other long-duration financing. The chapter also includes additional prudential provisions that will affect credit administration and risk management.

The chapter on **non-fund-based (NFB) credit facilities** governs guarantees, electronic guarantees (**e-guarantees**), co-acceptances, and guarantees involving overseas current or capital account transactions. UCBs must comply with the general conditions for issuing such exposures, and the document specifically addresses how guarantees may be issued, the use of e-guarantee systems, guarantees in favor of another regulated entity, and the regulatory treatment of co-acceptances. Compliance must ensure that contingent liabilities are tracked and approved under the prescribed framework, and that any cross-border or overseas-linked guarantee activity follows the RBI’s foreign-exchange and credit rules. This chapter is especially important because NFB exposures can create credit risk without immediate fund outflow and therefore require careful limit, documentation, and monitoring controls.

The **housing finance** chapter sets eligibility rules for borrowers, eligibility criteria for housing finance itself, and limits on loan amount and margin requirements. It also includes rules on **interest rates**, **foreclosure charges/prepayment penalties**, and the **reset of floating interest rates on EMI-based housing loans**, along with **penal charges** and a required **Key Facts Statement** regime. For compliance purposes, this means UCBs must ensure retail home-loan pricing and disclosures are transparent and consistent with RBI standards, and that borrowers receive the mandated pre-contract and ongoing disclosures. Because the document is a consolidated directions instrument, the effective obligations are not limited to one-off underwriting rules; they also govern how housing loans are priced, how prepayment is treated, and how changes to floating rates are communicated and implemented.

Overall, the document is a broad RBI credit-compliance framework for UCBs that requires banks to align board policies, lending workflows, outsourcing arrangements, collateral valuation, income assessment, project monitoring, contingent-credit issuance, and retail housing-loan disclosures with the specific prudential and customer-protection standards set out in the directions. A compliance officer should review each product line against the relevant chapter, confirm that internal policy, system controls, and customer disclosures match the RBI text, and verify that any activities involving digital platforms, precious-metal collateral, microfinance households, project disbursements, guarantees, or housing-loan repricing are operating within the prescribed limits and procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits” Directions, 2025, as updated on August 25, 2026, set the RBI’s binding framework for how urban co-operative banks may offer, calculate, pay, and disclose interest on deposit products, with separate rules for domestic rupee deposits, non-resident rupee deposits, and foreign-currency deposits. The directions are issued under the RBI’s regulatory authority and apply to urban co-operative banks covered by the framework; the document is organized as a comprehensive operational rulebook, so compliance teams should treat it as controlling both product design and day-to-day deposit operations from the commencement date stated in the instrument (not shown in the excerpt). It replaces or consolidates prior instructions through repeal-and-savings provisions, while preserving actions already taken under earlier directions where applicable.

For domestic rupee deposits, the directions govern current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, additional interest, overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, the periodicity of savings-interest crediting, payment on death of the depositor, and penalties for premature withdrawal. The bank must ensure interest is paid only in the manner and at the rates permitted by the RBI framework, with specific operational rules for when interest can be added to balances, when overdue deposits continue to earn interest, and how floating-rate term deposits are repriced and settled. The directions also require banks to follow RBI-prescribed treatment for deceased depositors’ accounts and to apply any premature-withdrawal penalty only as permitted under the applicable product terms and RBI rules.

For deposits held by non-residents, the document separately regulates rupee deposits and FCNR(B)-type foreign-currency deposits. It prohibits marking liens on certain non-resident deposit accounts, prescribes the interest treatment for NRE deposits and FCNR(B) deposits, and sets out the treatment when the depositor dies, when an NRI returns to India, or when funds are converted from FCNR(B) into Resident Foreign Currency (RFC) or resident rupee accounts. The directions also address premature withdrawal of non-resident and foreign-currency deposits and allow penalties only within the limits and conditions set by the RBI. Compliance teams must therefore verify that account opening, renewal, conversion, and closure workflows distinguish clearly between resident, NRI, returning Indian, and deceased-depositor scenarios.

The foreign-currency chapter covers FCNR(B) deposits in detail, including how interest is calculated, how interest applies on renewal, and what happens to deposits after the depositor’s death or return to India. It also includes the Resident Foreign Currency Accounts Scheme, so banks must ensure products and systems support the permissible conversion and payment rules across FCNR(B), RFC, and resident rupee accounts. The “Prohibitions and Exemptions” chapter indicates that some activities are expressly barred while certain entities or transactions may be exempted, and the final chapter clarifies repeal, savings, application of other laws, and interpretative rules. Because the excerpt does not reproduce the operative rate tables or specific numeric thresholds, a compliance officer should review the full body of the directions and any schedules for exact interest ceilings, permitted exceptions, and product-specific implementation details.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 16, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. They apply to all **Urban Co-operative Banks**, defined here as **Primary Co-operative Banks under section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the BR Act, 1949**. The directions establish the full capital adequacy framework for UCBs, including how capital is defined, what counts toward regulatory capital, how risk-weighted assets (RWAs) are computed, and how banks must report capital ratios.

At a high level, the document sets out the prudential capital rules that banks must use to determine **net worth, statutory requirements, minimum regulatory capital, and the composition of capital**. It splits capital into **Tier 1 capital** and **Tier 2 capital**, and then sets out the methodology for calculating RWAs for **credit risk** and **market risk**. It also introduces specific requirements on **share linking to borrowings**, **refund of share capital**, **protection of investors in regulatory capital instruments**, and **reporting**, including prescribed reporting formats in **Annex I** and **Annex II** for capital ratio monitoring.

The definitions section is relevant for compliance because it establishes the regulatory meaning of key terms used throughout the directions. For example, **credit risk** is the risk that a borrower or counterparty fails to meet agreed obligations or that their credit quality deteriorates; **market risk** is the risk of loss from movements in market prices affecting on- and off-balance-sheet positions; **derivatives** take the meaning given in **Section 45U(a) of the RBI Act, 1934**; and **DTA/DTL** are to be understood under applicable accounting standards. Compliance teams should treat these definitions as controlling for capital classification and RWA calculations under the directions.

Because the document is a full prudential capital framework, the compliance impact is not limited to a single filing or threshold; it affects **capital measurement, eligibility of instruments as regulatory capital, internal capital computation processes, and ongoing regulatory reporting**. The document also includes a **Repeal and Savings** chapter, indicating that prior provisions on the subject are being superseded to the extent specified, while preserving certain actions or rights under the savings clause.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**, effective **immediately** on issuance (**November 28, 2025**), and the version provided is **updated through August 25, 2026**. These Directions apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, defined as **Primary Co-operative Banks under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. They set out the framework for how UCBs must calculate, maintain, and report **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** and **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** requirements, and they also establish reporting formats, compliance procedures, and penalties for non-compliance.

For **CRR**, the Directions require UCBs to report CRR maintenance to RBI through the relevant statutory return: **Form B Return for Scheduled Co-operative Banks** for scheduled UCBs, and **Form I Return for non-scheduled Co-operative Banks under section 18 read with section 56** for non-scheduled UCBs. For **SLR**, all co-operative banks must report via the **Form I Return (for SLR)** under **section 24 read with section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The document also clarifies key calculation concepts, including **“aggregate deposits” as demand plus time deposits**, and provides the method for **apportioning savings bank balances between demand liability and time liability**: banks must compute the split as of **March 31 and September 30**, using the **average of the minimum balances maintained in each account during each month of the half-year** as the **time liability** portion, and the difference between that amount and the **average of actual balances maintained during the half-year** as the **demand liability** portion. The resulting proportions are then applied to all reporting fortnights in the **next half-year**.

The Directions also define what counts as **approved securities / SLR securities**. These include **dated Government of India securities issued under the market borrowing programme and Market Stabilization Scheme**, **Treasury Bills of the Government of India**, and **State Development Loans (SDLs) of State Governments** (the text continues beyond the excerpt, but these categories are expressly identified here). Compliance teams should note that the document is issued under RBI’s statutory powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, and it is structured to cover not only maintenance requirements but also computation procedures, reporting obligations, penalties for breaches, and repeal/transition provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Governance Directions, 2025** apply to all **Urban Co-operative Banks / Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under **section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they take **immediate effect** from the date of issuance (**November 28, 2025**). The directions are issued under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and are intended to set governance requirements for the board, committees, key officers, and related oversight processes.

A key change is the requirement that every UCB must, **at all times**, have **at least two professional directors** on its board—meaning directors with either **suitable banking experience at middle/senior management level** or a **relevant professional qualification in law, accountancy, or finance**. UCBs must ensure their **byelaws** contain a provision to support this requirement. This two-professional-director requirement **does not apply to Salary Earners’ Co-operative Banks**, which are expressly carved out of this obligation. The directions also reiterate that directors must satisfy the **eligibility, qualification, and disqualification criteria** under the **Banking Regulation Act and applicable co-operative laws**.

The document defines a **“Board”** broadly to include the Board of Directors or any governing body that manages the bank, and a **“Director”** includes directors appointed by **election, co-option, or any other lawful manner**. It also defines a **“Salary Earners’ Co-operative Bank”** as a primary co-operative bank whose membership is limited to persons who are or were employed in an institution or a group of institutions and that is recognized as such by RBI. Any undefined terms are to be interpreted using the **RBI Act, 1934**, the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, relevant statutory modifications/re-enactments, RBI’s glossary, or ordinary commercial meaning as appropriate.

Although the excerpt provided stops while introducing the disqualification rules for directors, the table of contents shows the wider governance framework covered by the Directions: the **constitution of the board and appointment of directors**, the **role of the board and individual directors**, a **calendar of reviews**, **board committees** including an **Audit Committee of the Board** and a **Risk Management Committee**, a **Board of Management**, appointment requirements for **Chief Executive Officer/Managing Director** and **Chief Risk Officer**, and **repeal/other provisions**. For compliance purposes, the immediate action point in the visible text is to confirm the board composition of each UCB, verify that the byelaws support the minimum professional-director requirement, and determine whether any institution qualifies for the Salary Earners’ Co-operative Bank exemption.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 27, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set applies to all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) in India, meaning Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. It is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025**, issued under sections 35A and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and became effective **immediately**; the document shown is an updated version **as of April 27, 2026**. The directions are intended to govern when and how UCBs may undertake or participate in financial-services-related activities, and the RBI expressly states that these directions override and consolidate the relevant regulatory framework for such activities.

The preliminary definitions are important for compliance because they determine the scope of restrictions and approvals. A **“debtor company”** is any company to which the UCB currently has, or had at any time in the preceding 12 months, a loan or investment exposure, excluding equity instruments. **“Equity instrument”** is defined narrowly to include equity shares, compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS), and compulsorily convertible debentures (CCD). A **“Financial Services Company”** is a company engaged in the business of financial services, and the definition expressly includes the forms of business listed in section 6(1)(a), (c), (d), (e) and clause (o) of section 6(1), as well as the forms of business listed in section 45I(c) and (f) of the RBI Act, 1934, read with the Banking Regulation Act. Compliance teams should treat these definitions as controlling for any proposed partnership, referral, distribution, or investment arrangement.

The directions also impose general governance expectations on the board and on investments in alternative investment funds (AIFs). Although the excerpt provided does not include the full operative text of Chapter II, it specifically flags that UCBs must follow board-level oversight requirements and comply with RBI’s restrictions on AIF investments. For a compliance officer, that means any UCB proposal to invest in an AIF, or to hold interests connected to AIFs, must be checked against the RBI’s current permitted/prohibited structure and board approval requirements, because these are not routine treasury investments.

Chapter III authorizes only specified financial services activities and imposes activity-specific conditions, so UCBs should not assume a general permission to sell third-party products or act as a financial-services intermediary. The directions cover: **mutual fund distribution as agents**, **insurance business as corporate agents without risk participation**, **insurance referral business without risk participation while sharing physical space**, **foreign exchange business**, **online trading facilities for demat account holders**, **Point of Presence (PoP) services under PFRDA**, **merchant acquisition business**, **acting as PAN Service Agents (PSA)**, and **issuance of prepaid payment instruments (PPIs)**. Each of these activities is subject to the RBI’s specific eligibility, conduct, and operational conditions in the relevant chapter provisions, so a UCB must confirm that its exact business model matches the permitted form and that it meets all prescribed safeguards before launch or continuation.

The document also contains repeal/saving language and clarifies that other laws continue to apply unless specifically barred. This means UCBs must comply not only with these RBI directions but also with the underlying laws and regulations governing securities distribution, insurance intermediation, foreign exchange, payments, pension services, PAN services, and any other applicable sectoral rules. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a permission-and-conditions framework: an activity is not allowed simply because it is mentioned in the directions; it is allowed only if the UCB fits within the defined category and satisfies the detailed requirements in the applicable chapter, with the directions in force from the date of issue and the updated text reflecting changes through **April 27, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025”** apply to **urban co-operative banks in India** (defined here as primary co-operative banks under **Section 5(cc) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**) and **take effect on January 1, 2026**. The Directions require every covered bank to maintain **comprehensive policies for all digital banking channels** that address all relevant statutory and regulatory requirements, including **liquidity risk and operational risk management** in a digital banking environment.

A key new authorization framework is introduced for **“view only banking facility”** over digital channels. A bank is eligible to provide view-only access for **internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital banking channels** only if it has **implemented Core Banking Solution (CBS)** and has enabled its **public-facing IT infrastructure to handle IPv6 traffic**. View-only access is limited strictly to non-transactional functions such as **balance enquiry, balance viewing, and account statement download**; it **cannot** be used to offer loans, funds transfers, or any other service that creates customer liability or moves funds, although downloadable application forms may still be provided for those services.

Banks that begin offering **view-only digital banking channels from the effective date onward** must **inform the Reserve Bank of India’s Department of Regulation via the PRAVAAH portal** and must submit a copy of the **“Gap Assessment and Internal Controls Adequacy” (GAICA) report** referenced in the Directions **within 30 days from the decision to launch** the service. In short, the document creates a formal authorization and control framework for digital banking by urban co-operative banks, with a specific eligibility gate (CBS plus IPv6 readiness), strict limits on what view-only channels may do, and a mandatory notification/reporting obligation tied to rollout.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** apply **with immediate effect** to **all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning **Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The directions govern **voluntary amalgamation of two or more UCBs** and define the key parties: the **“amalgamated entity”** is the bank transferring its business, and the **“amalgamating entity”** is the bank acquiring that business under the scheme. RBI states it will consider only proposals where the acquiring UCB commits to **protecting all depositors of the amalgamated UCB**, regardless of whether the amalgamated bank has a **positive or negative net worth**; if the net worth is negative, this protection must be provided either by the amalgamating UCB itself or **with upfront financial support from the State Government** as part of the amalgamation process. RBI will also only consider proposals where the **post-amalgamation CRAR** of the amalgamating UCB meets the **minimum regulatory requirement prescribed by RBI**.

At the governance stage, the decision to amalgamate must be approved by a **two-thirds majority of the total number of board members** of **both** the amalgamating and amalgamated UCBs; this is explicitly **not** limited to two-thirds of those present and voting. When boards consider the proposal, they must especially assess matters such as whether a due diligence exercise has been carried out and other prudential, financial, and operational considerations relevant to the merger. The directions then require **shareholder approval** and subsequent **RBI approval** before the amalgamation can proceed, and the RBI may sanction the scheme only after reviewing the proposal against the conditions set out in the directions.

The document also establishes a framework for the **sanction of the scheme of amalgamation** and for the **entitlement of dissenting shareholders**, meaning there is a formal process for handling shareholders who do not agree with the merger and determining their rights/consideration under the scheme. It further states that the directions **repeal and supersede earlier RBI directions on the subject to the extent of inconsistency**, while preserving actions already taken under the earlier framework. The directions also clarify that they do **not bar the application of other laws** where relevant, and that undefined terms will be interpreted using the RBI Act, the Banking Regulation Act, RBI’s Glossary of Terms, or ordinary commercial usage as appropriate.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Licensing, Scheduling and Regulatory Classification) Guidelines, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s 2025 guidelines state that it is **not considering any fresh proposals** to organize new Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) or to convert co-operative credit societies into UCBs. For these purposes, “Urban Co-operative Banks” are defined as **Primary Co-operative Banks** under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

The guidelines replace a one-size-fits-all approach with a **four-tier regulatory framework** based on deposit size and bank type. **Tier 1** covers all unit UCBs and salary earners’ UCBs regardless of size, plus all other UCBs with deposits of **up to ₹100 crore**. **Tier 2** covers UCBs with deposits of **more than ₹100 crore and up to ₹1,000 crore**. **Tier 3** covers deposits of **more than ₹1,000 crore and up to ₹10,000 crore**, and **Tier 4** covers UCBs with deposits of **more than ₹10,000 crore**. Deposits are to be measured using the **audited balance sheet as of 31 March of the immediately preceding financial year**. If a bank crosses into a higher tier because deposits increase, it is allowed a **glide path of up to two years**—the financial year in which the threshold is crossed and the following financial year—to meet any higher regulatory requirements of the new tier.

For inclusion in the **Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934**, licensed UCBs (other than **Salary Earners’ Banks**) may apply to the RBI’s Regional Office if they satisfy the RBI’s business authorisation eligibility criteria and three additional conditions. First, the bank must have maintained the **minimum deposits required for Tier 3 status for two consecutive years**. Second, its **CRAR** must be at least **3 percentage points higher than the minimum CRAR requirement applicable to that bank**. Third, the bank must have **no major regulatory or supervisory concerns**. The assessment must be based on the **latest** of the RBI inspection findings or the audited financial statements, and the application must include a **board/AGM resolution** authorizing the application and naming the officer(s) who may correspond with RBI, as well as **major financial details** and copies of the **published balance sheets for the last three years**.

From a compliance perspective, the document affects existing UCBs’ classification, capital planning, and schedule-inclusion readiness, but it does **not** open the door to new bank licensing or credit-society conversions. Firms operating or advising UCBs should verify current tier placement using the prior year’s audited 31 March balance sheet, monitor for threshold crossings, and, if applicable, track the two-year transition period for meeting more stringent requirements. They should also assess whether a bank is positioning for Second Schedule inclusion, particularly ensuring the Tier 3 deposit history, CRAR buffer, and supervisory-clean status are documented before any application is submitted.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) branch authorisation consolidate and replace the RBI’s existing branch-opening framework for UCBs, with effect from **December 04, 2025** (the date of the directions). They apply to **urban co-operative banks** and govern when and how they may open, shift, close, or operationalise places of business, including branches, extension counters, ATMs/CDMs/CRMs, as well as how they may use **Business Facilitators (BFs)** and **Business Correspondents (BCs)** and provide doorstep banking. The directions also establish reporting obligations through RBI’s **Central Information System for Banking Infrastructure (CISBI)** and expressly repeal the earlier branch-authorisation directions, while preserving actions already taken under the old framework and making clear that other applicable laws are not displaced.

A key governance requirement is that each UCB’s **Board of Directors must approve and periodically review** policies governing branch authorisation and related operational matters; the board is responsible for ensuring the bank complies with the RBI’s eligibility and procedural conditions before opening or relocating offices. The directions structure branch expansion around RBI-defined **Eligibility Criteria for Business Authorization (ECBA)** and the bank’s **area of operation**, meaning a bank cannot simply open a branch wherever it wants without first satisfying the relevant geographic and business parameters. UCBs must also follow specific RBI procedures for opening a **new place of business**, for selecting the route for opening a branch either under the **automatic route** or the **prior approval route**, and for opening an **extension counter** or operationalising an **ATM/CDM/CRM**. Likewise, there are separate compliance steps for **shifting a place of business**, **closing a place of business**, and dealing with **leased premises** where the bank does not comply with **section 11(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (as applicable to co-operative societies/AACS)**.

The directions also permit UCBs to engage third parties under two distinct outsourcing-style models: the **BF model** and the **BC model**. Only entities that meet the RBI’s eligibility requirements may be appointed, and the scope of activities is limited to the activities specifically permitted by the directions and the bank’s approved arrangements. The BC/BF framework includes detailed conditions on appointment, oversight, responsibility allocation, and operational controls, so a bank using these models must ensure written contractual arrangements, internal monitoring, and compliance with the RBI’s prescribed activity boundaries and risk-management expectations. Separate provisions also govern **doorstep banking**, indicating that UCBs offering such services must do so only within the operational framework set out by the RBI, rather than on ad hoc terms.

Finally, the directions require UCBs to submit **bank/branch information in the prescribed proforma through CISBI**, which creates an ongoing regulatory reporting obligation tied to branch authorisation status and infrastructure details. Because the document is a comprehensive replacement framework, compliance officers should treat it as controlling for all branch expansion, relocation, closure, outsourced banking-channel engagement, and infrastructure reporting decisions made **from December 04, 2025 onward**, while also verifying whether any existing branch-related arrangements need to be brought into conformity with the new procedures, board approvals, and reporting templates.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 23 read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and take **immediate effect on December 04, 2025**. They apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)** and **Central Co-operative Banks (CCBs)** as defined under the **NABARD Act, 1981**. Although the excerpt provided ends in the definitions section, the table of contents shows that the directions comprehensively regulate **branch authorisation, extension counters, ATMs/CDMs/CRMs, shifting or closure of business locations, doorstep banking, and reporting through the Central Information System for Banking Infrastructure (CISBI)**, replacing prior instructions through a repeal-and-savings framework.

From the structure of the document, the new framework is organized around **eligibility criteria for business authorization (ECBA)** and the **area of operation of District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)**, followed by detailed rules for opening new places of business. It distinguishes between a **branch opened under the automatic route** and one opened under a **prior approval route**, which indicates that some branch openings may proceed without case-by-case RBI approval if the bank satisfies the prescribed conditions, while others require RBI permission in advance. The directions also impose **additional conditions on StCBs** for opening branches, and separately regulate the opening and operation of **extension counters**, **ATMs/CDMs/CRMs**, and the **shifting of a place of business**, which suggests compliance obligations not only at branch-inception but also for subsequent changes to the network. The inclusion of a dedicated provision on **closure of a place of business** and **doorstep banking services** indicates that the RBI is also controlling service continuity and customer access, not just physical branch count.

A notable compliance point is the separate chapter on **reporting**, which requires banks to use a **proforma** and submit branch and bank details under **CISBI**, meaning branch authorization decisions and branch network changes are expected to be captured in the RBI’s central infrastructure reporting system. The document also anticipates situations where a co-operative bank **does not comply with Section 11(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (as applicable to co-operative societies)**, and contains special rules for **shifting, acquisition, surrender of leased premises, etc.** in those cases, implying enhanced restrictions or procedural safeguards for banks with capitalization/regulatory deficiencies. Finally, the directions preserve the application of other laws and include an interpretation clause, so compliance teams should treat these directions as operating alongside, not instead of, other banking and co-operative law requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025** (dated **December 4, 2025**, circular reference **DOR/2025-26/319 / DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.332/13-04-001/2025-26**) consolidates and updates compliance requirements for **rural co-operative banks**, covering **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs), District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs), and related rural co-operative banking entities** to the extent made applicable in the text. The directions take effect from the date specified in the operative provisions of the instrument and reorganize obligations across board governance, depositor education fund compliance, KYC outreach, legal/name-change matters, prohibited activities, staff leave, and business continuity planning.

A major compliance area is the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. Banks must transfer eligible unclaimed amounts to the Fund in accordance with the prescribed procedure, maintain records, and comply with refund and interest rules when a depositor later makes a valid claim. The directions set out detailed **registration, transfer, claim, reporting, disclosure, audit, record-retention, and information-furnishing requirements**, including specific **returns to RBI**, **notes-to-accounts disclosure**, and preservation of supporting records. Banks must also maintain contact details for claim handling and follow RBI’s interpretation of the scheme where clarification is needed.

The directions require **board-level governance controls**, including **board-approved policies** and periodic **board reviews** of specified compliance areas. They also mandate **camps and awareness campaigns for periodic updation of KYC**, meaning banks must actively conduct outreach to keep customer KYC information current rather than relying only on routine branch-level updates. In addition, banks must comply with the detailed rules on **change of name**, **display of the bank’s name**, and, where relevant, the **norms for inclusion of an StCB in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934**, as well as obey any **court directives** affecting operations.

The directions also reinforce prohibitions on certain **financial conduct and ancillary activities**. Rural co-operative banks are restricted from **holding shares in other co-operative societies**, must follow RBI’s rules on **payment of bonus**, and are prohibited from **accepting deposits at the instance of private financiers or unincorporated bodies**. They are also barred from **associating with prize chit schemes** or **selling lottery tickets**, which should be treated as prohibited business lines and compliance risks requiring internal monitoring and staff instruction.

On the operational side, the directions impose requirements for **mandatory leave** and a formal **business continuity planning (BCP)** framework, indicating banks must have workable continuity arrangements for disruptions and ensure leave practices are managed in accordance with the RBI’s prescribed norms. The final chapter contains **repeal and saving provisions**, meaning prior inconsistent instructions are superseded to the extent provided, while actions already taken or rights/obligations accrued under the earlier framework may be preserved where the savings clause applies.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025** on **28 November 2025**, and they take **immediate effect**. They apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined in the **NABARD Act, 1981**, and they cover **any outsourcing arrangement with a service provider located in India or abroad**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the RBI is imposing a formal risk-management framework for outsourcing by RCBs, with board-level accountability, management oversight, due diligence, contractual controls, ongoing monitoring, grievance handling, and specific restrictions on what can and cannot be outsourced.

The directions require each RCB’s **Board** to approve a **written outsourcing policy** and remain ultimately responsible for all outsourced activities; outsourcing does **not** transfer the bank’s regulatory responsibility or accountability. The policy must set out the bank’s risk appetite, the kinds of activities that may be outsourced, approval processes, due diligence standards, confidentiality and data-security expectations, business continuity requirements, and exit/termination planning. Senior management must implement the policy, maintain records, conduct risk assessments, and ensure that outsourced services remain subject to effective internal controls, auditability, and ongoing supervision.

A central requirement is that certain **core banking, decision-making, and fiduciary functions cannot be outsourced**. While the document must be read for the exact prohibited activities, the substance is that RCBs may not outsource functions that would undermine managerial control, regulatory compliance, or the bank’s ability to supervise and answer for the activity. Where outsourcing is permitted, the RCB must do prior evaluation of the vendor’s capability, financial soundness, reputation, internal controls, information security, ability to meet service levels, and ability to maintain business continuity and disaster recovery. The outsourcing agreement must be in writing and must clearly define scope, performance standards, access rights, confidentiality obligations, audit/inspection rights for the RCB and regulators, sub-contracting limits, incident reporting, data-handling rules, termination rights, and continuity/transition support.

The directions also require **continuous monitoring** of outsourced functions and formal procedures for handling service failures, breaches, and customer complaints arising from outsourced activity. RCBs must ensure that customers are not denied service or grievance redress merely because a function was outsourced; the RCB remains responsible for complaint handling and regulatory compliance. Special rules apply to **offshore outsourcing**, which is treated as a higher-risk arrangement and is subject to additional due diligence and control expectations, including ensuring that RBI access, audit, and supervisory needs are not impaired. The directions conclude by repealing prior inconsistent outsourcing guidance for RCBs while preserving actions already taken, and they clarify that other applicable laws continue to apply and that RBI’s interpretations govern any ambiguity.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI Direction, issued on **November 28, 2025** and titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025”** (updated as of **July 1, 2026**), applies to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) operating in India**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The Directions take effect **from the date of issue unless a specific provision states otherwise**, and they are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling powers. For compliance teams, this is a comprehensive conduct framework covering **customer service, customer protection, accessibility, payments/remittances, deposit accounts and liabilities, responsible lending, and miscellaneous operational obligations**, with detailed annexures containing prescribed forms and standards.

At a high level, the Directions require RCBs to implement a **formal institutional framework** for responsible business conduct, including governance arrangements, accountability, and internal processes to ensure that customer-facing activities are handled fairly and transparently. They also impose requirements on **branch customer service**, including clear customer guidance, disclosure practices, complaint-handling support, and service standards at the branch level. The customer-protection chapter expands these obligations by requiring banks to provide customers with understandable information about products and services, protect customers from unfair practices, and maintain procedures that reduce the risk of mis-selling or misunderstanding. The document further adds obligations related to **financial inclusion and accessibility**, indicating that RCBs must make services accessible to underserved or vulnerable customers and ensure that branch/service delivery arrangements do not exclude eligible customers.

The Directions also specifically regulate **payment and remittance services**, meaning RCBs must handle such services in a manner consistent with RBI’s conduct expectations, likely including proper disclosure, service reliability, and customer support for transaction issues. In the section on **deposit accounts and other liabilities**, the framework addresses account operations, claims, and liability-handling procedures; the annexes show that RBI has standardized several forms for **settlement of claims**, including cases involving **nomination or joint accounts with survivorship clauses** and cases where neither exists. The document defines “**accounts with survivorship clause**” as joint accounts styled as **“either or survivor,” “anyone or survivor,” “former or survivor,” “latter or survivor,” or similar wording**, which is important because those account types trigger specific claim-settlement procedures. The annexes also include prescribed formats for **inventory of locker contents**, **inventory of articles kept in safe custody**, and **indemnity/surety/disclaimer/affidavit forms**, showing that banks must follow standardized documentation when settling claims for deceased customers or releasing locker/safe-custody contents.

The most substantial operational change for lending is the chapter on **responsible lending conduct**, which indicates that RCBs must apply conduct controls throughout the lending lifecycle, from sourcing and disclosure to sanction, servicing, and recovery. The inclusion of a **Key Facts Statement** in the annexes indicates a requirement for standardized pre-disbursal disclosure of loan terms, likely to improve customer understanding of interest, fees, repayment obligations, and other material conditions. The “Rates at a quick glance” annex suggests RBI expects prominent disclosure of applicable rates/charges in a simplified form, while the “Comprehensive Notice Board” format indicates specific branch display requirements for customer-facing information. For compliance, this means product documentation, sanction letters, disclosures, and branch notice boards must be aligned to the prescribed RBI formats rather than left to bank discretion.

The document is organized into ten chapters, with **Chapter X – Repeal and Other Provisions** indicating that prior instructions on the subject are being superseded or consolidated, so compliance teams should verify which earlier circulars/instructions remain operative and which are replaced. The annexures are not merely illustrative; they include **mandatory formats** for notices, claim forms, affidavits, indemnities, and inventory records, all of which should be built into bank operating procedures. Because the Directions are updated as of **July 1, 2026**, compliance staff should treat the text as a living consolidation and confirm whether any provisions in the updated version carry later effective dates, transitional rules, or revised forms. Overall, the document establishes a detailed RBI conduct regime for RCBs that requires formal governance, transparent customer communication, standardized claim and locker procedures, accessibility measures, and more disciplined loan and deposit practices.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** are a consolidated KYC/AML/CFT framework for **rural co-operative banks**, issued under the RBI’s master-direction style rulemaking and updated as of **December 29, 2025**. The document is intended to prevent these institutions from being used for **money laundering (ML)** or **terrorist financing (TF)** and aligns bank procedures with India’s **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)** and **Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**, as well as FATF standards. For compliance teams, the key point is that the directions cover the full customer lifecycle: acceptance policies, customer identification, due diligence, beneficial ownership, ongoing monitoring, record retention, reporting to FIU-India, and handling of international-agency communications.

The directions apply specifically to **rural co-operative banks** and require them to maintain a formal **board-approved governance framework** for KYC/AML controls. Banks must have documented policies and procedures for customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification procedures (CIP), and customer due diligence (CDD), with higher scrutiny for riskier customers and simplified steps only where the rules expressly permit. The document also organizes obligations by customer type, including **individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial owners**, indicating that compliance officers must ensure the institution has distinct onboarding and verification workflows for each category rather than a single generic KYC process.

A major operational requirement is **ongoing due diligence** after account opening, not just at onboarding. Rural co-operative banks must monitor transactions and customer behavior for consistency with the expected profile, refresh KYC information as needed, and escalate unusual or suspicious activity through internal controls and reporting channels. The directions also require maintenance of KYC records and reporting obligations to **Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND)**, so institutions must be able to preserve identification, transaction, and due-diligence records in a way that supports regulatory inspection and suspicious activity analysis.

The document also addresses special handling for customers and situations subject to **international-agency communications** and other legal obligations, meaning banks must have a process to act on sanctions-style or cross-border regulatory inputs where applicable. Chapter XI indicates **repeal and saving** provisions, confirms that application of other laws is **not barred**, and provides interpretive guidance, so compliance teams should treat this as the controlling RBI KYC framework for rural co-operative banks while still continuing to apply other relevant statutory requirements. Because the excerpt provided is the table of contents and introduction, it does not show specific numeric thresholds, documentary standards, or exact deadlines for individual procedures, but it clearly signals a comprehensive, mandatory KYC/AML control regime that must be embedded across onboarding, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on “Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends” apply immediately upon issuance, and they govern all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs), meaning State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The directions replace and repeal the prior RBI directions, instructions, and guidelines on prudential norms for dividend declaration for RCBs, as referenced in the RBI circular dated November 28, 2025, subject to any saving provisions for actions taken before the new directions came into force.  

Under the new rules, an RCB may declare dividends only if it satisfies all of the following conditions for the financial year for which the dividend is proposed: it must meet the applicable regulatory capital requirement; its net non-performing asset (NNPA) ratio must be at or below 5%; it must have complied with Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements throughout that financial year; and it must have made all required provisions for impaired assets, income tax, employee benefits, and similar items. In addition, the dividend can only be paid out of the net profit of that same financial year, after making all statutory provisions and fully adjusting any accumulated losses.  

The directions also make clear that any prudential treatment involving reversal of excess provisions, dividend payments arising from such reversals, and unrealized profits from transfer of loans and Security Receipts guaranteed by the Government of India must be handled in accordance with the RBI’s separate “Rural Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk” Directions, 2025. When deciding whether to declare equity dividends, the Board of Directors must specifically assess the bank’s current and projected capital position against applicable capital requirements, the adequacy of provisions, and broader factors such as the economic environment and the bank’s profitability outlook.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational change is that dividend declaration is now explicitly conditioned on a documented prudential review of capital adequacy, asset quality, reserve/CRR/SLR compliance, provisioning completeness, and profitability, with a hard NNPA threshold of 5% for the relevant financial year. The directions took effect immediately on November 28, 2025, so any dividend decision made after issuance must conform to these requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025**, which apply specifically to **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**—that is, **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act, 1981**. The Directions **take effect on the day they are placed on RBI’s official website**; the title also notes an **“Updated as on April 1, 2026”** status, which is relevant for ensuring the version in use reflects subsequent updates by that date.

For financial statement preparation, every RCB must prepare its **Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account** for all business transacted **as on the last working day of the year or period concerned**, using the **forms in the Third Schedule of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, as substituted under Section 56. In compiling those statements, the bank must follow the **ICAI’s pronouncements on Accounting Standards**, but only **subject to RBI’s directions and guidelines**; in other words, where RBI has specific requirements, those override general ICAI guidance to the extent of any inconsistency.

The document then establishes a detailed framework for **presentation and disclosure in notes to accounts** and later adds **other compliance instructions** affecting items such as **inter-branch account provisioning for net debit balances, reconciliation of Nostro accounts and treatment of outstanding entries, transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds, provisioning for fraud, unreconciled balances, deferred tax liability on special reserves created under Section 36(1)(viii) of the Income Tax Act, payment of fees and allowances to directors, and restrictions on window dressing**. It also contains a **repeal and saving** section, indicates that the application of other laws is **not barred**, and provides interpretive guidance, meaning compliance teams should read these Directions alongside the Banking Regulation Act and other applicable law rather than treating them as the sole rulebook.

The operative legal basis is important: RBI states it is acting under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, along with other enabling provisions, and frames the Directions as necessary in the public interest. For compliance purposes, the key action point is that affected RCBs must ensure their statutory financial statements and disclosures are formatted and compiled in line with the specified BR Act forms and RBI-prescribed disclosure rules, and must also implement the separate controls and accounting treatments required for the other specified items once the Directions are in force.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** take **immediate effect** and apply to **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** (collectively, “RCBs”) as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The Directions are intended to create a system for disseminating credit information on wilful defaulters so lenders can prevent further institutional finance from being extended to them. Although issued for RCBs, the document states that the restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters and the provisions on large defaulters apply to **all Reserve Bank-regulated entities**, even if they are not “lenders” within the Directions’ defined term.

For **wilful defaulters**, an RCB must not grant any additional credit facility to a person/entity classified as a wilful defaulter by any lender, and this prohibition also extends to any **associated entity**. The restriction remains in place for **one year after the wilful defaulter’s name is removed** from the List of Wilful Defaulters. RCBs are also barred from granting credit for the **floating of new ventures** to the wilful defaulter or any associated entity for **five years after removal** from the list. If an associated entity is no longer associated with the wilful defaulter, the penal restrictions cease to apply to that entity. Restructuring of wilful defaulters or their associated entities must follow the Reserve Bank’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025**.

The Directions define when an entity is “associated” with a wilful defaulter. If the wilful defaulter is a **company**, association includes a **subsidiary**, a **joint venture**, or an **associate company** under the Companies Act, 2013. If the wilful defaulter is a **natural person**, then all entities where the person is a **promoter**, **director**, or otherwise **in charge of and responsible for management** are deemed associated. This means the credit restrictions can reach multiple related entities, not just the named defaulter.

The document also includes a reporting framework for **wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, indicating that RCBs will have specific reporting obligations, including submission of a **List of Large Defaulters** in the prescribed format set out in **Annex I**. However, the excerpt provided cuts off before the detailed reporting requirements, thresholds, or timelines in Chapter III are fully visible, so a compliance team should review the full text to confirm the exact reporting triggers, due dates, and submission mechanics. There is also a Chapter IV on **repeal and other provisions**, but the substantive content is not shown in the excerpt.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025**, issued on **November 28, 2025** and updated as of **July 1, 2026**, set out a comprehensive framework for **early identification, reporting, and time-bound resolution of stressed assets** in rural co-operative banks. The directions also **rationalize and harmonize rules on compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, with the stated goal of improving resolution outcomes across the sector. RBI notes that some RCBs may be involved in state government **Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)** that waive or sacrifice debt obligations for targeted borrowers in exchange for fiscal support, and it highlights the prudential and credit-discipline risks if such schemes are frequent or poorly designed, including delayed recoveries, mismatches between amounts claimed and amounts admitted by government, and mandatory requirements to extend fresh credit.

For compliance purposes, the document applies to **Rural Co-operative Banks** and establishes a requirement for **board-approved policies** governing stress recognition and resolution, which means each bank must have formally approved internal policies rather than ad hoc case handling. It requires **early identification of stress** and **reporting**, so institutions must monitor accounts proactively and escalate signs of stress before default becomes severe. The directions also impose **disclosure obligations**, meaning banks must make the prescribed stress/resolution information available in the manner required by the RBI framework. Where an account is being restructured, the prudential norms in the document govern how restructuring may be done, implying that restructuring cannot be used informally to mask asset quality issues.

The directions contain specific treatment for **special cases**, including **compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, which are now brought within a harmonized RBI framework. They also create a dedicated chapter for **resolution of accounts impacted by calamities**, assigning roles to the **State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC)**, **Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committee (UTLBC)**, and **District Consultative Committee (DCC)** in coordinating responses. Banks must then **implement the resolution plan** in accordance with the directions, use the specified **ancillary measures**, and comply with **reporting requirements** for such calamity-affected accounts. The structure indicates that relief in disaster situations is not discretionary or informal; it must follow a documented committee-led process and bank implementation steps.

The document also addresses **Government Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)** and sets prudential treatment for those schemes, reflecting RBI’s concern that relief measures should not undermine credit discipline or create unrecognized exposure. In addition, it includes **special trade relief measures**, though the excerpt does not give the detailed mechanics in the text provided. Finally, the directions include standard legal clauses on **repeal and saving**, confirm that **other applicable laws are not barred unless expressly overridden**, and reserve RBI’s power of interpretation. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that RCBs must align internal policies, monitoring, reporting, restructuring, write-off, compromise settlement, and government-relief handling processes to this RBI framework, and should ensure board approval, documentation, and timely reporting are in place across all stressed-asset workflows.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI circular issues the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025**, and states that they **came into force immediately** on **28 November 2025**.
