The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026** apply specifically to **all Payments Banks** and cover the banks’ **digital payment products and services**, whether provided directly by the bank or through an RBI-operated system or a system operated by an RBI-authorised Payment System Operator (PSO). The scope is broad and includes both **financial and non-financial transaction functionality**, such as **balance enquiry, PIN set/change, mobile banking registration, OTP generation, mini-statements, transaction status checks, and customer dispute/grievance raising**, along with the related **IT assets, applications, systems, and infrastructure** supporting those services. The Directions are issued under RBI’s powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **Chapter IV of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.

The Directions are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Supervisory Directions, 2026** and **take effect immediately upon issuance**. The document is structured around board governance, general security controls, internet banking controls, mobile payments application controls, card payment controls, and repeal/saving provisions, indicating that compliance is not limited to one channel but extends across the full digital payments ecosystem of a payments bank. Although the excerpt provided does not yet detail the substantive control requirements chapter-by-chapter, it makes clear that the Directions establish a supervisory framework for **security risk governance, authentication, fraud risk management, reconciliation, customer protection, awareness, and grievance redressal** in relation to covered digital payment activities.

A compliance team should note that the document expressly treats the covered services and the associated technical environment as part of the regulated scope, so obligations will likely attach not only to customer-facing features but also to the supporting infrastructure and control environment. The definitions section begins by adopting terms from the **Financial Stability Board (FSB) Cyber Lexicon** unless otherwise stated, including key cyber-risk concepts such as **availability** and **confidentiality**, signaling that the directions are intended to be interpreted using a cyber-security and operational-risk lens. No specific deadline beyond immediate commencement is stated in the provided text, but the immediate-effect language means payments banks would need to assess current digital payment offerings and supporting systems against the Directions without waiting for a phased implementation date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Payments Banks - Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026”** sets a comprehensive, mandatory technology-risk and cybersecurity regime for **payments banks**. It is issued by the RBI Department of Supervision and is dated **July 31, 2026**; the document is intended to replace or formalize the minimum governance, security, resilience, and assurance expectations that payments banks must implement across their technology stack and third-party arrangements. The directions cover board oversight, senior-management responsibilities, IT governance, risk management, baseline cybersecurity controls, logging/monitoring, patch and vulnerability management, customer authentication, secure communications, crypto controls, straight-through processing, and continuous surveillance.

A major focus is **board-level accountability**. Payments banks must have **board-approved policies** for IT, information security, cybersecurity, risk management, and resilience, and the board is expected to oversee these through dedicated committees and formal reporting. The framework requires clear assignment of roles across the **Board, IT Strategy Committee, senior management, IT Steering Committee, Information Security Committee, Head of IT, and Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)**, with the CISO having a defined assurance and security leadership role rather than a purely operational one. The document also requires structured IT governance, IT project management, architecture control, and IT services management, meaning technology decisions are not left to ad hoc operational teams.

The directions impose a **formal IT and information-security risk management process**. Payments banks must periodically review IT-related risks, maintain an IT/security risk management framework, and document risk identification and assessment in a way that supports ongoing oversight and auditability. The document goes beyond general risk statements and requires specific baseline cybersecurity and resilience controls, including **inventory management of information assets, data leak prevention, controls over data migration, prevention of unauthorized software execution, physical/environmental safeguards, capacity management, secure configuration, network security, application security life-cycle controls, audit-log monitoring, patch/vulnerability/change management, user-access controls, teleworking controls, customer authentication, secure mail/messaging, removable-media controls, third-party controls, cryptographic controls, straight-through processing controls, and continuous surveillance**.

The third-party provisions are especially important for compliance teams: any outsourcing or external technology arrangement must be governed through formal controls, not treated as a substitute for the bank’s own accountability. The framework makes clear that security obligations continue even when services are delivered by vendors, cloud providers, or other outsourced parties, so contracts, oversight, monitoring, and assurance mechanisms must be in place. The presence of requirements on **secure configuration, logging, patching, access management, and continuous surveillance** indicates an expectation of active, ongoing defense and detection rather than a one-time implementation exercise.

Because the text provided is only the table of contents and introductory header, **no specific effective date, grace period, numerical threshold, or deadline is visible in the excerpt** beyond the document date itself (**July 31, 2026**). For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these directions are a broad and detailed supervisory framework for payments banks’ technology and cybersecurity programs, and they likely require a gap assessment against existing policies, board governance, security tooling, monitoring practices, and vendor-management controls to determine what must be updated to meet RBI expectations.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks - Compliance Function Directions, 2026** establish mandatory minimum standards for the **compliance function of all Payments Banks** in India, effective **immediately upon issuance on July 31, 2026**. The RBI frames compliance as a core part of corporate governance and assurance, alongside internal audit and risk management, and states that although the directions set minimum standards, each bank must organize its compliance framework in a way that is proportionate to its **size, complexity, risk profile, and organizational structure**. The directions are issued under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply specifically to **Payments Banks**, referred to collectively as “banks” and individually as “bank.”

For governance, the document requires the **Board** to approve and oversee the compliance policy and ensure the bank has an effective compliance function, while **senior management** must implement the policy and maintain an effective compliance culture. The bank must adopt a formal **compliance policy** that covers the structure, roles, responsibilities, escalation procedures, staffing, reporting lines, monitoring, and governance of the compliance function. The directions also extend the compliance expectation to **bank-led Financial Conglomerates**, requiring group-wide compliance risk management where relevant.

The document sets out requirements on the **scope, structure, staffing, and responsibilities** of the compliance function, including clear segregation of duties and defined accountability across the organization. It also requires the bank to maintain a **compliance culture**, meaning compliance obligations should be embedded in business processes and staff conduct, not treated as a standalone checklist. In addition, the bank must have **quality assurance** over the compliance function and integrate compliance oversight with **internal audit** arrangements to ensure ongoing effectiveness.

A significant governance requirement is the appointment of a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**. The CCO must have appropriate **authority, stature, independence, and access to the Board/senior management**, and the directions prescribe reporting requirements and specific responsibilities for that role. The bank must ensure the CCO’s position is sufficiently senior and independent to supervise compliance risk and raise issues without undue interference, and the CCO is expected to be a central point for compliance reporting and oversight.

The directions also require the use of **technology for monitoring compliance**, indicating that banks should employ technological tools to help identify, track, and manage compliance risk and obligations more effectively. Finally, the document includes **repeal and saving provisions**, states that other applicable laws are **not barred** by these directions, and provides interpretation provisions to clarify how the directions should be read and applied.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Local Area Banks (Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026** under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (and other enabling powers), addressed to **local area banks (LABs)**. The document is a supervisory directions compendium that brings together requirements on fair-practice interest charging, treatment of inoperative/unclaimed accounts, fraud prevention, protected disclosures, vigilance, network management, and cyber-security controls for third-party ATM switch application service providers. It appears to be a binding supervisory framework for LABs, with the stated date of issuance being **31 July 2026**.

For compliance purposes, the most immediate takeaway from the excerpt is that LABs must follow RBI requirements on **charging interest fairly**, and on **identifying, handling, and reporting inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits** in accordance with the specific chapter-level directions referenced in the table of contents. The directions also impose a detailed **fraud-prevention framework**, including controls for frauds involving **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, **fake title deeds of property**, **safe custody of critical documents**, and **accounts opened by employees**; these topics indicate that LABs must maintain formal preventive controls, document custody safeguards, and employee-account monitoring processes. In addition, the RBI has included a **Protected Disclosure Scheme**, which means banks must have a mechanism for receiving and processing complaints/whistleblower disclosures under a protected reporting framework, along with a protected disclosure policy and a defined complaint procedure.

The document also contains extensive **vigilance requirements**, including rules on the **Chief of Internal Vigilance** (appointment, tenure, involvement in sensitive matters, and reporting/review of returns), as well as **preventive vigilance**, **staff rotation**, and **mandatory leave**. LABs will need to maintain complaint-handling and investigation arrangements, including the use of an **investigation agency** where applicable, periodic **review of cases entrusted to investigating agencies**, procedures for action against persons making **false complaints**, and liaison with external agencies. These obligations suggest a formal internal-control and disciplinary architecture that compliance, HR, audit, and vigilance teams would need to coordinate and evidence through policies, records, and periodic reporting.

The directions further address **network management** and, importantly, **cyber-security controls for third-party ATM switch application service providers**, indicating that LABs that outsource ATM switching functions must ensure appropriate cyber controls, oversight, and governance over those vendors. The final chapter also includes **repeal and saving** provisions, an **application-of-other-laws-not-barred** clause, and an **interpretation** section, which means the new directions are intended to sit alongside other applicable legal/regulatory requirements rather than replace them entirely. Because the excerpt provided is largely the table of contents and introductory citation, it does not show the chapter-by-chapter operational thresholds or specific technical parameters, but it clearly establishes that LABs are subject to a comprehensive RBI compliance regime across deposits, fraud, vigilance, and outsourced technology oversight, effective from the date of the 2026 directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Supervisory Returns Directions, 2026** apply **only to Local Area Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related RBI enabling powers, and they define “supervisory returns” broadly to cover **all periodic and ad-hoc data submitted to RBI**, regardless of the technology platform, frequency, or submission method. They also define **CIMS** as RBI’s online platform for return submission and related data dissemination.

From a governance perspective, the document requires the **Board and senior management** of each LAB to treat **data quality risk** as part of the overall risk management framework. That framework must explicitly cover standards for **in-house and outsourced data-related processes**, and include policies addressing **data confidentiality, integrity, availability, and risk management**. The bank must also ensure that its **risk data aggregation capabilities and risk reporting practices are fully documented** and subject to **high validation standards**; the visible text cuts off after this point, so additional detail may appear later in the document.

Because the document is titled “Supervisory Returns,” the main compliance impact is that LABs must follow RBI’s prescribed processes for submitting returns and data, including any return formats, periodicity, and ad hoc reporting instructions that RBI may specify from time to time. Compliance teams should note that the directions are not limited to a particular return type or filing channel; they appear designed to impose an umbrella framework over all supervisory data submissions made by LABs to RBI. The table of contents also shows separate chapters on **filing of supervisory returns**, **timelines**, **exceptions**, **penalties**, and **other instructions**, indicating that the final document includes operational submission requirements and consequences for non-compliance, though those specific provisions are not contained in the excerpt provided.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** apply to all **Local Area Banks** and govern the **appointment and reappointment of Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs)** and **Statutory Auditors (SAs)**, with SCAs used for banks that also appoint separate **Statutory Branch Auditors (SBAs)**. The Directions were issued under **Section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **come into effect immediately upon issuance**; the document is dated **July 31, 2026**.  

At a high level, the RBI is establishing a formal audit-governance framework for LABs covering board and senior management oversight, auditor eligibility and independence, professional standards, tenure and rotation, audit fees/expenses, appointment procedures, and detailed requirements for the **Long Form Audit Report (LFAR)**. The table of contents shows that the Directions require specific procedures for both the **Statutory Central Auditor LFAR** and the **Statutory Branch Auditor LFAR**, including objectives, strategy, scope, coverage, and indicative coverage requirements, indicating that audit work must be documented in a structured and prescribed manner rather than left to bank discretion.  

The document also makes clear that it is not just advisory guidance: it is a binding regulatory direction intended to standardize how LAB statutory audits are carried out and how auditors are selected, retained, and supervised. Compliance teams should therefore treat the issuance date as the operative effective date for any new appointment or reappointment decisions, and ensure the bank’s audit governance, auditor due diligence, and LFAR reporting processes are aligned to the new RBI framework.  

Only the opening portion of the document is visible in the provided text, so the specific numerical limits, eligibility thresholds, rotation periods, fee rules, or detailed LFAR content are not available here; however, the structure shows those substantive requirements are covered in the later chapters and annexes and would need to be reviewed in full before finalizing any audit appointment or compliance implementation plan.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026** on **July 31, 2026**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance**. They apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)**, which are referred to collectively as “banks” in the directions. The core policy change is that LABs are required to move away from a purely transaction-checking internal audit model and instead adopt a **Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework that evaluates risk management systems and internal controls, while still performing selective transaction testing.

From a compliance and governance standpoint, the document establishes that internal audit is a key part of the bank’s internal control and risk management architecture, and it is being mandated under **Section 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling RBI powers. The directions are structured to require board-level oversight, senior management execution, a formal RBIA policy, functional independence of the audit function, periodic risk assessment, defined audit scope and communication standards, performance evaluation of the internal audit function, and rules for outsourcing. Although the excerpt shown stops before the detailed chapter provisions, the table of contents and introduction make clear that the full directions also require appointment, authority, tenure, and reporting-line arrangements for the **Head of Internal Audit**, plus repeal/saving and interpretive provisions.

For a compliance team, the immediate action implication is that an LAB’s internal audit framework must be reviewed or redesigned to ensure it is explicitly **risk-based**, not merely transaction-oriented, and aligned with RBI expectations and broader governance standards. The board is expected to have oversight responsibility, while senior management must operationalize the framework, including controls around independence, scope setting, reporting, and evaluation. Because the directions are effective immediately, banks should treat implementation as an immediate compliance obligation rather than a future-dated transition requirement.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks (LABs) – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026**, issued on **July 31, 2026** and cited as **RBI/DoS/2026-27/446** / **DoS.CO.FMG.40/23.04.001/2026-27**, establish a mandatory fraud-risk framework for LABs covering **prevention, early detection, and timely reporting** of fraud to both **law enforcement agencies (LEAs)** and the **RBI**, along with RBI-led dissemination of fraud information. The Directions are issued under the RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and apply specifically to **Local Area Banks**. They replace or consolidate prior RBI instructions on this subject through a **repeal-and-saving** framework, while preserving actions already taken under earlier directions.

At a governance level, LABs must maintain a formal **fraud risk management governance structure** and an **early warning signals (EWS)/red-flagging framework** to detect potential fraud in time. The document distinguishes between (i) **credit facilities/loan accounts** and (ii) **other banking / non-credit related transactions**, and requires LABs to build processes that identify suspicious patterns and escalate them promptly. Once a credit facility or loan account is classified as a **red-flagged account**, the bank must follow the prescribed fraud-reporting and escalation process, and the Directions also address how accounts under resolution are to be treated to avoid inappropriate delay or dilution of fraud action.

The Directions require LABs to **report fraud incidents to law enforcement agencies** and separately **report frauds to the Reserve Bank of India**, including via the **Central Fraud Registry**. They also set out the **modalities for reporting incidents of fraud** and the **closure process for fraud cases already reported**, meaning banks must ensure their internal case-management and regulatory-reporting workflows are aligned so that reports are accurate, timely, and capable of being updated or closed in accordance with RBI procedure. A separate chapter specifically covers **cheque-related frauds**, requiring reporting to both LEAs and RBI under the dedicated framework, rather than treating them as ordinary operational incidents.

The Directions also impose several related compliance obligations beyond core reporting: LABs must carry out a **legal audit of title documents** in respect of **large value loan accounts**, and they must apply the prescribed treatment when accounts classified as **fraud** are **sold to other lenders or asset reconstruction companies (ARCs)** so that fraud tagging and regulatory consequences are not lost in transfer. The document also sets out the **role of auditors**, indicating that audit functions are part of the fraud-control architecture and not merely a retrospective review. Additionally, there are specific provisions for reporting **theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**, reflecting that not all loss events are handled identically and that these incidents have their own reporting expectations.

Finally, the Directions include **staff accountability and penal measures**, meaning individual employee involvement, negligence, or lapses in fraud handling may trigger internal accountability actions, and the bank must have procedures to enforce consequences where required. The document also states that its provisions coexist with **other applicable laws**, so compliance with these Directions does not displace criminal, civil, or other regulatory obligations arising under separate statutes. For a compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that LABs need a documented, end-to-end fraud framework spanning detection, internal escalation, regulatory and police reporting, account tagging/classification controls, audit verification, and closure tracking, all implemented under the 2026 RBI Directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Concurrent Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Concurrent Audit Directions, 2026** apply to **all Local Area Banks** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. RBI issues them under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and related enabling powers, with the stated objective of ensuring that concurrent audit serves as an early-warning control mechanism to detect serious errors, irregularities, fraudulent transactions, and other control failures quickly.

For governance, the **Audit Committee of the Board (ACB)** must **approve the detailed scope** of the concurrent audit. The ACB is also required to set both **the maximum tenure for external concurrent auditors** and **their remuneration**, and it must **review the effectiveness of the concurrent audit system and the auditors’ performance annually**, taking whatever corrective or strengthening measures are needed. This makes the ACB directly responsible for the design, oversight, and periodic reassessment of the audit function.

The document defines an **“Audit Firm”** broadly to include a **proprietorship firm, partnership firm, or LLP**. It also states that unless otherwise defined, terms carry the meanings given under the **RBI Act, 1934**, **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **Companies Act, 2013**, any statutory modification or re-enactment, other RBI regulations, RBI’s Glossary of Terms, or ordinary commercial usage as applicable.

Although the excerpt provided cuts off at the start of Chapter III’s “Coverage” section, the operative requirements visible already establish that Local Area Banks must have a board-approved concurrent audit framework, that external concurrent auditors are subject to ACB-determined tenure and pay, and that the ACB must conduct an annual effectiveness review. A compliance team should therefore treat these directions as immediately binding on LABs and ensure the bank’s governance documents, audit charter, and ACB processes reflect these responsibilities.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Compliance Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Compliance Function) Directions, 2026**, dated **July 31, 2026**, under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling powers. These Directions apply specifically to **Local Area Banks (LABs)** and are effective **immediately upon issuance**. RBI states that the compliance function is a core part of corporate governance and an assurance function alongside internal audit and risk management, and that the framework is aligned with the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision** but adapted for the Indian environment, including **bank-led financial conglomerates** for group-wide compliance risk management.

The core requirement is that each LAB must maintain a **formal compliance function** with governance, staffing, independence, monitoring, and reporting arrangements that are **commensurate with the bank’s size, complexity, risk profile, and organisational structure**. The Board is responsible for oversight of the compliance framework, senior management must implement it, and the bank must have a **compliance policy** and defined compliance structure with clear responsibilities. The document indicates dedicated chapters on the **scope, structure, staffing, roles and responsibilities, compliance culture, quality assurance, and internal audit interface**, meaning compliance cannot be treated as an informal or purely control-room activity; it must be embedded in governance and operational processes.

A key named requirement is the appointment of a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)**, with specific provisions on **appointment, authority, stature, independence, reporting lines, and responsibilities**. The Directions also include a chapter on the **use of technology for monitoring**, indicating that banks are expected to employ technology-enabled compliance monitoring rather than relying solely on manual review. Although the excerpt does not reproduce the detailed definitions or chapter rules, the table of contents shows that the Directions also address **group-wide compliance**, implying obligations may extend beyond the standalone bank to entities within a bank-led group where applicable.

The document also contains a **repeal and saving** section, a statement that other laws are **not barred**, and an **interpretations** section, which means these Directions are intended to operate alongside existing legal/regulatory requirements rather than replace them entirely. In compliance terms, LABs should treat this as a new minimum supervisory framework requiring immediate gap assessment of current governance, policy documentation, CCO status, reporting lines, staffing adequacy, monitoring tools, and board/senior management oversight to ensure alignment with RBI’s prescribed compliance-function standards.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** were issued on **31 July 2026** and **take effect immediately upon issuance**. They apply to **all Regional Rural Banks** as defined under **section 5(ja) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The directions are issued under **section 35A read with section 51 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and related enabling powers.

The main substantive requirement is that every RRB must **review and, where needed, correct its lending and interest-charging practices** to ensure fairness and transparency. RBI specifically flags as unfair: charging interest **from the date of sanction or loan agreement instead of actual disbursement**; for cheque disbursements, charging interest **from the date the cheque is issued even if handed over later**; charging EMIs on the **sanctioned amount rather than the actual amount disbursed without borrower knowledge or consent**; failing to communicate any **changes to the amortisation schedule in the Key Facts Statement (KFS)** when a loan is disbursed in parts; charging **full-month interest when disbursement or repayment occurs partway through a month** instead of only for the period outstanding; and taking **advance instalments while still charging interest on the full loan amount**. RBI states these and similar non-standard interest practices are inconsistent with fair treatment of customers, so RRBs must make whatever **corrective action and system-level changes** are necessary to stop them.

The directions also indicate that RRBs **may use online account transfers instead of cheques for loan disbursal**, which is presented as an acceptable operational alternative to reduce the risk of the cheque-based interest issue. In the fraud-related provision, where there is a **prima facie case against loan-dealing officials**, the RRB must initiate action under **Central Vigilance Commission guidelines** for placing those officers in the **list of officers with doubtful integrity**, and this must be done **in consultation with the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)**. The final chapter also repeals prior directions to the extent specified while preserving actions already taken under them, and clarifies that these directions do not bar application of other laws or RBI powers, with interpretive issues to be resolved in accordance with the stated RBI/legal framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026** establish a mandatory framework for **prevention, early detection, red-flagging, investigation support, and timely reporting of fraud incidents** by RRBs to **law enforcement agencies (LEAs)** and **NABARD**, with NABARD also expected to disseminate relevant fraud information. The directions are issued under RBI’s powers under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and they **take effect immediately upon issuance** (dated **July 31, 2026**). They apply to **Regional Rural Banks**, and the document is structured to cover governance, early warning signals, red-flagged accounts, fraud reporting, treatment of resolved accounts, interactions with third parties/professionals, staff accountability, auditor roles, and reporting of theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery.  

A key compliance requirement is that RRBs must maintain a **board-level or equivalent governance structure** for fraud risk management, with defined internal responsibilities for monitoring, escalation, and reporting. The framework specifically requires banks to implement **Early Warning Signal (EWS)** mechanisms and a **Red Flagging of Accounts (RFA)** process for both **credit facilities/loan accounts** and **other banking/non-credit transactions**, so institutions must be able to detect suspicious conduct early, classify accounts appropriately, and trigger investigative and reporting actions without delay. The directions also require **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where those parties are used in connection with fraud-risk related work, which means banks cannot rely solely on internal assertions when validating facts relevant to fraud detection or reporting.  

For accounts identified as suspicious or fraudulent, the directions require a formal process to **classify a credit facility or loan account as a red-flagged account** and to **report fraud** in accordance with the prescribed framework. They also address **staff accountability and penal measures**, meaning employee involvement, negligence, or complicity in fraud-related events must be examined and may lead to disciplinary or other punitive action under the bank’s internal and regulatory processes. Where an account is under **resolution**, the directions provide specific treatment rules so that fraud-risk handling does not stop simply because recovery or restructuring is underway; compliance teams should assume fraud monitoring and reporting obligations continue notwithstanding resolution status.  

The directions also impose obligations on **reporting frauds to LEAs** and on **reporting incidents of fraud** more generally, including a separate chapter on **cheque-related frauds** that must be reported both to **law enforcement agencies** and to **NABARD**. Additional instructions cover the **legal audit of title documents for large-value loan accounts**, reflecting heightened due diligence expectations for collateral-backed exposures. If an account already classified as fraud is **sold to another lender or to an asset reconstruction company**, the document specifies how that account must continue to be treated, so sale/assignment does not eliminate fraud classification consequences. Finally, the directions recognize the role of **auditors** in fraud oversight and require reporting of **theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery** incidents as distinct events, indicating the bank’s incident-reporting obligations extend beyond classic fraud to other criminal losses as well.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** take effect **immediately upon issuance** and apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks**, defined as Primary Co-operative Banks under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 as applicable to co-operative societies. A key applicability carve-out is for **Chapter III (Prompt Corrective Action Framework)**: it applies only to **Tier 2, Tier 3, and Tier 4 UCBs**, **excluding banks currently under All Inclusive Directions (AID)**; **Tier 1 UCBs are not covered by Chapter III**, though they remain under enhanced supervisory monitoring, and **UCBs under AID continue under their existing AID conditions** until they exit AID, after which RBI will provide a suitable transition period before Chapter III applies.

The directions are issued under **Section 35-A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and supersede prior directions to the extent covered by the new framework (with repeal/saving provisions in Chapter VIII). The document consolidates several supervisory topics into one set of directions, including **core banking solution implementation**, the **prompt corrective action framework**, **fair practices in charging interest**, **nomination facility requirements**, **fraud prevention measures**, and **vigilance-related requirements**. For compliance teams, the practical significance is that the bank must map its obligations against these chapters based on its **tier classification** and whether it is under **AID**, because obligations differ materially by category.

Chapter III is the only part whose applicability is explicitly limited by tier, so compliance officers should verify whether the institution is in **Tier 2/3/4** and not under AID to determine whether the new PCA triggers, escalation, and supervisory response requirements apply. The direction also signals that **Tier 1 UCBs are not exempt from supervision**, but will be managed through the existing supervisory framework rather than the new Chapter III PCA provisions. Since the document states that the directions are effective on issuance, institutions should treat the requirements as immediately operative unless a specific chapter or provision elsewhere provides a transition arrangement.

If you want, I can also turn the full text into a **chapter-by-chapter compliance checklist** for UCB operations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
These Directions, issued by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 27 and Section 35-A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling provisions, are titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026** and **take effect immediately upon issuance** on **31 July 2026**. They apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The Directions define **“Supervisory Returns”** broadly to include **all periodic and ad-hoc data** submitted to RBI in the prescribed formats, regardless of the technology platform, submission frequency, or mode of submission, and define **CIMS** as RBI’s online platform for return submission and related data dissemination.

From a governance perspective, the document requires the **Board and Senior Management** of each UCB to explicitly include **identification, assessment, and management of data quality risks** as part of the bank’s overall risk management framework. It also places responsibility on the bank to maintain appropriate **data architecture and IT infrastructure** to support accurate supervisory reporting, and to ensure **accuracy and integrity in reporting**. In practical compliance terms, this means supervisory return submission is not treated as a purely operational task; it is a governance and control obligation requiring board-level oversight, management accountability, and robust reporting controls.

The Directions establish that UCBs must follow RBI-prescribed **operational guidelines** for filing supervisory returns, and they must comply with the **list of applicable returns** and associated **timelines** set out in the Directions and any related RBI instructions. The document indicates that there are specific provisions for **exceptions**, **penalties**, and **other instructions**, which means compliance teams must monitor whether a particular return is required, whether any exemption or special treatment applies, and whether delays, omissions, or inaccuracies could trigger consequences. Because “supervisory returns” includes both periodic and ad-hoc submissions, the obligation is ongoing and extends beyond routine scheduled reporting to any RBI-requested data submission.

The Directions also contain a **repeal and saving** framework, meaning prior inconsistent provisions are superseded to the extent covered by the new Directions, while certain prior actions or instructions may remain effective where preserved. They further state that the Directions do **not bar application of other laws**, so UCBs must continue to comply with other applicable legal and regulatory requirements in parallel. For compliance officers, the key operational takeaway is that the bank should ensure its reporting governance, systems, and escalation processes are aligned immediately with the new RBI framework, with particular attention to data quality controls, board oversight, and adherence to RBI-prescribed submission requirements through CIMS or other applicable channels.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI direction, issued on 31 July 2026 and effective immediately upon issuance, applies to Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and governs the appointment and reappointment of their statutory auditors. It distinguishes between UCBs that appoint separate Statutory Branch Auditors, where the lead auditor is referred to as a Statutory Central Auditor (SCA), and all other UCBs, where the term Statutory Auditor (SA) applies. The document is issued under section 30(1A) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, read with section 56 of the Act as applicable to co-operative societies, and states that it supersedes prior RBI directions on this subject subject to saving provisions, while leaving other laws and interpretations not barred by the directions applicable.

The document’s scope is broader than just appointment mechanics: it establishes governance and oversight expectations for the board and senior management, and sets out eligibility, independence, professional standards, tenure/rotation, audit fees and expenses, and the appointment procedure for auditors. The compliance team should note that the directions are intended to govern both initial appointment and reappointment of auditors, so annual or periodic auditor renewal decisions must be aligned with these requirements. The text also defines relevant institution categories such as All India Financial Institutions, including NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, EXIM Bank, and NaBFID, as well as other banking and co-operative banking terms used throughout the directions.

Although the excerpt provided cuts off before the substantive clauses and Annexures, the table of contents shows that the operative requirements are organized around: board/senior management responsibilities; the permissible number of SCAs/SAs and branch coverage; auditor eligibility criteria; independence requirements; professional standards; tenure and rotation rules; fee and expense rules; and the formal appointment process. For compliance purposes, this means the bank should expect explicit restrictions and procedural steps around how many audit firms may be engaged, which firms are eligible, how independence is assessed, how long auditors may serve before rotation is required, and what governance approvals/documentation are needed for appointment or reappointment. Because the Directions took effect immediately on issuance, UCBs should treat the rules as currently binding from 31 July 2026 onward and ensure audit-planning, board approvals, and audit committee processes are aligned without delay.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026** on **31 July 2026** under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, to establish a harmonized, risk-based internal audit framework for **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**. The stated purpose is to strengthen internal audit as the **third line of defence** and ensure the Board and senior management receive assurance on the adequacy and effectiveness of internal controls, risk management, and governance. These Directions replace fragmented practices with a uniform set of requirements covering governance, audit design, independence, staffing, reporting, outsourcing, and audit coverage.

The Directions apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks**, with the internal audit function required to be structured around a **Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA)** framework. UCBs must have a formal internal audit policy approved by the Board, and the policy must define the objectives, scope, authority, independence safeguards, risk assessment process, annual audit planning, compliance monitoring, and any outsourcing arrangements. The Board remains responsible for overseeing the internal audit function, while senior management must ensure implementation, adequate staffing, and timely remediation of audit observations.

A key requirement is that internal audit must be **independent, sufficiently empowered, and not be assigned operational responsibilities that could compromise objectivity**. The Head of Internal Audit must have appropriate stature, direct reporting access, and independence from the activities being audited, with a defined reporting line to the Board/Audit Committee as specified in the Directions. The audit plan must be risk-based, derived from periodic risk assessments, and should focus audit resources on higher-risk areas rather than relying solely on fixed-cycle reviews.

The Directions also require UCBs to establish a clear system for **monitoring compliance with audit findings**, including tracking of exceptions, overdue rectifications, and reporting of unresolved issues to governance bodies. Where internal audit work is outsourced, the bank remains fully responsible for the quality, independence, confidentiality, and oversight of the outsourced function, and outsourcing cannot dilute management or Board accountability. The document further prescribes periodicity and minimum coverage expectations for inspection/internal audit activities, permits **special audits** where needed, and includes repeal/saving provisions along with interpretative rules for applying the Directions alongside other laws and RBI instructions.

In practical compliance terms, UCBs should expect to review and, if necessary, redesign their internal audit governance, risk assessment methodology, annual audit planning, reporting structure, and follow-up mechanisms to ensure alignment with these Directions by their effective date and any implementation timeline specified in the operative chapters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026** establish a mandatory fraud-risk framework for UCBs aimed at **prevention, early detection, prompt reporting to law enforcement agencies (LEAs), and reporting/dissemination to the RBI**. The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling powers, and they apply specifically to **urban co-operative banks**; the document is organized around governance, early warning signals, fraud reporting, cheque frauds, audit requirements, and treatment of fraud cases.

For compliance purposes, the most important operational requirement is that UCBs must maintain a **formal fraud risk management governance structure** and an **early warning signal (EWS) framework** to detect suspicious activity in both **credit facilities/loan accounts** and **other banking or non-credit transactions**. The bank must have procedures to identify and investigate indications of fraudulent activity, and it must obtain **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, where relevant. The directions also address **staff accountability** and **penal measures** where employee conduct is implicated, and they provide specific treatment rules for **accounts under resolution** that are relevant to fraud classification and reporting.

The directions require UCBs to report fraud incidents to both **LEAs and the RBI** using prescribed modalities, and they also create a separate reporting framework for **cheque-related frauds** to LEAs and RBI. They additionally require banks to report **cases of theft, burglary, dacoity, and robbery**, indicating that the framework is broader than classic credit fraud and covers physical loss/criminal incidents that may affect banking operations. The document also includes instructions on **closure of fraud cases reported to RBI**, meaning banks must follow a defined process before a reported case can be treated as closed in regulatory reporting.

Several other compliance points are expressly addressed: UCBs must carry out a **legal audit of title documents for large-value loan accounts**, and there are specific instructions for the **treatment of accounts classified as fraud and then sold to other lenders or asset reconstruction companies (ARCs)** so that the fraud classification and related obligations are not lost in transfer. The directions also describe the **role of auditors**, indicating that audit functions are expected to support fraud detection and compliance verification rather than being purely retrospective. A repeal-and-saving section is included, along with a statement that the directions do not bar the application of other laws, so UCBs must comply with these directions **in addition to** any applicable criminal, banking, or regulatory obligations.

The excerpt provided does **not include the detailed effective date, transition deadlines, numeric thresholds, or reporting timelines**, but the document title and issuance date indicate it is the **2026 RBI framework** and is intended to be immediately relevant to UCB fraud governance once in force. A compliance team should therefore review the full text for any exact timelines, thresholds, and form requirements embedded in the chapter provisions, especially those governing EWS triggers, fraud classification, LEA/RBI reporting, cheque fraud reporting, and closure procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026** were issued on **31 July 2026** and take effect **immediately upon issuance**. They apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks / Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under **Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and cover **digital payment products and services** offered by the UCB whether delivered directly by the bank or through RBI-operated systems or systems operated by RBI-authorised **Payment System Operators (PSOs)**. The scope explicitly includes both **financial and non-financial transactions**, such as **balance enquiry, PIN set/change, mobile banking registration, OTP generation, mini-statements, transaction status checks, and customer dispute/grievance raising**, along with the related IT assets supporting those services, including applications, systems, and infrastructure.

At a high level, the directions create a mandatory security framework for UCB digital payment activity and are organized around board oversight, governance and risk controls, application security, authentication, fraud management, reconciliation, customer protection, and channel-specific controls for internet banking, mobile apps, and card payments. The document states that the RBI is issuing these requirements under its authority in **Section 35-A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, and other enabling laws, indicating they are binding supervisory directions rather than advisory guidance.

The opening provisions also make clear that the directions incorporate technical definitions, largely drawn from the **Financial Stability Board (FSB) Cyber Lexicon**, unless otherwise specified. Although the excerpt provided does not yet include the detailed control prescriptions in later chapters, the table of contents shows that the regulations will require UCBs to implement formal **board-approved policies**, **general security controls**, an **application security lifecycle**, an **authentication framework**, **fraud risk management**, **reconciliation mechanisms**, and **customer protection/awareness/grievance redressal procedures**, plus distinct controls for **internet banking**, **mobile payment applications**, and **card payment security**.

From a compliance perspective, the key immediate takeaway is that this is a **bank-wide mandatory security control regime for UCB digital payment offerings**, effective immediately, with applicability tied to whether the bank offers any of the covered digital payment services or related transaction-support functions. UCBs should treat the issuance date as the start of the compliance clock and assess all impacted products, channels, outsourced or platform-dependent payment flows, and supporting IT assets against the eventual chapter-by-chapter requirements of the Directions.

Introduction Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are expected to lay down, with the approval of their boards, transparent policies and guidelines for credit dispensation, in respect of each broad category of economic activity, keeping in view the credit exposure norms and various other guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India from time to time. In order to ensure that the loan policy of the UCB reflects approved internal risk appetite and remains in alignment with the extant regulations, it shall be reviewed by the Board at least once in a financial year. 2. Working Capital Requirements 2.1 The assessment of working capital requirement of borrowers, other than micro and small enterprises, requiring fund based working capital limits up to ₹1 crore and micro and small enterprises requiring fund based working capital limits up to ₹5 crore from the banking system may be made on the basis of their projected annual turnover. 2.2 In accordance with these guidelines, the working capital requirement is to be assessed at 25% of the projected turnover to be shared between the borrower and the UCB, viz. borrower contributing 5% of the turnover as Net Working Capital (NWC) and UCB providing finance at a minimum of 20% of the turnover. Projected turnover may be interpreted as 'Gross Sales' including excise duty. 2.3 The UCBs may, at their discretion, carry out the assessment based on projected turnover basis or the traditional method. If the credit requirement based on traditional production / processing cycle is higher than the one assessed on projected turnover basis, the same may be sanctioned, as borrower must be financed up to the extent of minimum 20% of their projected annual turnover. The projected annual turnover would be estimated on the basis of annual statements of accounts or other documents such as returns filed with sales-tax / revenue authorities. Actual drawals may be allowed on the basis of drawing power to be determined by UCBs after excluding unpaid stocks. 2.4 Drawals against the limits should be allowed against the usual safeguards including drawing power and it is to be ensured that the same are used for the purpose intended. UCBs will have to ensure regular and timely submission of monthly statements of stocks, receivables, etc., by the borrowers and also periodical verification of such statements vis-à-vis physical stocks by their officials. 2.5 In respect of borrowers other than micro and small enterprises, requiring working capital limits above ₹1 crore and for micro and small enterprises/units requiring fund based working capital limits above ₹5 crore, UCBs may determine the working capital requirements according to their perception of the credit needs of borrowers. UCBs may adopt turnover method or cash budgeting method or any other method as considered necessary. However, UCBs may ensure that the book- debt finance does not exceed 75% of the limits sanctioned to borrowers for financing inland credit sales. The remaining 25% of the credit sales may be financed through bills to ensure greater use of bills for financing sales. Withdrawn 4 3. General 1.1 The role of primary (urban) co-operative banks (UCBs) in providing housing finance has been reviewed from time to time. These banks, with their vast network, occupy a very strategic position in the financial system and have an important role to play in providing credit to the housing sector. Further, housing finance to specified categories up to prescribed limits is treated as priority sector lending, and the need for UCBs providing credit to priority sector has come to be increasingly recognised consistent with the social objectives placed before the banking system. 1.2 Therefore, with a view to enabling the UCBs to play a more positive role in providing finance for housing schemes, particularly to the weaker sections of the community, these banks are permitted to grant loans for housing schemes up to certain limits from their own resources subject to the guidelines detailed hereunder. 1.3 Bigger banks that have large surplus resources may undertake larger lending for housing, as this will provide a remunerative avenue for investment of their surplus funds. 1.4 Wherever banks are still required to obtain special permission of the Registrar for financing housing societies, it is suggested that these banks should obtain general permission to finance housing societies subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed for the purpose. 2. (b) Housing boards undertaking housing projects or schemes for economically weaker sections (EWS), low income groups (LIG) and middle income groups (MIG). (c) Owners of houses / flats for extension and up-gradation, including major repairs. 3. Introduction Capital acts as a buffer in times of crisis or poor performance by a bank. Sufficiency of capital also instills depositors' confidence. As such, adequacy of capital is one of the pre- conditions for licensing of a new bank as well as its continuance in business. 2. Statutory Requirements In terms of the provisions contained in Section 11 of Banking Regulation Act (AACS), no co-operative bank shall commence or carry on banking business unless the aggregate value of its paid-up capital and reserves is not less than one lakh of rupees. In addition, under Section 22(3)(d) of the above Act, the Reserve Bank prescribes the minimum entry point capital (entry point norms) from time to time, for setting-up of a new Primary (Urban) Cooperative Bank. 3. Net Worth UCBs shall have minimum net worth as under: • Tier 1 1 UCBs operating in a single district shall have minimum net worth of ₹2 crore. • All other UCBs (of all tiers) shall have minimum net worth of ₹5 crore. • UCBs which currently do not meet the minimum net worth requirement, as above, shall achieve the minimum net worth of ₹2 crore or ₹5 crore (as applicable) in a phased manner. Such UCBs shall achieve at least 50 per cent of the applicable minimum net worth on or before March 31, 2026 and the entire stipulated minimum net worth on or before March 31, 2028. The computation of “Net worth” in this context is provided in Annex 1 . 4. Constitution of Board of Directors 1.1 Primary (urban) co-operative banks (UCBs or banks) have been functioning under the regulation and supervision of Reserve Bank of India (Reserve Bank or RBI) in terms of the powers vested in it inter alia under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (BR Act) and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (RBI Act). 1.2 The directors on the boards of UCBs must be knowledgeable and persons of high integrity. To ensure professionalism in the Board, banks should, at all times, have at least two professional directors, i.e., persons with suitable banking experience (at middle/senior management level) or with relevant professional qualification in the fields of law, accountancy or finance. Banks should also have a suitable provision in their byelaws to ensure this. However, these instructions would not be insisted upon in case of Salary Earners' Banks in view of the nature of their membership. 1.3 UCBs (other than those having deposit size less than Rs.100 crore and salary earners’ banks) are also required to constitute a Board of Management (BoM) to facilitate professional management and focused attention to their banking-related activities, by making suitable amendments to their bye-laws, in accordance with the guidelines contained in RBI circular DoR(PCB).BPD.Cir.No.8/12.05.002/2019-20 dated December 31, 2019. 1.4 Since the directors are elected from amongst the members (except co-opted and nominated directors), the persons who are not eligible for admission even as members cannot become directors of UCBs. In particular, persons engaged in money lending, financing and investment activities, either in individual capacity or as proprietor/partner/employee/director of any concern as also those convicted of any criminal offences including moral turpitude are ineligible in terms of clause b (ii) of the model by-law no.9 and/or the provisions contained in the co-operative societies law concerned. Besides, certain eligibility/qualification/disqualification criteria for becoming director in a UCB are also prescribed in the BR Act and the co-operative laws concerned. Withdrawn - 4 - 1.5 The recommendations made by the “Committee on Urban Co-operative Banks”, headed by Shri Madhava Das, regarding the Board of Directors of UCBs and recommended by the Reserve Bank for adoption by the banks are given in Annex 1. 1.6 It was observed during the course of supervisory reviews that some of the UCBs have adopted the practice of creating honorary designations (remunerated or otherwise) / conferring titles at Board level, such as Chairman Emeritus, Group Chairman, etc., which are not recognised in applicable statutes or regulations. While such positions/titles may be indicative of certain privileges/rights for the incumbent to access all board materials and participate in board/committee meetings, enforcing liability or obligations on such person may be difficult. Such positions may be seen as creating conflicts of interest as well as creation of a parallel or shadow authority impeding effective and independent functioning of the legally constituted board in the best interest of all its stakeholders. As such, UCBs are directed not to create any honorary positions/titles at Board level or confer such titles that are non-statutory in nature 1 . 2. Role of directors 2.1 The Board of Directors (BOD or Board) is primarily concerned with formulation of policies keeping in view the applicable statutory provisions and the guidelines issued by the RBI. The Board should also exercise overall supervision and control over the functioning of the bank, leaving the day-to-day administration to the Managing Director

INTRODUCTION Banks, with their vast branch network throughout the length and breadth of the country, occupy a very strategic position in the financial system and have an important role to play in providing credit to the housing sector. 2. VARIOUS REGULATIONS While formulating their policies, banks have to take into account the following RBI guidelines and ensure that bank credit is used for production, construction activities and not for activities connected with speculation in real estate. (A ) ACQUISITION OF LAND Bank finance can be granted only for purchase of a plot, provided a declaration is obtained from the borrower that he intends to construct a house on the said plot, with the help of bank finance or otherwise, within such period as may be laid down by the banks themselves. (B ) CONSTRUCTION OF BUILDING / READY-BUILT HOUSE (i) Banks may grant loans to individuals for purchase/construction of dwelling unit per family and loans for repairs to the damaged dwelling units of families. (ii) Banks may extend finance to a person who already owns a house in town/village where he resides, for buying/ constructing a second house in the same or other town/ village for the purpose of self-occupation. (iii) Banks may extend finance for purchase of a house by a borrower who proposes to let it out on rental basis on account of his posting outside the headquarters or because he has been provided accommodation by his employer. (iv) Banks may extend finance to a person who proposes to buy an old house where he is presently residing as a tenant. (v) Banks may finance for construction meant for improving the conditions in slum areas for which credit may be extended directly to the slum-dwellers on the guarantee of the Government, or indirectly to them through the State Governments. (vi) Banks may provide credit for slum improvement schemes to be implemented by Slum Clearance Boards and other public agencies. Withdrawn 5 (vii) Banks are advised to also adhere to the following conditions, in the light of the observations of Delhi High Court on unauthorized construction: (a) In cases where the applicant owns a plot/land and approaches the banks/FIs for a credit facility to construct a house, a copy of the sanctioned plan by competent authority in the name of a person applying for such credit facility must be obtained by the Banks/FIs before sanctioning the home loan. (b) An affidavit-cum-undertaking must be obtained from the person applying for such credit facility that he shall not violate the sanctioned plan, construction shall be strictly as per the sanctioned plan and it shall be the sole responsibility of the executants to obtain completion certificate within 3 months of completion of construction, failing which the bank shall have the power and the authority to recall the entire loan with interest, costs and other usual bank charges. The enclosed Master Circular consolidates the circulars issued by Reserve Bank on the subject till date, as listed in the Appendix. Yours faithfully, (R. Giridharan) Chief General Manager , � ,10 , , , � � . 10014, -400001 Financial Inclusion & Development Dept., Central Office,10th Floor, Central Office Building, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg,P.B.No.10014,Mumbai-1 Tel:022-22601000 � 91-22-22621011/22610943/22610948 - : cgmincfidd@rbi.org.in , “ : - � , � �� , " Caution: RBI never sends mails, SMSs or makes calls asking for personal information like bank account details, passwords, etc. It never keeps or offers funds to anyone. Please do not respond in any manner to such offers. 2 Master Circular - Credit Facilities to Scheduled Castes (SCs) & Scheduled Tribes (STs) Banks should take the measures indicated below to step up their advances to SCs/STs. 1. Planning Process 1.1 The District Level Consultative Committees formed under the Lead Bank Scheme should continue to be the principal mechanism of co-ordination between banks and development agencies in this regard. The district credit plans formulated by the Lead Banks should clearly indicate the linkage of credit with employment and development schemes. 1.2 Banks will have to establish closer liaison with the District Industries Centres, which have been set up in different districts for promoting self-employment. 1.3 At the block level, a certain weightage is to be given to SCs/STs in the planning process. Accordingly, the credit planning should be weighted in their favour and special bankable schemes suited to them should be drawn up to ensure their participation and larger flow of credit to them for self-employment. It will be necessary for the banks to consider their loan proposals with utmost sympathy and understanding. 1.4 Banks should periodically review their lending procedures and policies to see that loans are sanctioned in time, are adequate and production-oriented and that they generate incremental income to make them self-liquidating. 1.5 While formulating the Block/ District Credit Plan, special focus may be given to villages with sizeable population of SC/ST communities/ specific localities (bastis) in the towns/villages having a concentration of these communities. 3 2. Role of Banks 2.1 Bank staff may help the borrowers in filling up the forms and completing other formalities so that they are able to get credit facility within a stipulated period from the date of receipt of applications. 2.2 In order to encourage SC/ST borrowers to take advantage of credit facilities, greater awareness among them about various schemes formulated by banks needs to be created through various means such as brochures, visits by field staff etc so that salient features of the schemes, as also the advantages that will accrue to them are known to such borrowers. Banks should advise their branches to organize meetings more frequently exclusively for SC/ST beneficiaries to understand their credit needs and to incorporate the same in the credit plan. 2.3 Circulars issued by RBI/NABARD should be circulated among the staff for compliance. 2.4 Banks should not insist on deposits while considering loan applications under Government sponsored poverty alleviation schemes/self-employment programmes from borrowers belonging to SCs/STs. It should also be ensured that applicable subsidy is not held back while releasing the loan component till the full repayment of bank dues. Non-release of subsidy upfront amounts to under-financing and hampers asset creation/income generation. 2.5 The National Scheduled Tribes Finance & Development Corporation and National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation have been set up under the administrative control of Ministry of Tribal Affairs and Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment, respectively. Banks should advise their branches/controlling offices to render all the necessary institutional support to enable these institutions to achieve the desired objectives. 2.6. Loans sanctioned to State Sponsored Organisations for Scheduled Castes/ Scheduled Tribes for the specific purpose of purchase and supply of inputs and/or the marketing of the outputs of the beneficiaries of these organisations are eligible for priority sector classification. 4 2.7 Rejection of SC/STs’ loan applications under government programmes should be done at the next higher level instead of at the branch level and reasons of rejection should be clearly indicated. 3. Role of SC/ST Development Corporations The

information/data 2.3.6 Liaison with State Government 2.3.7 Capacity Building/Training/Sensitization Programmes 3 Implementation of Lead Bank Scheme 3.1 Preparation of credit plans 3.2 Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs) 3.3 Monitoring the performance of credit plans 3.4 Revised mechanism of Data Flow for LBS fora meetings 4 Assignment of Lead Bank Responsibility 5 Banking Penetration 5.1 Roadmap for provision of banking services in unbanked villages 5.2 Roadmap for opening brick and mortar branches in villages with population more than 5000 without a bank branch of a scheduled commercial bank 5.3 Aligning roadmap for unbanked villages having population more than 5000 with revised guidelines on Branch Authorisation Policy 5.4 National Strategy for Financial Inclusion (NSFI): 2019-2024 – Universal Access to Financial Services 6 Credit Deposit Ratio 6.1 CD Ratio of banks in Rural and Semi-Urban Areas 6.2 Implementation of the recommendations of Expert Group on CD Ratio 7 Direct Benefit Transfer 8 Service Area Approach (SAA) 8.1 Dispensing with ‘No Due Certificate’ 9 Enhancing Farmers’ Income 10 Expanding and Deepening of Digital Payments Ecosystem 3 Introduction (i) The genesis of the Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) can be traced to the Study Group headed by Prof. D. R. Gadgil (Gadgil Study Group) on the Organizational Framework for Implementation of the Social Objectives, which submitted its report in October 1969. The Study Group drew attention to the fact that commercial banks did not have adequate presence in rural areas and also lacked the required rural orientation. The Study Group, therefore, recommended the adoption of an 'Area Approach' to evolve plans and programmes for the development of an adequate banking and credit structure in the rural areas. (ii) A Committee of Bankers on Branch Expansion Programme of Public Sector Banks (PSBs) appointed by the Reserve Bank of India under the Chairmanship of Shri F. K. F. Nariman (Nariman Committee) endorsed the idea of an ‘Area Approach’ in its report (November 1969), recommending that in order to enable the PSBs to discharge their social responsibilities, each bank should concentrate on certain districts where it should act as a 'Lead Bank'. (iii) Pursuant to the above recommendations, the LBS was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in December 1969. The Scheme aims at coordinating the activities of banks and other developmental agencies through various fora to achieve the objective of enhancing the flow of bank finance to the priority sector and other sectors and to promote banks' role in the overall development of the rural sector. For coordinating the activities in a district, a particular bank is assigned ‘Lead Bank’ responsibility of the district. The Lead Bank is expected to assume a leadership role for coordinating the efforts of the credit institutions and the Government. (iv) In view of the several changes that had taken place in the financial sector, the LBS was last reviewed by the High Level Committee headed by Smt. Usha Thorat, former Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of India in 2009. (v) The Committee held wide ranging discussions with various stakeholders, viz., State Governments, banks, development institutions, academicians, NGOs, MFIs, etc. and noted that the scheme has been useful in achieving its original objectives of improvement in branch expansion, deposit mobilisation and lending to the priority sector, especially in rural/semi urban areas. There was overwhelming consensus that LBS needs to continue. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, guidelines 4 were issued to State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) Convenor banks and Lead Banks for implementation. (vi) Envi
rows.summary: RBI consolidated all Lead Bank Scheme rules through March 31, 2025, updating compliance requirements for bank coordination forums and credit-planning processes.

The enclosed Master Circular consolidates and updates all the instructions/guidelines on the subject issued till date and replaces the earlier Master Circular issued on the subject. Please do not respond in any manner to such offers. 2 Master Circular Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM) 1. Background The Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD), Government of India launched the National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM) by restructuring Swarnajayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) with effect from 01st April 2013 ( RBI Circular No. RBI/2012-13/559 dated 27 June 2013). NRLM was renamed as DAY-NRLM (Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission) w.e.f. March 29, 2016. The DAY-NRLM is the flagship program of Government of India for promoting poverty reduction through building strong institutions of the poor, particularly women, and enabling these institutions to access a range of financial services and livelihoods. DAY-NRLM adopts a demand driven approach, enabling the States to formulate their own State specific poverty reduction action plans. The key features of DAY-NRLM have been furnished in Annex I. 2. Women SHGs and their Federations 2.1 DAY-NRLM promotes affinity-based women Self Help Groups (SHGs). However, only in case of groups to be formed with persons with disabilities and other special categories like elders and transgenders, DAY-NRLM may have both men and women in the Self-Help Groups. 2.2 Women SHGs under DAY-NRLM consist of 10-20 members. In case of special SHGs i.e., groups in the difficult areas, groups with disabled persons, and groups formed in remote tribal areas, this number may be a minimum of 5 members. 2.3 Federations of Self Help Groups formed at village, gram panchayat, cluster or higher level may be registered under appropriate Acts prevailing in their respective states. Financial Assistance to the SHGs 3. Revolving Fund DAY-NRLM, MoRD, will provide Revolving Fund (RF) support as corpus ranging between ₹20,000 - ₹30,000 per SHG to strengthen their institutional and financial management capacity and build a good credit history within the group. SHGs in existence for a minimum period of 3/6 months and follow the norms of good SHGs known as ‘Panchasutras’, viz., regular meetings, regular savings, regular internal lending, regular recoveries and maintenance of proper books of accounts, and which have not received any RF earlier will be eligible for such support. 3 4. Capital Subsidy No capital subsidy would be sanctioned to any SHG under DAY-NRLM. 5. Community Investment Support Fund (CIF) CIF will be provided by MoRD to the SHGs promoted under DAY-NRLM in all blocks and will be routed through the village level/cluster level federations, to be maintained in perpetuity by the federations. The CIF may be used by the federations to advance loans to the SHGs and/or to undertake common/collective socio-economic activities. 6. Interest Subvention DAY-NRLM has a provision for interest subvention for women SHGs. Salient features of the Scheme are enclosed in Annex II. 7. Role of banks: 7.1 Opening of S avings/Current A ccounts: The role of banks would commence with opening of accounts for all the SHGs including those having members with disability and for the federations of SHGs. (i) The SHGs engaged in promoting of savings habits among their members would be eligible to open savings bank accounts. (ii) For KYC verification pertaining to SHG members, instructions in the Master Direction on KYC ( dated February 25, 2016, as updated from time to time) shall be adhered to. As regards submission of PAN/Form 60 by SHGs, banks shall be guided by Section 33A(b) of the Master Direction on KYC. (iii) Business Correspondents deployed by b anks may also be authorized to open saving bank accounts of the SHGs, subject to adherence to extant BC guidelines and in accordance with the bank’s Board approved policy on Business Correspondents.
