This is a PCAOB public inspection report for Rosenberg Rich Baker Berman, P.A., headquartered in Somerset, New Jersey, covering the firm’s 2024 inspection and issued June 26, 2025. The PCAOB reviewed two issuer audits for fiscal years ending in 2022, using a risk-based selection approach, and also evaluated portions of the firm’s system of quality control; the report stresses that the findings relate only to the specific audit areas reviewed and are not a full evaluation of all audit work. The report notes that the firm had 18 total issuer audit clients in 2024 and 15 in 2021, with 4 total engagement partners on issuer audit work in 2024 and 5 in 2021, and that two audits were reviewed in both years. One key metric shown in the overview is that 50% of the 2024 audits reviewed had Part I.A deficiencies, versus 0% in 2021, although the report explains that a Part I.A deficiency does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate it and may have taken corrective action after identification.

For compliance purposes, the important substantive point is that the PCAOB’s 2024 inspection assessed whether the firm complied with applicable laws, PCAOB rules, and professional standards in public-company audits, and it identified inspection observations in the report sections for unsupported opinions, other PCAOB non-compliance, independence, and quality control. The report does not provide the detailed findings in the excerpt you supplied, but it clearly indicates that the firm had at least one audit deficiency severe enough to be reflected in Part I.A of the report. No new rules, monetary thresholds, or filing deadlines are announced in the excerpt itself; rather, the document is a regulatory oversight report that signals inspection findings and potential remediation expectations for the audit firm. Compliance teams that rely on this auditor should treat the report as a PCAOB oversight action focused on selected 2022 issuer audits and on the firm’s quality control environment, with the practical implication that the firm may need to demonstrate remediation of identified deficiencies and continued compliance in future inspections.

rows.title: Pannell Kerr Forster of Texas, P.C
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report for Pannell Kerr Forster of Texas, P.C. covers the firm’s **2024 inspection**, issued **June 26, 2025**. The PCAOB reviewed the firm’s compliance with applicable laws, rules, and professional standards in public company audits, focusing on **one issuer audit** (the firm’s audit work was reviewed only in part) and also evaluating selected elements of the firm’s **system of quality control**. The report makes clear that PCAOB inspection selections are **risk-based** and are not a representative sample of all the firm’s audits; findings apply only to the portions actually reviewed.

On the firm’s 2024 profile, Pannell Kerr Forster of Texas had **5 total issuer audit clients** where it served as principal auditor and **4 total engagement partners on issuer audit work**. The PCAOB reviewed **2 audits** in total in 2024, including **1 integrated audit of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR)**, and identified **Part I.A deficiencies in 2 audits**, meaning **100% of the audits reviewed had Part I.A deficiencies**. The report also provides a comparison to the prior inspection year (2022), noting the firm then had **6 issuer audit clients**, **4 engagement partners**, and **2 audits reviewed**, with a **100% Part I.A deficiency rate** as well.

The report does **not** state a new rule or forward-looking compliance deadline for the firm; instead, it is an inspection finding that signals where the PCAOB believed the firm’s audit work did not conform to standards in the reviewed areas. It also notes that a Part I.A deficiency **does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate it**, because firms may later perform additional procedures, inform the issuer’s management of needed financial statement or ICFR changes, or take steps to prevent reliance on prior audit reports. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB identified material audit-quality concerns in the specific reviewed engagements and that the firm’s audit population is small, so inspection outcomes can change significantly year to year depending on which engagements and audit areas are selected.

rows.title: Banks Finley White & Company, CPAs
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report covers Banks Finley White & Company, CPAs (headquartered in Birmingham, Alabama) and was issued June 26, 2025 under PCAOB Release No. 104-2025-107. In the 2025 inspection, PCAOB reviewed two issuer audits for fiscal years ended in 2023, using a risk-based selection approach; the firm had 2 total issuer audit clients, 1 engagement partner on issuer audit work, and 2 audits reviewed, with no integrated audits of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting. The report emphasizes that the inspection did not examine every aspect of the audits or represent a statistically representative sample, and that findings apply only to the portions reviewed.

For the reviewed audits, the report shows no Part I.A deficiencies and a 0% deficiency rate for audits reviewed. The document also states that PCAOB evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control, but the excerpt provided does not list any specific quality control criticisms or remedial mandates. Because the firm’s 2025 inspection selected only portions of audits and used a risk-based method, the absence of deficiencies in the public portion does not mean the audits were fully free of issues outside the reviewed areas.

From a compliance perspective, the practical takeaway is that this report is an oversight outcome rather than a rulemaking change: it does not create new filing deadlines or numeric thresholds for issuers, but it is relevant to any entity using Banks Finley White & Company as its auditor because it reflects PCAOB oversight of the firm’s issuer-audit practice. The firm remains subject to PCAOB inspection and the standards and rules applicable to issuer audits, and the report signals that the PCAOB may scrutinize future audits using a similar risk-based, selective review model.

rows.title: Schechter Dokken Kanter Andrews & Selcer Ltd.
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 26, 2025 public inspection report for Schechter Dokken Kanter Andrews & Selcer Ltd. (headquartered in Minneapolis, Minnesota) describes the firm’s 2024 inspection of its public-company audit practice. PCAOB reviewed one issuer audit, for a fiscal year ended 2022, and examined only a portion of that audit as well as elements of the firm’s quality control system; the report emphasizes that its inspection approach is risk-based, not a representative sample of all audits, and that findings apply only to the portions reviewed. The firm had one issuer audit client and one engagement partner on issuer audit work, and one audit was reviewed; that audit was an integrated audit of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR).

The most significant result is that the one audit reviewed contained Part I.A deficiencies, meaning the PCAOB concluded there were issues that led to an unsupported audit opinion in the reviewed portion. As a result, 100% of the audits reviewed had Part I.A deficiencies. The report also notes that a Part I.A deficiency does not automatically mean the firm failed to remediate it afterward; the firm may have already performed additional audit procedures, informed management of needed financial statement or ICFR changes, or taken steps to prevent reliance on the prior audit report.

For compliance purposes, the report is not itself a new rule with a separate future effective date or deadline, but it is a formal PCAOB enforcement/oversight finding that should prompt review of audit execution and quality control processes. The inspection report also states that the PCAOB evaluated only selected areas, that inspection results may not be comparable across years or firms because the scope changes over time, and that omitted portions exist in the public version to comply with Sarbanes-Oxley Act confidentiality provisions.

rows.title: KPMG SA (France)
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report for KPMG SA, headquartered in Paris La Défense, France, covers the firm’s 2024 inspection and was issued June 26, 2025. The PCAOB, working with the French High Authority for Audit, evaluated KPMG SA’s compliance with applicable laws, PCAOB rules, and professional standards for audits of public companies, and also reviewed elements of the firm’s quality control system. The inspection was risk-based and focused only on selected portions of three issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2023, so the findings apply to the specific audit areas reviewed and are not a full assessment of all of the firm’s work.

For 2024, KPMG SA reported 5 issuer audit clients where it was the principal auditor, 26 issuer audits where it was not the principal auditor, and 128 engagement partners on issuer audit work. The PCAOB reviewed 3 total audits: 2 where KPMG SA was the principal auditor and 1 where it was not. Of the audits reviewed, 67% had a Part I.A deficiency, meaning the PCAOB identified at least one audit area with unsupported opinions in the reviewed portion; the report notes that such findings do not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate, because firms may perform additional procedures, require financial statement or ICFR changes, or otherwise take corrective action after deficiencies are identified.

The report does not, in the excerpt provided, state any new rule, mandatory filing deadline, or formal sanction; rather, it is an inspection finding that highlights compliance weaknesses in specific audit work. Compliance staff should note that the PCAOB explicitly warns that inspection results are not comparable across firms or years because the inspection mix, risk focus, and firm circumstances can change. The report’s practical implication is that KPMG SA should review the cited audit deficiencies and the related quality-control observations in Part II, and ensure corrective actions are implemented for future public-company audits and any related independence or professional-standard issues identified in the full report.

rows.title: PricewaterhouseCoopers Incorporated (South Africa)
rows.summary:
This is a PCAOB public inspection report for PricewaterhouseCoopers Incorporated, headquartered in Johannesburg, South Africa, covering the firm’s 2024 inspection and issued June 26, 2025. The PCAOB, working with the South African Independent Regulatory Board for Auditors, reviewed three issuer audits for fiscal years ending in 2023 and evaluated parts of the firm’s quality control system; the inspection was risk-based and was not a full review of all audits or all procedures. The report states that PwC South Africa had 4 issuer audit clients where it was the principal auditor, 8 additional issuer audits where it was not the principal auditor, and 14 total engagement partners involved in issuer audit work; of the 3 audits reviewed, 1 was a principal-auditor engagement and 2 were not.

The excerpt provided does not show any Part I.A “unsupported opinion” deficiencies, and it indicates 0 audits with Part I.A deficiencies, which is 0% of the audits reviewed. The report also notes that inspection findings are limited to the specific portions of the audits selected for review and should not be read as an assessment of the firm’s entire audit practice. Because the content excerpt ends in the middle of a footnote, it does not include the substantive Part I.B, Part I.C, or Part II findings, if any, nor any remediation directives, deadlines, or sanctions. From a compliance perspective, the key point from the visible text is that this is an oversight/inspection outcome rather than a rulemaking change, and the firm should expect that any actual compliance obligations would be stated in the omitted portions of the report or in the firm’s response appendix.

rows.title: Marcum LLP
rows.summary:
This is a public PCAOB inspection report for Marcum LLP, headquartered in New York, New York, covering the firm’s 2024 inspection and issued June 25, 2025. The PCAOB reviewed 26 issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2023 and evaluated selected portions of those audits as well as elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report is not itself a new rulemaking document, but it is a regulatory finding about audit quality and compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional requirements.

The PCAOB found that 21 of the 26 reviewed audits were serious enough to be included in Part I.A, meaning the deficiencies were significant enough that, in the PCAOB’s view, Marcum had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its audit opinion(s) on the issuer’s financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting at the time the opinions were issued. The most common problems in these Part I.A audits involved testing controls over or substantive testing of revenue and related accounts, goodwill and intangible assets, and long-lived assets; the PCAOB specifically noted recurring deficiencies in how the firm performed substantive procedures to address risks of material misstatement, tested estimates, and tested data or reports used in substantive testing.

The report also identifies Part I.B deficiencies, which are other noncompliance issues with PCAOB standards or rules that did not rise to the level of unsupported audit opinions. These included deficiencies related to consideration of fraud, engagement quality review, audit committee communications, risk assessment, management communications, critical audit matters, the audit report itself, and Form AP. In addition, the report lists Part I.C independence issues, including audit committee pre-approval, financial relationships, partner rotation, and tax services provided to persons in financial reporting oversight roles. The report expressly states that inclusion of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that a material weakness in ICFR exists, that the Board concluded the firm lacked objectivity and impartiality, or that the firm has not already addressed the deficiency.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB is signaling elevated risk in Marcum’s audit methodology and independence practices, especially around revenue, estimates, and audit evidence reliability. There are no explicit remediation deadlines, effective dates, monetary penalties, or mandated corrective actions in the excerpt provided, but the inspection findings are significant because they may affect regulatory scrutiny of the firm’s issuer audits, its quality control remediation efforts, and any issuer or audit committee decision-making regarding engagement oversight, independence monitoring, and audit evidence standards.

rows.title: Baker Tilly US, LLP
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report for Baker Tilly US, LLP (headquartered in Chicago, Illinois) is the firm’s 2024 inspection, released June 25, 2025 under PCAOB Release No. 104-2025-106, and it evaluates the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards and rules and other applicable regulatory/professional requirements in connection with issuer audits. The PCAOB reviewed 12 issuer audits, generally for fiscal years ending in 2023, and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control.

The most significant findings are in Part I.A: seven of the 12 audits reviewed were cited for deficiencies serious enough that the PCAOB believed the firm, when it issued its audit reports, had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s) on the financial statements and/or ICFR. The report says these Part I.A deficiencies primarily involved testing controls over and/or substantive testing of revenue and inventory, with the most common problems being testing data or reports used in substantive testing, testing estimates, and performing substantive procedures to address risks of material misstatement. The report cautions that the presence of a Part I.A deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated or that a material weakness in ICFR existed, except in cases where the report specifically identifies an incorrect opinion.

Part I.B identifies other PCAOB standard/rule compliance issues not tied to insufficient audit evidence, and the 2024 issues in this category related to consideration of fraud, the audit report, critical audit matters, and Form AP. Part I.C identifies apparent independence issues, specifically involving non-audit services and the use of a non-independent firm on an engagement. The report also notes that a cited deficiency does not necessarily mean the PCAOB concluded the firm was not objective and impartial throughout the audit and professional engagement period, and it does not necessarily mean the firm has not already corrected the deficiency.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that Baker Tilly’s 2024 inspected engagements showed repeated weaknesses in core audit execution areas—especially revenue, inventory, data/report testing, estimate testing, and substantive procedures addressing material misstatement risks—plus separate issues in fraud procedures, audit reporting, CAMs, Form AP, and independence controls. The document is a public inspection summary only; it omits portions of the complete report under Sarbanes-Oxley confidentiality provisions, and it does not itself impose a new rule or deadline, but it is a formal regulator finding that the firm’s audit quality controls and engagement performance were deficient in the areas described.

rows.title: Moss Adams LLP
rows.summary:
This PCAOB inspection report, issued June 25, 2025, summarizes the Board’s 2024 inspection of Moss Adams LLP, headquartered in Seattle, Washington, and evaluates the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards and rules and other applicable regulatory and professional requirements in its issuer audit practice. The PCAOB reviewed 12 issuer audits, generally for fiscal years ending in 2023, and also assessed elements of the firm’s system of quality control. Of the 12 audits reviewed, 6 were included in Part I.A because the deficiencies were significant enough that, in the PCAOB’s view, the firm had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its audit opinions on the financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting when the audit reports were issued.

The report says the Part I.A deficiencies were driven primarily by the firm’s testing of controls over and/or substantive testing of revenue and inventory. The most common serious deficiencies in 2024 involved inadequate substantive testing to address a risk of material misstatement and failures in testing estimates. This means compliance and audit leadership should focus on whether the firm’s audit methodology, execution, and review procedures sufficiently address high-risk revenue, inventory, and estimate areas before opinions are issued.

The report also identifies Part I.B deficiencies, which were noncompliance with PCAOB standards or rules that were not framed as unsupported-opinion issues. In 2024 these related to fraud consideration, Form AP, and audit committee communications. The Part I.C independence findings involved audit committee pre-approval, use of a non-independent firm on an engagement, and financial relationships, which means the firm must ensure engagement acceptance and continuation controls, affiliate/vendor independence vetting, and personal/firm financial relationship checks are functioning before and during issuer audit engagements.

The report is explicit that inclusion of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that a material weakness in ICFR exists, or that the firm was ultimately not objective and impartial; it also does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate the issue. Appendix A contains Moss Adams LLP’s response to the draft inspection report.

rows.title: Forvis Mazars, LLP
rows.summary:
This is a PCAOB public inspection report dated June 25, 2025 covering Forvis Mazars, LLP’s 2024 inspection, based on 14 issuer audits with fiscal years generally ending in 2023. The PCAOB’s review was limited to portions of selected audits and also included an evaluation of elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report is an inspection finding, not a new rule, but it identifies areas where the PCAOB believes the firm did not fully comply with applicable auditing, independence, and professional requirements.

The most significant findings are in Part I.A: 10 of the 14 audits reviewed were placed in this category because the deficiencies were serious enough that the PCAOB believed the firm, at the time it issued its audit reports, had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s) on the issuer’s financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The report says these deficiencies primarily involved testing controls and/or substantive testing of allowance for credit losses, business combinations, revenue, and related accounts. The most common issues were failures in testing the design or operating effectiveness of selected controls, inadequate testing of estimates, insufficient testing of data or reports used in substantive procedures, and failure to identify controls related to significant accounts or relevant assertions.

Part I.B identifies other PCAOB standard/rule compliance problems that were not framed as unsupported-opinion issues. These related to audit committee communications, the firm’s audit report, and consideration of fraud. Part I.C identifies one independence-related issue, specifically involving audit committee pre-approval. The report emphasizes that inclusion of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that undisclosed material weaknesses in ICFR exist, or that the PCAOB concluded the firm was not objective and impartial throughout the engagement period.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB expects stronger audit evidence around high-risk areas such as allowance for credit losses, business combinations, and revenue, and better execution of control testing, estimate testing, and reliance on system-generated data/reports. The report does not state a remediation deadline or impose a direct penalty in the text provided, but it serves as a formal regulatory signal that the firm’s audit methodology, documentation, and independence governance were deficient in multiple engagements during the 2024 inspection cycle.

rows.title: ARK PRO CPA & CO (Hong Kong)
rows.summary:
PCAOB’s 2024 inspection of ARK PRO CPA & Co. (formerly HKCMCPA Company Limited), headquartered in Hong Kong SAR, was issued on June 12, 2025 as a public inspection report. The PCAOB reviewed three issuer audits, generally for fiscal years ending in 2022, using a risk-based selection process focused on higher-risk, more complex, or recurring-deficiency audit areas; the report expressly notes that the selected audits are not a representative sample of the firm’s full issuer-audit population and that findings apply only to the reviewed portions of the audits. In the firm data summarized in the report, ARK PRO had 6 total issuer audit clients as principal auditor, 0 issuer audits as non-principal auditor, and 1 engagement partner on issuer audit work; of the three audits reviewed, all three were principal-auditor audits, none were integrated audits of financial statements and ICFR, and 67% of the reviewed audits had Part I.A deficiencies.

The report does not announce a new rule or threshold applicable to all firms; rather, it records inspection findings about this firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and applicable laws in public company audits. A compliance team should note that the PCAOB’s observations include “audits with unsupported opinions,” “other instances of non-compliance with PCAOB standards or rules,” independence issues, and quality-control observations, which means the report is not limited to one isolated technical issue but potentially spans audit execution, independence, and firm-wide control processes. The report also states that deficiencies identified in Part I.A do not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate them, because firms may have already taken corrective action after the deficiency was identified.

The inspection was conducted in cooperation with the China Securities Regulatory Commission, the Ministry of Finance of the People’s Republic of China, and the Accounting and Financial Reporting Council of Hong Kong. The report is a public version and omits portions to comply with Sections 104(g)(2) and 105(b)(5)(A) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB’s 2024 review found deficiencies in a majority of the small set of audits reviewed, and the firm should treat the report as evidence that its audit methodology, documentation support, independence controls, and quality-control system were all areas of regulatory scrutiny.

rows.title: WithumSmith+Brown, PC
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report on WithumSmith+Brown, PC, issued May 22, 2025 (Release No. 104-2025-102), summarizes the PCAOB’s 2024 inspection of the Princeton, New Jersey-headquartered audit firm and its compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional requirements. The PCAOB reviewed portions of 15 issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2023 and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report is important for compliance purposes because it identifies inspection observations in three categories: Part I.A for audit deficiencies so significant that the PCAOB believed, at the time the reports were issued, the firm had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinions on the financial statements and/or ICFR; Part I.B for other standards/rules violations not rising to that level; and Part I.C for apparent independence-rule issues. The report expressly notes that a deficiency finding does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated, a material weakness existed, the firm lacked objectivity and impartiality, or that the firm has not already remediated the issue.

Substantively, nine of the 15 audits reviewed were included in Part I.A because of the severity of the deficiencies. The PCAOB says those deficiencies primarily involved the firm’s substantive testing of revenue, business combinations, warrants, and equity. The most common Part I.A problems were failures in substantive testing to address identified risks of material misstatement, insufficient testing of estimates, and inadequate testing of data or reports used in substantive procedures. In two audits, the inspection work was tied to the issuer restating its financial statements to correct misstatements, and the firm revised and reissued its audit report on those financial statements.

The Part I.B deficiencies concerned audit-process and standards issues, specifically retention of audit documentation, engagement quality review, audit committee communications, auditor tenure, and critical audit matters. The Part I.C independence issues related to audit committee pre-approval and financial relationships. The report also signals that the PCAOB assessed the firm’s quality control system, so these findings are not limited to individual engagements and may indicate broader control weaknesses that compliance leadership should evaluate for remediation, training, supervision, documentation retention, independence monitoring, and audit committee communication controls.

rows.title: Cohen & Company, Ltd.
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report, issued May 22, 2025, covers Cohen & Company, Ltd.’s 2024 inspection and evaluates the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional and regulatory requirements for issuer audits. The PCAOB reviewed nine issuer audits, generally with fiscal years ending in 2023, and also assessed elements of the firm’s system of quality control. One of the nine audits was placed in Part I.A because the identified deficiency was serious enough that the PCAOB believed that, at the time the audit report was issued, the firm had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion; the underlying issue involved substantive testing of expenses in response to a risk of material misstatement.

The report also identifies Part I.B deficiencies, which are noncompliance with PCAOB standards or rules that did not rise to the level of unsupported audit opinions. For 2024, those Part I.B items related specifically to audit committee communications and critical audit matters. The PCAOB states that it did not identify any Part I.C deficiencies, and the firm did not bring any independence-related deficiencies to the PCAOB’s attention, so no apparent violations of independence requirements were reported in this inspection.

From a compliance perspective, the report does not set a new deadline or rule change for issuers, but it does flag the areas where the firm’s audit execution fell short and where compliance teams should expect heightened scrutiny: substantive testing over expense accounts when material misstatement risk is present, timely and complete audit committee communications, and proper treatment/disclosure of critical audit matters. The report also notes that the presence of a deficiency does not necessarily mean the financial statements were materially misstated, that internal control over financial reporting contained an undisclosed material weakness, or that the firm failed to remediate the issue, but the Part I.A finding is significant because it indicates the PCAOB believed audit evidence was insufficient at the time of issuance.

rows.title: RSM US LLP
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report, issued May 22, 2025, covers RSM US LLP’s 2024 inspection and evaluates the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional and regulatory requirements in audits of issuers. PCAOB inspectors reviewed 17 issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2023 and evaluated portions of those audits as well as elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report is not a finding that the financial statements were necessarily materially misstated or that internal control over financial reporting necessarily contained undisclosed material weaknesses; rather, it identifies areas where the PCAOB believes audit evidence or compliance was insufficient in the reviewed work.

The most significant findings were placed in Part I.A: seven of the 17 audits reviewed were included there because the deficiencies were significant enough that, in the PCAOB’s view, RSM had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its audit opinions on the issuer’s financial statements and/or ICFR when those reports were issued. The report says those Part I.A deficiencies primarily involved testing controls and/or substantive testing of revenue and related accounts, inventory, and long-lived assets. The most common specific problems in 2024 were failure in testing an estimate and failure in testing data or reports used in substantive audit procedures. Because these are Part I.A matters, they are the most serious observations in the report and indicate unsupported opinions for the affected audits.

Part I.B addresses other PCAOB standards or rule violations that did not rise to the level of unsupported audit opinions. For 2024, those deficiencies involved audit committee communications, fraud consideration, communications with management, management’s annual report on ICFR, and critical audit matters. The report separately notes one Part I.C deficiency relating to independence, specifically involving non-audit services, meaning the firm had an apparent non-compliance issue with PCAOB independence rules during the audit and professional engagement period. The report also emphasizes that a Part I.C deficiency does not automatically mean the Board concluded the firm lacked objectivity and impartiality throughout the engagement, but it does signal a compliance concern that should be addressed.

From a compliance perspective, the report is a warning that the firm’s audit methodology and execution need attention in recurring risk areas: revenue, inventory, long-lived assets, estimation testing, and the reliability of data/reports used in substantive procedures. It also indicates the firm should ensure strict adherence to required communications with audit committees and management, proper fraud procedures, complete and timely ICFR reporting, careful handling of critical audit matters, and robust independence controls over non-audit services. The report includes a quality control section, reflecting that the PCAOB also assessed firm-level controls, so compliance teams should expect the inspection findings to inform remediation efforts not only at the engagement level but also in firmwide quality-control and independence processes.

rows.title: Crowe LLP
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s May 22, 2025 2024 inspection report on Crowe LLP (Chicago) describes the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional requirements in audits of issuers, based on review of 17 issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2023. The report’s most serious findings are in Part I.A: three of the 17 audits reviewed contained deficiencies significant enough that the PCAOB believed Crowe had **not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence** to support its audit opinions on the issuer financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting at the time the opinions were issued. The principal problem areas were Crowe’s **testing of controls over, and substantive testing of, the allowance for credit losses**.  

The report says the most common Part I.A issues involved failures in testing the **design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing**, failures to test controls over the **accuracy and completeness of data or reports** used in operating controls, and deficiencies in testing an **estimate**. For compliance purposes, this signals heightened risk around audit evidence and control testing for credit loss estimation processes, especially where the firm relies on system-generated reports or data inputs. The report also cautions that a Part I.A deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated or that an undisclosed material weakness existed, but it does mean the PCAOB concluded the audit evidence was insufficient for the issued opinion.  

Part I.B identifies other PCAOB standards/rule violations that did not rise to the level of unsupported opinions. In 2024, those deficiencies related to **consideration of fraud, retention of audit documentation, audit committee communications, and risk assessment**. These are important compliance points because they indicate weaknesses in audit planning, documentation discipline, governance communications, and fraud/risk procedures, even where the PCAOB did not conclude the opinion was unsupported.  

Part I.C identifies apparent independence violations tied to **audit committee pre-approval**. For a compliance team, that means the report also raises issues around ensuring required audit committee authorization procedures were followed before audit services were performed. The report notes that inclusion of a deficiency in Part I.C does not necessarily mean the PCAOB concluded the firm was not objective and impartial, but it does indicate a potential failure to comply with independence-related pre-approval requirements.  

No specific remediation deadline or monetary penalty is stated in the excerpt provided; the report is an inspection finding document rather than an enforcement order. However, the inspection date is **May 22, 2025**, and the audited periods reviewed were **fiscal years ending in 2023**, so the compliance significance is immediate for any Crowe audit clients and for firms with similar control-testing and audit committee approval processes.

rows.title: SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co. (Philippines)
rows.summary:
This PCAOB inspection report for SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co. covers the firm’s 2024 inspection results, issued publicly on May 22, 2025, and is based on three issuer audits for fiscal years ending in 2023. The PCAOB states that it reviewed only portions of those audits, using a risk-based selection approach focused on higher-risk or more complex audit areas, so the findings are limited to the specific areas reviewed and are not a conclusion about all of the firm’s issuer audit work. The report also notes that the inspection evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control.

For 2024, the firm had 1 issuer audit client where it served as principal auditor and 18 additional issuer audits where it was not the principal auditor; the report also lists 12 total engagement partners on issuer audit work. The PCAOB reviewed 3 audits total in 2024, including 1 where the firm was principal auditor and 2 where it was not, and all 3 were integrated audits of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). One of the three audits had Part I.A deficiencies, meaning 33% of the reviewed audits were found to have unsupported opinions in the reviewed areas.

The report’s structure indicates additional findings sections on unsupported opinions, other non-compliance with PCAOB standards or rules, independence, and quality control observations, but the excerpt provided does not include the underlying deficiency narrative or any specific remediation deadlines or mandated corrective actions. From a compliance perspective, the key takeaway is that the firm had a material inspection issue in one-third of the inspected engagements, and the PCAOB’s comments are tied to the particular audit portions reviewed rather than the full population of the firm’s audits. If your team is assessing vendor or auditor risk, the relevant impact is that the firm is under PCAOB scrutiny for at least one audited engagement from the 2023 fiscal-year cycle reviewed in the 2024 inspection.

rows.title: KPMG Samjong Accounting Corp. (South Korea)

Even so, for a compliance team, the practical implication is that the firm’s audit methodology and execution were found insufficient in every reviewed issuer engagement, which raises a high-risk indicator for audit quality and potential opinion reliability.

The inspection report also notes that the PCAOB reviewed only portions of each audit and did not inspect every area, so the findings are not a complete assessment of all work performed on those audits or of the firm’s full audit portfolio. Because the PCAOB uses a risk-based selection process, the inspected areas were those deemed more complex, more significant, or more likely to involve material misstatement risk, and the report cautions that results are not necessarily comparable across firms or over time. The report’s table shows the firm had two total issuer audit clients, one total engagement partner on issuer audit work, and zero issuer audits where it was not the principal auditor.

No specific monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or prescriptive remediation deadlines are stated in the excerpt provided. The document is primarily an inspection finding report rather than a rulemaking or enforcement order, so its operational effect for compliance is to signal that the firm had significant audit-quality deficiencies in the inspected engagements and that any organization relying on Bansal & Co LLP’s public company audit work should review the implications for audit reliability, oversight, and vendor/engagement risk management.

rows.title: GreenGrowth CPAs

Because this is a public PCAOB inspection report, firms subject to PCAOB oversight should treat it as a signal that similar control or engagement-level weaknesses, if present in their own practice, can lead to inspection findings and should be addressed through enhanced audit documentation, partner supervision, independence controls, and remediation tracking.

rows.title: MaloneBailey, LLP

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB identified a high rate of audit-quality deficiencies in a sampled set of issuer audits, which may indicate heightened regulatory scrutiny of the firm and possible implications for issuers relying on MaloneBailey for public-company audit services.

rows.title: Salberg & Company, P.A
rows.summary:

PCAOB reviewed two issuer audits performed by the firm—one for a fiscal year ended in 2023 and one for a fiscal year ended in 2022—and also evaluated selected elements of the firm’s system of quality control. No specific new rule, fee, threshold, or future compliance deadline is imposed by this report itself; instead, it is an oversight finding that should be used to assess the firm’s audit quality controls and remediation efforts. The document is relevant to any internal compliance, audit quality, or vendor oversight review involving Salberg & Company, P.A., especially if the firm is used for public company audits or other engagements subject to PCAOB standards.

rows.title: Grant Thornton LLP
rows.summary:
This PCAOB inspection report, issued February 26, 2025, covers Grant Thornton LLP’s 2024 inspection and assesses the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards and rules, as well as other applicable regulatory and professional requirements, in audits of issuers. The PCAOB reviewed portions of 27 issuer audits, generally for fiscal years ending in 2023, and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control.

The report states that 13 of the 27 audits reviewed were included in Part I.A because the deficiencies were significant enough that, in the PCAOB’s view, Grant Thornton had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence at the time it issued its audit opinions, including on financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The most common Part I.A problems involved the firm’s testing of controls over the accuracy and completeness of data or reports used in controls, testing the design or operating effectiveness of selected controls, and performing substantive audit procedures to respond to risks of material misstatement. The report specifically says these deficiencies primarily related to revenue and related accounts and inventory.

Part I.B identifies other PCAOB standards/rules noncompliance that did not rise to the level of unsupported audit opinions; in 2024 these involved audit committee communications, risk assessment, evaluation of management’s ICFR report, management communications, and the firm’s audit report. Part I.C addresses apparent independence violations and, for 2024, those related to audit committee pre-approval and non-audit services. The report cautions that inclusion of a deficiency in Part I.A, I.B, or I.C does not automatically mean the financial statements were materially misstated, that undisclosed material weaknesses in ICFR existed, that the Board concluded the firm was not objective and impartial, or that the firm has not already addressed the issue.

rows.title: PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP
rows.summary:
This is a public PCAOB inspection report issued on February 26, 2025 for PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (PwC), headquartered in New York, covering the firm’s 2024 inspection and focused on audits of issuers with fiscal years generally ending in 2023. The report does not create new rules for issuers, but it identifies the kinds of audit failures and compliance weaknesses the PCAOB observed, which is relevant for any company audited by PwC or by similarly regulated firms because it signals where audit quality and independence controls may be scrutinized.

The PCAOB reviewed 64 issuer audits and placed 10 of them in Part I.A because the deficiencies were significant enough that, at the time PwC issued its audit report(s), the PCAOB believed the firm had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s) on the financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The report says these Part I.A deficiencies were driven mainly by insufficient testing of controls over and/or substantive testing of revenue and related accounts and of the allowance for credit losses; the most common issues were failure to perform substantive testing responsive to a material misstatement risk, inadequate testing of an estimate, and inadequate testing of the design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing. In one of the reviewed audits, the issuer disclosed during the inspection process that its financial statements would be restated to correct misstatements.

The report also identifies Part I.B deficiencies, which are noncompliance with PCAOB standards or rules not rising to the level of unsupported audit opinions. Those issues involved retention of audit documentation, audit committee communications, audit planning, risk assessment, communications to management, critical audit matters, and Form AP filings. For compliance teams, the practical implication is that audit firms are expected to maintain complete workpapers, make required communications to audit committees and management, properly plan and assess risk, appropriately report critical audit matters, and file Form AP accurately and on time.

Finally, Part I.C notes apparent independence-related noncompliance, including employment relationships, audit committee pre-approval, and financial relationships. The report emphasizes that a deficiency finding does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that a material weakness in ICFR necessarily exists, or that PwC was ultimately not objective and impartial throughout the engagement period; it also does not necessarily mean the firm has not already addressed the issue. The report is therefore best read as a warning signal on audit quality and independence controls, especially for entities relying on PwC audits or monitoring their external auditor’s regulatory history.

rows.title: Ernst & Young LLP
rows.summary:
This is the PCAOB’s public 2024 inspection report for Ernst & Young LLP (EY), issued February 26, 2025, and it summarizes deficiencies the PCAOB identified in EY’s audit work and compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and related professional requirements. The report is organized into three main categories: Part I.A covers the most serious deficiencies—those significant enough that PCAOB concluded the firm had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support one or more audit opinions on issuer financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR); Part I.B covers other PCAOB noncompliance that did not rise to that level; and Part I.C covers apparent independence violations. The report expressly states that inclusion of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated, that an undisclosed material weakness existed in ICFR, that EY failed to remain objective and impartial, or that EY has not already addressed the issue.

For 2024, the PCAOB reviewed 64 EY audits, and 18 were included in Part I.A because of the severity of the deficiencies. The most significant recurring problem areas were testing controls and substantive testing over revenue and related accounts, inventory, and long-lived assets. The report says the most common Part I.A issues involved EY’s testing of the design or operating effectiveness of selected controls, testing the accuracy and completeness of data or reports used to operate controls, and in some cases overreliance on controls when performing substantive procedures. In one of the reviewed audits, the issuer restated its financial statements to correct a misstatement and EY revised and reissued its audit report; in that same matter, and in another audit, the issuer revised its ICFR report and EY revised and reissued its ICFR opinion to include one or more additional material weaknesses.

Part I.B deficiencies related to audit committee communications, audit planning, management communications, fraud considerations, the audit report itself, critical audit matters, Form 2, and Form AP. Part I.C deficiencies were concentrated in independence matters, specifically financial relationships, business relationships, and non-audit services. The report does not set out a new compliance deadline or rule change; rather, it flags EY’s inspection findings and areas where the firm’s audits and related filings did not comply with applicable PCAOB requirements during the 2024 inspection period. The practical compliance takeaway is that EY and similarly situated audit teams should treat controls testing over data reliability, revenue, inventory, and long-lived assets, along with independence and required filing/communication obligations, as high-risk areas requiring tighter documentation, evidence, and review.

rows.title: Deloitte & Touche LLP
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report, issued February 26, 2025 for Deloitte & Touche LLP’s 2024 inspection, summarizes the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards/rules and other applicable professional requirements for issuer audits, and it is based on review of 63 issuer audits, generally with fiscal years ending in 2023, plus selected quality-control elements. The report is not itself a rulemaking document or enforcement finding, but it identifies audit and independence deficiencies that compliance teams should treat as indicators of regulatory risk and possible remediation issues. It also notes that the public version omits portions of the complete report under Sarbanes-Oxley Act sections 104(g)(2) and 105(b)(5)(A).

The most consequential findings are in Part I.A: nine of the 63 audits reviewed were included because the deficiencies were significant enough that PCAOB believed Deloitte, at the time it issued the audit reports, had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s) on the issuer’s financial statements and/or ICFR. The deficiencies most often involved testing of controls over and/or substantive testing of revenue, allowance for credit losses, and leases. PCAOB specifically highlighted recurring problems in performing substantive testing to address a risk of material misstatement, testing the design or operating effectiveness of selected controls, and testing controls over the accuracy and completeness of data or reports used in operating controls.

Part I.B identifies other noncompliance with PCAOB standards or rules that did not rise to the level of unsupported opinions. The report says these deficiencies related to retention of audit documentation, audit committee communications, consideration of fraud, auditor tenure, and critical audit matters. For a compliance team, this means the report points to process failures in core audit documentation and governance communications, not just isolated technical issues.

Part I.C addresses apparent independence issues. The most common independence-related deficiencies in 2024 involved financial relationships, employment relationships, and audit committee pre-approval. The report cautions that inclusion of a Part I.C deficiency does not automatically mean the Board concluded the firm was not objective and impartial throughout the audit and professional engagement period, but it does signal possible violations of independence rules that may require internal review, monitoring, and remediation.

Finally, the report states that the PCAOB also evaluated elements of Deloitte’s system of quality control as part of the inspection, with Part II devoted to those observations, and Appendix A contains the firm’s response to the draft inspection report. No specific remediation deadlines, monetary penalties, or new firm-wide compliance dates are set in the excerpt provided; the operative compliance takeaway is that Deloitte was found to have multiple significant audit, documentation, communications, and independence issues in the 2024 inspection cycle, and these areas should be targeted for corrective action and enhanced controls.

rows.title: BDO USA, P.C.
rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report for BDO USA, P.C. (headquartered in Chicago, Illinois) was issued on February 26, 2025 and covers the firm’s 2024 inspection. It is an oversight report assessing BDO’s compliance with PCAOB standards and rules, as well as other applicable regulatory and professional requirements, for issuer audits; the report is specifically organized to distinguish between deficiencies serious enough to indicate insufficient audit evidence for the reported opinion (Part I.A), other PCAOB non-compliance not rising to that level (Part I.B), and apparent independence violations (Part I.C). The report cautions that the presence of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that an undisclosed material weakness in ICFR exists, or that the firm ultimately failed to remain objective and impartial.

The most material findings are that 18 of the 30 audits reviewed in 2024 were included in Part I.A because the identified deficiencies were significant enough that PCAOB inspectors believed BDO, at the time it issued its audit reports, had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinions on financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting. The deficiencies concentrated in audits involving testing of controls and/or substantive testing over revenue and related accounts, goodwill and intangible assets, and business combinations. The most common Part I.A issues were failures in testing an estimate, testing data or reports used in substantive procedures, identifying controls tied to a significant account or relevant assertion, testing the design or operating effectiveness of selected controls, and testing controls over the accuracy and completeness of data or reports used in control operation.

The report also notes a significant ICFR development during the inspection: for one audit, the issuer revised its ICFR report and BDO revised its ICFR opinion to an adverse opinion and reissued its report. Beyond the unsupported-opinion matters, Part I.B deficiencies involved fraud considerations, audit committee communications, audit planning, risk assessment, the audit report itself, and Form AP filings. Part I.C deficiencies involved audit committee pre-approval requirements and partner rotation, which are independence-related compliance obligations.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that PCAOB scrutiny focused heavily on audit evidence quality, especially around estimates and data/report reliability, as well as on control testing over key financial statement areas and ICFR. The report does not announce a new rule or firmwide deadline, but it documents inspection findings that may indicate areas where BDO’s methodologies, audit documentation, independence tracking, and audit committee communication procedures needed remediation or enhancement following the 2024 inspection.

rows.title: KPMG LLP
rows.summary:
This PCAOB inspection report for KPMG LLP, issued February 26, 2025, summarizes the PCAOB’s 2024 review of the firm’s issuer-audit practice and its compliance with applicable PCAOB standards, rules, and broader professional and regulatory requirements. The inspection covered 64 issuer audits, generally for fiscal years ending in 2023, and the PCAOB reviewed only portions of each audit rather than performing a full-file re-audit.

The most serious findings are in Part I.A: 13 of the 64 audits were cited because the PCAOB believed the deficiencies were significant enough that, at the time KPMG issued its audit opinions, the firm had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s) on the financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The report says these deficiencies were concentrated primarily in the firm’s work on revenue and related accounts, and on the allowance for credit losses. The most common problems were failures in testing the design or operating effectiveness of controls chosen for testing, failures to test the accuracy and completeness of data or reports used in controls, failures to identify the controls tied to a significant account or relevant assertion, and failures to perform substantive testing sufficient to address identified risks of material misstatement.

Part I.B covers other PCAOB standard/rule violations that did not rise to the level of unsupported opinions; these related to audit documentation retention, audit committee communications, audit planning, risk assessment, the audit report itself, and critical audit matters. Part I.C covers apparent independence-related rule violations, and the most common issues in 2024 involved audit committee pre-approval, financial relationships, non-audit services, and indemnification clauses. The report also notes that these findings do not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated, that a material weakness existed, or that KPMG was conclusively not objective and impartial; similarly, inclusion of a deficiency does not necessarily mean the firm has not already addressed it.

For compliance purposes, the document is primarily a supervisory/regulatory signal rather than a new rule with a separate effective date or deadline: it does not impose a new compliance deadline, but it is a public PCAOB finding that should prompt the firm and related stakeholders to review audit methodology, controls testing, revenue and ACL audit procedures, documentation retention, audit committee communication practices, independence pre-clearance, and non-audit service/indemnification safeguards.

rows.title: Freed Maxick P.C.
rows.summary:

For the 2024 inspection, the PCAOB reviewed two issuer audits—one for a fiscal year ended in 2023 and one for a fiscal year ended in 2022—and evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control; the report emphasizes that only portions of those audits were reviewed, so the findings are limited to the selected audit areas and are not a blanket assessment of all of the firm’s audit work. The PCAOB explains that its audit selection is risk-based, focusing on areas it believes pose heightened risk of material misstatement, including challenging or significant audit areas and areas with recurring deficiencies, and that the selected audits are not necessarily representative of the firm’s entire issuer audit population.

The report’s summary data show that Freed Maxick was the principal auditor for 17 issuer audit clients in 2024, down from 21 in 2021, and that it had 1 engagement partner on issuer audit work in 2024 compared with 6 in 2021 and 5 in 2020. The PCAOB reviewed 2 audits in 2024, both principal-auditor engagements, and identified Part I.A deficiencies in 1 of the 2 audits, meaning 50% of the audited engagements reviewed had at least one unsupported-opinion finding; the historical table shows the same 50% rate in 2021 as well. The report notes that a Part I.A deficiency does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remedy the issue, because firms may take post-identified remedial actions such as performing additional audit procedures, advising the issuer to change the financial statements or ICFR reporting, or taking steps to avoid reliance on the prior audit report.

From the firm data included in the report, PricewaterhouseCoopers Japan LLC had 2 issuer audit clients where it was the principal auditor and 52 issuer audits where it was not the principal auditor, with 36 engagement partners on issuer audit work. Of the 3 audits reviewed, 1 was a principal-auditor engagement and 2 were not; all 3 were integrated audits of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The report states that 33% of the audits reviewed had Part I.A deficiencies, meaning one of the three reviewed audits contained the type of deficiency described in that section.

The report also makes clear that the presence of a deficiency in Part I.A does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate it, because firms often perform corrective actions after issues are identified, including additional audit work depending on the circumstances. The inspection is not described as imposing a new rule change or deadline on the firm in the text provided; rather, it documents PCAOB inspection findings and quality-control observations for the 2023 inspection cycle. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB identified deficiencies in one-third of the reviewed engagements and that the report is an official public inspection outcome relevant to the firm’s audit quality, inspection response, and remediation processes.
